A seller who produces photocopies every time and originals never. Land on a prohibited-property list — the Sub-Registrar will refuse it until the restriction resolves. And resistance to a NEWSPAPER NOTICE: publishing one inviting objections before closing is ordinary practice — a seller who argues against it is telling you something. Bottom line Chain, EC, courts, record, zoning, survey — six checks, each catching what the others miss, none substituting for the rest. 2026-09-07|ls-ceiling: Agricultural land ceiling limits by state: how much you can own Land School — an original Deccan Ledger lesson · source & further reading: Agricultural Land Ceiling Limits by State: How Much You Can Own — 1acre.in Key Highlights Ceiling laws cap the agricultural land any person or family may hold — and they are still enforced today. No national number exists: land is a state subject, and limits run from ~7.5 acres to over 50 by state. Many states measure in STANDARD acres — irrigated land counts for more ceiling than dry land. The FAMILY often matters more than the individual: several acts aggregate the household’s holdings. Exceed the cap — even unintentionally — and the state can take the excess as surplus. What ceiling laws actually do Born of the post-independence land-reform agenda, ceiling acts cap agricultural holdings and redistribute the surplus to the landless — an answer to a world where a large landlord held roughly 45 times a marginal farmer’s land. Every state had passed one by the early 1960s, tightened again around 1971. They never expired: exceeding the ceiling remains a live legal problem, not a historical footnote. Why there is no single national limit Land is a state subject, so each state wrote its own act with its own numbers. Kerala’s figure tells you nothing about Telangana’s. The only safe move before a large purchase is a state-specific check of the CURRENT limit — amendments happen, and working from an outdated figure is working from the wrong law. The standard acre — the concept that trips buyers A stated ceiling does not always mean physical acres. A standard acre weights land by productivity and irrigation: under Madhya Pradesh’s act, for instance, one double-cropped irrigated acre equals 1.5 single-crop irrigated acres, or three dry acres. So a “30 standard acre” ceiling could allow far more physical dry land — or far less irrigated land — than the headline number suggests. Definition — Standard acre: a productivity-weighted unit for measuring ceiling compliance. Always ask of any ceiling figure: standard or physical? And of any parcel: what irrigation class does the record show? How family-unit calculation changes your real limit In several states the ceiling applies to the HOUSEHOLD as a unit — everyone’s holdings aggregate against one shared cap, with shares proportioned across members. A common exception: major (adult) sons in some states count as independent holders, subject to filing declarations. The classic ambush: a joint family where each member holds comfortably under the limit individually — but the family total quietly crossed it, discovered during inheritance or partition. Example: A family holding 20 irrigated acres buys 15 more “dry” acres — but 6 turn out irrigation-classified in the record. Converted to standard acres, the household crosses the cap, and the excess is exposed to surplus proceedings. The fix — splitting across eligible holders/entities — costs nothing at agreement stage and is miserable after registration. Red flags Combined family holdings crossing the cap even though no individual does; land in OTHER states not factored (some acts count out-of-state land in the calculation even though only in-state land can be declared surplus); relying on a pre-amendment ceiling figure; and misclassified irrigation status flipping the standard-acre conversion entirely. Individual-basis vs family-basis states Aspect Individual basis Family basis What is capped What one person holds What the whole household holds combined Source The same state ceiling act — differing in how it defines the holding unit Same Practical effect Each person’s limit stands alone All members aggregate against one shared limit Diligence needed Your own holdings The household’s TOTAL in-state holdings, before your share Who actually needs to worry For most buyers of 1–10 acres, this is genuinely a non-issue. It bites in two places: buyers already holding substantial land approaching the cap, and joint families whose aggregate has never been totalled. If either describes the deal, run the numbers before the agreement. What happens if you exceed the ceiling A notice arrives requiring declaration of total holdings and a choice of which land to retain within the cap. The excess vests in the state, compensation is paid — typically below market — and the land is redistributed to landless labourers. An active mechanism, not a museum piece. Pre-purchase checklist ☐ The CURRENT ceiling for the exact state — never borrowed from elsewhere. ☐ The family’s total existing holdings, not just yours. ☐ The parcel’s irrigation classification confirmed (it drives the conversion). ☐ A revenue lawyer’s calculation when buying as a joint family or near the limit. ☐ Figures verified with the local revenue department. Quick answers (FAQ) Is the ceiling per person or per family? Depends on the state’s act — several aggregate the household. Do these laws still apply? Fully. Does irrigated land have a lower effective ceiling? Yes — through the standard-acre conversion. What if I inherit my way over the cap? The surplus machinery applies to inherited excess too — total the family holdings at every succession. Bottom line No single number answers “how much can I own” — the state, the household structure, and the irrigation class together decide. Run the family-level calculation BEFORE a large purchase, and the ceiling stays a footnote instead of a surplus notice. For you: When someone offers 80 clean acres under one name in a low-ceiling state, the right reaction is not excitement — it is “show me how this holding is legal.” And any parcel whose chain touches ceiling-surplus declarations gets treated like assigned land: radioactive until a lawyer clears it. The working standard is 30 years back; 12–13 years is the accepted floor where older records are gone. Land pulls in checks a flat never needs: zoning, NA conversion, and a physical boundary survey. Mutation records and the EC are supporting evidence — neither is proof of title on its own. Land disputes are a huge share of India’s pending civil cases — the whole case for spending a sliver of the deal on verification. What a title search is It answers one question with evidence: is the seller legally entitled to sell? A deed in his name is not enough — his claim depends on everyone BEFORE him having transferred correctly. Four terms, kept straight: title — the underlying right of ownership; registration — the record of a transaction (evidence something happened, not proof the title behind it was clean); mutation — the revenue-record update that follows registration; patta/khata — who is liable for tax, supporting evidence only. The search pulls the threads together: every transfer traced, each one’s registration confirmed, every break flagged. What the search covers Chain of ownership — every recorded transfer, 30 years back where records permit, starting from the mother deed. Inheritance links — succession papers, and confirmation ALL legal heirs signed. Encumbrances — pulled independently, never from the seller’s copy. Litigation — any live case or stay. Revenue consistency — name, survey number and extent agreeing across deed, mutation and portal. Definition — Mother deed: the root document where the ownership story begins. A chain that cannot be traced to a credible root is treated as broken. Why it is required Before the agreement, a buyer can simply walk away from a defect; after registration, unwinding is litigation. Banks run exactly this check before lending — no lender touches unclear title. And the risk concentrates outside city limits: assigned land, government-reserved parcels and record mismatches appear disproportionately in agricultural and peri-urban belts — precisely the plotting developer’s hunting ground. How the process works, step by step 1. Collect the paper: deeds and prior deeds, tax receipts, conversion/approval certificates. 2. Trace the chain at the SRO, 30 years or as far as records go. 3. Pull the EC yourself. 4. Cross-check revenue and mutation records against the deed. 5. Verify zoning against the master plan; confirm NA conversion where the land was agricultural. 6. Put a licensed surveyor on the ground for boundaries and encroachment. 7. Resolve every gap BEFORE payment — the cheapest moment it will ever have. Red flags, severity, and where to check Red flag What it signals Severity Where to check Revenue record mismatch Name, survey number or extent disagreeing High Deed vs mutation vs state portal Assigned / government land Cannot legally be sold at all Critical Assignment records; prohibited list Gap in the chain A transfer missing or unclear High Trace every link the full 30 years Unapproved construction/layout Structures without sanction Medium–High Municipal / panchayat records Pending litigation A live case rides on the land Critical eCourts + EC attachments No NA conversion on former agri land Use is not legal yet High The Collector’s conversion order Zoning mismatch The master plan disagrees with the pitch Medium The development authority’s plan Is a title search reliable on its own? It de-risks enormously, but is not infallible: records can be genuinely outdated (rural digitisation is patchy), and a seller’s copies can be curated or forged — which is why every document is pulled INDEPENDENTLY, and why the physical survey rides alongside the paper. State systems differ too — Telangana’s portal records, Maharashtra’s 7/12, Tamil Nadu’s patta — same logic, different desks. Example: Title is a relay race run over thirty years: the baton must pass cleanly at every exchange. One fumbled pass — a sister’s missing signature in 2003 — and everyone downstream is running confidently with a dead baton. Pre-purchase checklist ☐ EC pulled by YOU, never the seller’s copy. ☐ Chain traced 30 years or as far as records allow. ☐ Zoning + NA status confirmed for former agricultural land. ☐ Licensed surveyor on the boundaries. ☐ Mutation and survey numbers matching the deed. ☐ Lawyer BEFORE the agreement to sell, not after. Quick answers (FAQ) How many years back? 30 standard; 12–13 the floor. Is the EC proof of clear title? No — supporting evidence. Can mutation substitute for the search? No — it is a tax record. Which flags stop a purchase outright? Assigned-land taint and live litigation — the two Criticals. What does professional diligence cost? A small fraction of one percent of any real deal — the cheapest insurance in property. Bottom line Everything downstream — approvals, loans, resale — sits on the title. The search costs a sliver of the deal; skipping it stakes the whole deal. Do it first, do it independently, and make the seller’s paper prove itself. 2026-09-08|ls-sale-deed: The Sale Deed: what it is, how registration works, and why it matters Land School — an original Deccan Ledger lesson · source & further reading: Sale Deed: What It Is, How Registration Works, and Why It Matters for Land Buyers — 1acre.in Key Highlights The sale deed — not the agreement to sell — is the document that legally transfers ownership (Section 54, Transfer of Property Act, 1882). Registering it at the Sub-Registrar’s office is compulsory (Registration Act, 1908). No registration, no transfer. An agreement to sell only gives you the right to DEMAND a future sale. It moves no ownership. The Supreme Court said it again as recently as 2025: unregistered papers cannot stand in for a registered deed. A buyer who has paid fully and moved in — but holds no registered deed — is still legally exposed. What a sale deed is The sale deed is the legal instrument that actually moves ownership of immovable property from seller to buyer. It works under Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, and it comes alive only when it is signed AND registered under the Registration Act, 1908. Three words get mixed up constantly, and the mix-up is expensive. An agreement to sell is a contract (under the Indian Contract Act, 1872) fixing price, payment schedule and possession date — a binding promise, but only a promise. The sale deed is the transfer document that follows once the promise’s conditions are met. And “registry” , the word everyone uses loosely, is not a third document at all — it is the ACT of registering the sale deed. Only the registered sale deed changes whose name the law recognises. Definition — Sub-Registrar Office (SRO): the government office where property documents are recorded. The moment the deed is registered at this counter is the moment ownership legally changes hands. What a sale deed covers A properly drafted deed is the complete record of the transaction. It contains: Party details — full names, addresses and ID of buyer and seller. Property description — survey number, boundaries, area and location exactly as the revenue records show them. Sale consideration — the price and how it was paid. Possession clause — when and how possession passes. Title and indemnity clause — the seller’s written confirmation that the title is clean and free of encumbrances, and his liability if that turns out false. Registration particulars — stamp duty paid, registration number and SRO details, which anchor the deal in the public record. Definition — Indemnity clause: the seller’s promise inside the deed to compensate you if the title is defective. If trouble ever comes, this clause is what your lawyer sues on — read it before signing, not after. Why a sale deed is required Indian law treats REGISTRATION — not payment, not possession — as the trigger for ownership. Without the registered deed, your claim rests only on contract, which is a far weaker seat in any dispute. It matters at three stages. Before buying: part of due diligence is confirming the SELLER’S own deed was properly registered — his weakness becomes yours. At registration: the deed formally transfers ownership. After buying: the registered deed is what you use for mutation, for a loan against the property, and for reselling later. Example: Ravi pays ₹80 lakh, takes possession, builds a compound wall, and holds a signed agreement to sell. Years later the seller’s heirs register a sale deed for the same plot to someone else. The registered deed wins; Ravi’s money and wall buy him a court case, not a plot. How the registration process works, step by step 1. Buyer and seller sign the agreement to sell — price, payment schedule, timelines. 2. The buyer uses this window for due diligence: title documents, Encumbrance Certificate, tax records. 3. The deed is drafted and stamp duty calculated — a state-set percentage of the HIGHER of the official value and the deal price. 4. Both parties appear before the Sub-Registrar with two witnesses: signatures, biometric verification, registration fee. 5. The office checks and registers the deed; the buyer receives the certified registered copy. Timeline: typically a few days to a few weeks, depending on the state and how ready the papers are. Cost: stamp duty plus a registration fee — the fee is a smaller percentage on top of the duty. Definition — Stamp duty: the state’s tax on the transaction, paid before registration. In Telangana the working total for a sale deed is about 7.5% including transfer duty and registration; it varies by state (roughly 4–8% across India). Regulatory red flags — and what to check for each Risk What it means What to check Unregistered sale deed Ownership never legally moved, even if possession changed hands Ask for the registered copy bearing the SRO stamp and registration number Under-valued stamp duty A deed declared below the circle rate can be penalised or challenged Compare the declared value against the state’s current circle/market value Missing Encumbrance Certificate The property may carry undisclosed loans or claims Demand an EC covering at least 13–30 years Seller delaying execution You stay stuck at a contractual claim instead of ownership Write a hard registration deadline into the agreement itself Forged or altered documents The deed may collapse as evidence of title Verify authenticity directly at the Sub-Registrar’s office (certified copies) Sale deed vs agreement to sell — the key differences Aspect Agreement to sell Sale deed Purpose Records the terms of an INTENDED sale Legally transfers ownership Where it happens Signed between buyer and seller Registered at the Sub-Registrar’s office Legal force Enforceable as a contract Conclusive evidence of title once registered Typical use Fixes price, payment schedule, possession date The formal transfer of property rights Cost Nominal stamping Full stamp duty — roughly 4–8% of value by state Use the agreement during negotiation and due diligence, when both sides need something binding before completion. The moment you want actual enforceable ownership rather than a promise — you need the deed. Is a sale deed always reliable? It carries strong weight — under conditions. It must be REGISTERED (an unregistered deed transfers nothing, whatever it says). Stamp duty must be correctly paid (under-stamped deeds face penalties and can be refused as evidence). And the seller’s own CHAIN must be clean — every earlier deed in the property’s history properly registered — because a break anywhere upstream weakens your title downstream. Example: Simple memory test: if the dispute went to court tomorrow and each side placed its papers on the table, which paper wins? The registered one, standing on a registered chain. Always be the person holding that paper. Pre-purchase checklist ☐ The agreement to sell states price, payment schedule and possession date clearly. ☐ The seller’s title verified — EC plus his prior registered deeds. ☐ Possession or full payment is never treated as ownership. ☐ The deed is executed and registered as soon as conditions are met. ☐ No long, open-ended gap between agreement and registration. ☐ A property lawyer is called the moment a seller resists or delays registration. Quick answers (FAQ) Is registering a sale deed mandatory? Yes — without registration the transfer simply has not happened in law. Can possession alone prove ownership? No. Possession supports other evidence but cannot substitute for a registered deed. What if the seller refuses to execute the deed after the agreement? The agreement gives you the right to sue for “specific performance” — a court can compel the sale. Slow, but real; the deadline clause in your agreement is what makes it strong. Does an unregistered agreement have ANY value? As a contract, yes — you can sue on it. As ownership, none. What should I verify before registering? The seller’s chain, the EC, the survey-number match across all records, and the current circle value your duty will be computed on. Bottom line The sale deed is what actually places property in your name; the agreement to sell only holds your place in the queue. Treat registration as the finish line — never as a formality to get to later. For you: In your plotting business this cuts both ways: never leave your own purchases parked on agreements, and never let your plot buyers sit on them either — their limbo matures into your dispute. The date that matters in every deal file is the SRO appointment. This is an original Deccan Ledger lesson; full source article: 1acre.in (link above). Glossary — every term, simply MLC vs MLA An MLA is directly elected by voters in a constituency to the Legislative Assembly (the lower, more powerful House). An MLC sits in the Legislative Council (the upper House), usually elected indirectly — by local bodies, graduates, teachers, or by nomination — or appointed. Both arrested legislators here are MLCs, not MLAs. Example: it’s like the difference between a directly-elected town councillor and a state-level appointee to an advisory upper chamber — both have real power, but answer to different constituencies. Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) India’s new criminal code, in force since mid-2024, replacing the 160-year-old Indian Penal Code (IPC). Same broad idea — a single law listing crimes and punishments — renumbered and partly rewritten. Example: what used to be IPC Section 504 (insult intended to provoke a breach of peace) now lives under a renumbered BNS section. SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act A 1989 central law creating specific, tougher offences and procedures for crimes committed against Scheduled Caste or Scheduled Tribe individuals, in recognition of India’s history of caste-based violence and discrimination. Example: an insult that might otherwise draw a fine or short-term charge under ordinary law can become a much more serious, harder-to-bail offence if it targets someone specifically because of their SC/ST status. Remand A police request to a magistrate for permission to keep an arrested person in custody — police or judicial — while investigation continues. A court can reject it if it isn’t convinced custody is necessary, as happened here. Example: think of remand as police asking a judge, “let us keep holding this person a bit longer to investigate” — the judge can simply say no. Bail / personal bond Release from custody on a promise (sometimes backed by a money bond and sureties) to appear in court when required. It is not an acquittal or a finding of innocence — the case continues; the person is simply not held in jail meanwhile. Preventive custody Police temporarily detaining someone not because they’re formally charged with a crime, but to prevent an anticipated problem — here, BRS leaders reaching an active confrontation zone at Erravalli. It is meant to be short and typically doesn’t result in a criminal case. Adjournment motion A formal notice an MLA files demanding the House immediately drop scheduled business to debate an urgent matter. The Speaker or Chairman can accept or reject it outright, with no appeal — filing one is a way of forcing an issue onto the record even if it’s likely to be refused. Privilege / breach of privilege A formal complaint that someone has insulted or obstructed the dignity of the House or one of its members acting in that capacity. A Speaker or Chairman can refer it to a Privileges Committee, which can recommend censure — a step short of, but related to, what happened here via the criminal complaint route instead. Business Advisory Committee (BAC) A cross-party committee in each House that plans the session’s calendar — which bills get discussed on which days. Tabling its decisions mid-chaos is a government’s way of visibly sticking to a pre-agreed plan. “Dushasana” and the Mahabharata reference Dushasana is a villain in the Hindu epic Mahabharata who tried to forcibly disrobe the queen Draupadi in open court — one of Indian literature’s most infamous scenes of gendered public humiliation. Invoking his name against police accused of manhandling women legislators is about as severe a cultural comparison as Indian political rhetoric offers. President’s Rule A constitutional provision (Article 356) letting the Union government take direct control of a state when its constitutional machinery is said to have broken down, dismissing the state government. It is rare, politically explosive, and requires central government and often judicial scrutiny — an opposition demanding it is usually making a rhetorical point about the severity of a crisis, not expecting it to actually happen. 2026-09-09|ls-plot-safe: How to check if a plot is legally safe to buy Land School — an original Deccan Ledger lesson · source & further reading: How to Check If a Plot Is Legally Safe to Buy in India — 1acre.in Key Highlights With plots, nobody upstream has checked anything — legal verification is entirely your job. The 30-year title chain proves a seller CAN sell; the latest deed alone proves little. An EC only catches REGISTERED transactions — deposit-of-deeds mortgages and court cases need separate searches. ULPIN, the 14-digit parcel ID, catches an altered survey number. The whole drill costs a few thousand rupees; a disputed title costs years. Why verification matters MORE for plots Buy a flat and a builder, a lender and usually a RERA registration have each done a slice of checking before you arrived. Buy a plot and NONE of that happened. Vacant land also carries a messier past — split among siblings after a death, handed around inside a family, converted from farmland years ago with paperwork that never caught up. Every one of those moments is a place a defect could have entered the record and stayed. Verification is finding them BEFORE you pay. Start with the title chain, not the latest deed A sale deed tells you who holds the land — nothing about whether the person BEFORE them had any right to hand it over, and that gap is where most disputes begin. Ask for the Mother Deed, then trace every sale, gift, partition and inheritance forward. Thirty years is the working standard — your bank will stop at a 13-year EC, but that is a LENDING threshold, not a title standard. Inheritance deserves special attention: in ancestral property every coparcener holds a share and ALL must sign; a guardian selling a minor’s share needs court permission; one absent signature can unwind a sale a decade later. The EC catches less than you think Owning land and being FREE to sell it are separate things. Pull the EC yourself from the sub-registrar for the full 30 years — in most southern states a clean result returns as Form 16, while Form 15 lists whatever is registered against the property. Now the part sellers rarely volunteer: the EC shows only REGISTERED transactions. A mortgage created by depositing title deeds with a bank often never reaches the register; neither will an unregistered sale agreement, an oral family partition, or unpaid dues. So run two more searches: the e-courts portal for litigation on the survey number, and the state land-records portal for the latest revenue record — comparing owner name, survey number, extent and classification against the deed. Any mismatch: investigate before proceeding. Definition — Equitable mortgage (deposit of title deeds): a loan secured by simply handing the original deeds to the bank — legally valid, and frequently invisible on the EC. It is why “show me the ORIGINALS” is a due-diligence question, not rudeness: a seller without originals may have a banker holding them. Zoning, conversion and RERA: what you can actually build Start with the master plan — how is the parcel classified? Farmland once? Ask for the conversion ORDER and the fee receipt; a seller’s assurance is not a document. Then RERA: larger plotted developments generally must register, and an unregistered one becomes a problem YOU inherit. Then who may buy at all — agricultural-land eligibility varies by state. And layout approval sits with the planning authority — verified separately, on its portal, by its LP number. Legal checks vs physical checks Check What it proves Where you get it 30-year title chain The seller’s right to sell Sub-registrar copies + your advocate EC (30 years) Registered loans/claims Sub-registrar / online e-courts search Pending litigation ecourts portal, by survey number/parties Revenue record State’s view of owner + classification State land-records portal (Dharani in TG) Licensed survey Ground matches paper Surveyor on site ULPIN check Parcel identity not altered State records where rolled out Walk the boundary before you pay A licensed surveyor measures the plot against the deed AND the revenue record — paper and ground drift apart more often than buyers expect. Where your state has rolled it out, check ULPIN — the 14-digit parcel ID under the national land-records programme, sometimes called Bhu-Aadhaar — which nails the parcel’s identity against an altered or misquoted survey number. Warning signs of a risky purchase Survey numbers that DISAGREE across deed, revenue record and EC. A PoA sale where the PoA is unregistered or does not explicitly authorise sale. A seller who produces photocopies every time and originals never. Land on a prohibited-property list — the Sub-Registrar will refuse it until the restriction resolves. And resistance to a NEWSPAPER NOTICE: publishing one inviting objections before closing is ordinary practice — a seller who argues against it is telling you something. Example: The newspaper notice is the cheapest trap-detector in the kit: ₹3,000, one column, fifteen days. A silent fortnight closes the deal with confidence; a phone call from an unknown “co-owner” just saved you the whole purchase price. Quick answers (FAQ) How far back should the chain go? 30 years. Does the EC show every loan? No — registered ones only; deposit-of-deeds mortgages hide. Do all plots need RERA? Larger plotted developments generally yes; small ones may be exempt — check the threshold. Is patta proof of ownership? Supporting evidence only. Do I need a lawyer for a small plot? Yes — defect risk does not scale down with plot size; a small plot with a bad title is 100% bad. Bottom line Chain, EC, courts, record, zoning, survey — six checks, each catching what the others miss, none substituting for the rest. A few thousand rupees of verification against years of litigation: the cheapest insurance in real estate. For you: This lesson is the customer’s-eye view of everything your school has covered — use it as your master checklist template. Better: run the six checks on your OWN ventures and publish the results as a buyer pack. In a market where verification is “entirely the buyer’s job”, the developer who does the job FOR the buyer owns the trust premium. 2026-09-09|ls-ceiling: Agricultural land ceiling limits by state: how much you can own Land School — an original Deccan Ledger lesson · source & further reading: Agricultural Land Ceiling Limits by State: How Much You Can Own — 1acre.in Key Highlights Ceiling laws cap the agricultural land any person or family may hold — and they are still enforced today. No national number exists: land is a state subject, and limits run from ~7.5 acres to over 50 by state. Many states measure in STANDARD acres — irrigated land counts for more ceiling than dry land. The FAMILY often matters more than the individual: several acts aggregate the household’s holdings. Exceed the cap — even unintentionally — and the state can take the excess as surplus. What ceiling laws actually do Born of the post-independence land-reform agenda, ceiling acts cap agricultural holdings and redistribute the surplus to the landless — an answer to a world where a large landlord held roughly 45 times a marginal farmer’s land. Every state had passed one by the early 1960s, tightened again around 1971. They never expired: exceeding the ceiling remains a live legal problem, not a historical footnote. Why there is no single national limit Land is a state subject, so each state wrote its own act with its own numbers. Kerala’s figure tells you nothing about Telangana’s. The only safe move before a large purchase is a state-specific check of the CURRENT limit — amendments happen, and working from an outdated figure is working from the wrong law. The standard acre — the concept that trips buyers A stated ceiling does not always mean physical acres. A standard acre weights land by productivity and irrigation: under Madhya Pradesh’s act, for instance, one double-cropped irrigated acre equals 1.5 single-crop irrigated acres, or three dry acres. So a “30 standard acre” ceiling could allow far more physical dry land — or far less irrigated land — than the headline number suggests. Definition — Standard acre: a productivity-weighted unit for measuring ceiling compliance. Always ask of any ceiling figure: standard or physical? And of any parcel: what irrigation class does the record show? How family-unit calculation changes your real limit In several states the ceiling applies to the HOUSEHOLD as a unit — everyone’s holdings aggregate against one shared cap, with shares proportioned across members. A common exception: major (adult) sons in some states count as independent holders, subject to filing declarations. The classic ambush: a joint family where each member holds comfortably under the limit individually — but the family total quietly crossed it, discovered during inheritance or partition. Example: A family holding 20 irrigated acres buys 15 more “dry” acres — but 6 turn out irrigation-classified in the record. Converted to standard acres, the household crosses the cap, and the excess is exposed to surplus proceedings. The fix — splitting across eligible holders/entities — costs nothing at agreement stage and is miserable after registration. Red flags Combined family holdings crossing the cap even though no individual does; land in OTHER states not factored (some acts count out-of-state land in the calculation even though only in-state land can be declared surplus); relying on a pre-amendment ceiling figure; and misclassified irrigation status flipping the standard-acre conversion entirely. Individual-basis vs family-basis states Aspect Individual basis Family basis What is capped What one person holds What the whole household holds combined Source The same state ceiling act — differing in how it defines the holding unit Same Practical effect Each person’s limit stands alone All members aggregate against one shared limit Diligence needed Your own holdings The household’s TOTAL in-state holdings, before your share Who actually needs to worry For most buyers of 1–10 acres, this is genuinely a non-issue. It bites in two places: buyers already holding substantial land approaching the cap, and joint families whose aggregate has never been totalled. If either describes the deal, run the numbers before the agreement. What happens if you exceed the ceiling A notice arrives requiring declaration of total holdings and a choice of which land to retain within the cap. The excess vests in the state, compensation is paid — typically below market — and the land is redistributed to landless labourers. An active mechanism, not a museum piece. Pre-purchase checklist ☐ The CURRENT ceiling for the exact state — never borrowed from elsewhere. ☐ The family’s total existing holdings, not just yours. ☐ The parcel’s irrigation classification confirmed (it drives the conversion). ☐ A revenue lawyer’s calculation when buying as a joint family or near the limit. ☐ Figures verified with the local revenue department. Quick answers (FAQ) Is the ceiling per person or per family? Depends on the state’s act — several aggregate the household. Do these laws still apply? Fully. Does irrigated land have a lower effective ceiling? Yes — through the standard-acre conversion. What if I inherit my way over the cap? The surplus machinery applies to inherited excess too — total the family holdings at every succession. Bottom line No single number answers “how much can I own” — the state, the household structure, and the irrigation class together decide. Run the family-level calculation BEFORE a large purchase, and the ceiling stays a footnote instead of a surplus notice. For you: When someone offers 80 clean acres under one name in a low-ceiling state, the right reaction is not excitement — it is “show me how this holding is legal.” And any parcel whose chain touches ceiling-surplus declarations gets treated like assigned land: radioactive until a lawyer clears it. 2026-09-10|ls-death-transfer: How to transfer land ownership after the owner’s death Land School — an original Deccan Ledger lesson · source & further reading: How to Transfer Land Ownership After the Owner's Death — 1acre.in Key Highlights Title does not shift automatically at death — the record keeps the dead owner’s name until someone files for mutation. Probate stopped being MANDATORY anywhere in India on 20 December 2025 (Repealing and Amending Act, 2025 removed Section 213) — but banks and buyers still ask for it. Without a will, PERSONAL law decides: Hindu, Muslim and Christian families on the same street follow different rules. A succession certificate covers bank accounts and securities — NOT land. India has no transfer-on-death deed; the nearest equivalent is a registered settlement or gift deed made while the owner is alive. Why ownership does not transfer automatically An heir does not become the recorded owner by grief alone — someone has to FILE, and the filing is mutation: updating the revenue and municipal record so the state knows who now owes land revenue and property tax. The application goes to the concerned revenue authority with the death certificate, proof of heirship, and the existing land records. With a will vs without one With a will: land passes directly to named beneficiaries through the executor — sometimes involving probate. Without a will (intestate): ownership follows the personal succession law of the deceased’s religion — the Hindu Succession Act for Hindus (daughters holding EQUAL coparcenary rights since 2005), Muslim personal law with its fixed shares, the Indian Succession Act for Christians and Parsis. The intestate route usually needs court-issued heirship paperwork, making it slower — which is the practical argument for a will. Definition — Probate: a court’s certification that a will is genuine. Since 20 December 2025 it is mandatory NOWHERE in India — the old Section 213 requirement (which bound certain wills, notably in the presidency towns) was repealed. But the market has memory: banks and cautious buyers still ASK for probate on willed property, so sometimes heirs obtain it for smoothness even though the law no longer compels it. Legal-heir certificate vs succession certificate Constantly confused, differently scoped. A legal-heir certificate establishes WHO the heirs are — used for utility transfers, pensions, bank formalities, and as the heirship proof in land mutation. A succession certificate , issued by a civil court, authorises the holder to collect the deceased’s DEBTS, SECURITIES and MOVABLE assets — it does not itself convey land. For immovable property, courts and offices weigh the succession certificate alongside other documents, but the land transfer runs on heirship proof + mutation (or a court partition where heirs contest). Documents required ☐ Death certificate — first, everything waits on it. ☐ Legal-heir certificate (or the will + executor papers). ☐ The land records — deed, RoR/passbook, tax receipts. ☐ Co-heirs’ written NOCs where one heir applies. ☐ EC — checking for loans or claims riding on the land. ☐ For heirs abroad: a PoA that SPECIFICALLY authorises applying for the heir certificate and mutation — generic property clauses stall at the counter. Why India has no transfer-on-death deed — and the substitute Several countries let owners name a death-beneficiary on the deed itself; India does not. The working equivalent: a registered settlement or gift deed executed while the owner is alive , reserving a LIFE INTEREST — the owner keeps possession until death, and the property vests in the named person automatically afterwards. Stamped, registered, and it takes effect without anyone approaching a court later. For families who know exactly where land should go, it converts a future dispute into a present document. The steps, in order 1) Death certificate. 2) Establish heirship — get the legal-heir certificate proactively, not when an office finally asks. 3) Co-heirs’ NOCs in writing BEFORE filing — one heir applying alone invites an objection. 4) Pull the EC and revenue record — surface any loan or claim now. 5) File mutation with the revenue authority. 6) Only then list, sell, or borrow. Example: Three siblings inherit; the eldest files mutation alone “to keep it simple”. A sister objects, the revenue officer freezes the entry, and the file crosses into civil-court territory — two years gone. The written NOCs would have cost a week. Selling inherited land Most inherited land eventually reaches the market — and that is where unfinished mutation surfaces, because any buyer’s verification matches seller against record, and the record still names the deceased. Heirs who complete mutation BEFORE listing sell on their own timeline; those who do not discover the gap at the sub-registrar, in front of their buyer. Quick answers (FAQ) Does ownership pass automatically to heirs? By succession law, beneficially yes — but the RECORD moves only on filing. Is probate mandatory? No, since 20 Dec 2025 — though lenders and buyers may still request it. No will? Personal law distributes; heirship certificate + mutation execute. Transfer-on-death deed? Not in India — use a registered settlement/gift deed with life interest. Do daughters have equal rights? Yes — equal coparcenary rights in Hindu law since 2005. How long does it take? Clean, cooperative files: weeks to a few months; contested ones: years. Bottom line Death moves rights; paperwork moves records. Certificate, heirship, NOCs, EC, mutation — done early, in order, it is administration; done late or out of order, it is litigation. For you: Half the parcels you negotiate are inherited — so your first question to any selling family is “is mutation complete in the CURRENT generation’s names?”. If not, your timeline is not theirs to promise. And structurally: an incomplete heir set signing your agreement is a future injunction on your layout — collect every heir’s signature or a court partition first. Transfers are prohibited or void under state land-reform laws; a registered sale deed changes nothing. The government can RESUME the land at any time, with no compensation to the buyer — and buying it can carry up to six months’ jail. Narrow exceptions: inheritance by heirs, bank mortgages, and good-faith pre-Act purchases by landless poor persons. The whole defence is two checks: the revenue record’s remarks and the Section 22-A prohibited list. What assigned land is Government surplus or wasteland handed to landless poor persons — typically agricultural labourers or SC/ST families — for cultivation or as a house site, under land-reform and welfare schemes. What transfers is possession and limited use rights; ownership stays CONDITIONAL with the state. The condition that matters to every buyer: the grant usually prohibits sale. Why the law bans its sale The point of assignment is welfare — land in the hands of the landless. If assignees could sell, the poor would be bought out for quick cash and the policy would defeat itself; so state laws (in Telangana, the Assigned Lands (Prohibition of Transfers) Act) bar selling, gifting, leasing or otherwise transferring without government permission, and declare violating transfers invalid. What “void ab initio” means Treated as if the transaction never legally happened — no title passes, ever. Even land that changed hands TEN times through ten registered deeds: every link is equally invalid. A registered document does not make you the owner here; the paper has no legal weight at all. One narrow protection exists: a landless poor person who bought in good faith, for value, from the original assignee BEFORE the Act commenced and was in possession on that date — it protects the poor, not an investor. Definition — Void ab initio: void “from the beginning” — not cancelled later, but never valid at any moment. Nothing downstream of it can be valid either. What happens if it is sold anyway The government can resume the land at ANY time — no limitation period runs in its favour going away — and reassign it to another eligible landless family. The buyer gets no compensation; no civil court can decree the sale into existence. And the consequence sellers never mention: acquiring assigned land in breach of the prohibition is an OFFENCE carrying up to six months’ imprisonment. The buyer is not just a victim in this law’s eyes. Transferability by land category Category Freely transferable? Notes Patta (private) land Yes Ordinary sale deed + registration Assigned land No Transfer void; resumption + penal risk Tribal-area land Highly restricted Transfers to non-tribals barred in scheduled areas Ceiling-surplus land No Vested in government for redistribution Endowment (temple) land No Alienation needs statutory sanction, rarely given Forest land No Central law bars de-reservation without approval What an assignee CAN do Cultivate for the family; pass the land to legal heirs (inheritance is generally not a prohibited transfer); mortgage it to a scheduled bank, co-operative or notified institution — the one security the Act permits; build a house where the assignment was a house site. And in some states, apply to the Collector for DE-RESTRICTION — converting it into regular patta land eligible for sale once eligibility conditions are met. Rules vary; the revenue authority’s word is the only one that counts. How to check whether a plot is assigned Pull the latest Record of Rights from the state revenue department and read the REMARKS column for “assigned”, “granted” or restriction notes. Check the state’s prohibited-property register (Section 22-A list) for the survey number. Ask the local revenue office directly. And read the original ASSIGNMENT ORDER — it states plainly whether transfer is prohibited. Fifteen minutes of record-reading is the difference between owning land and owning a legal dead end. Example: The classic Hyderabad-belt trap: a corridor plot at 40% below market, seller waving a registered deed from a 2009 purchase. The RoR remarks column reads “asgd”. That deed — and the one before it — are both void; the discount was the disclosure. Walk away; no lawyer can cure it. If you are the assignee wanting to sell Apply to the competent revenue authority for removal of the transfer restriction where state law permits, BEFORE entering any agreement. For SC/ST or tribal-origin land, confirm whether Collector approval is mandatory. Selling first and regularising later is not a sequence the law recognises. Quick answers (FAQ) Can assigned land be sold after N years? No automatic ripening — only formal de-restriction changes its status. Why do registered deeds exist on assigned land? Because registration only blocks parcels actually on the prohibited list; the registrar’s stamp never validates a void transfer. Can family inherit it? Yes — heirs succeed; that is not a prohibited transfer. Can it be mortgaged? Only to banks/institutions the Act permits. Can it ever become freehold? In some states, via Collector-approved conversion to patta land. Bottom line Assigned land is the one category where late homework has NO remedy — no cure, no compensation, no sympathetic court. The RoR remarks and the 22-A list, checked before any money moves, are the entire safeguard. For you: For a plotting developer this is the first gate on every parcel — before price, before layout dreams: Dharani/RoR remarks + 22-A check on each survey number. One assigned survey number inside an assembled venture can poison the whole layout’s marketability. Make the check a fixed line item in your acquisition template. 2026-09-11|ls-circle-vs-market: Circle rate vs market value vs guidance value: what decides stamp duty Land School — an original Deccan Ledger lesson · source & further reading: Circle Rate vs Market Value vs Guidance Value: What Decides Stamp Duty — 1acre.in Key Highlights Circle rate, guidance value, ready-reckoner rate, jantri — one government benchmark under four names. Market value is what buyer and seller actually agree — moving daily, unlike the fixed benchmark. Stamp duty is ALWAYS charged on the higher of the two. Declaring low never helps. In hot localities the official rate can lag the street by 30–50%; in dead pockets it can sit ABOVE the market. A big gap between price and benchmark triggers income-tax consequences for BOTH sides. What the three names actually mean All one thing: the minimum property value per unit area set by the state for an area — the government’s floor for duty purposes even when the declared price is lower. Delhi and UP say circle rate; Karnataka and Tamil Nadu say guidance value; Maharashtra says ready reckoner; Gujarat says jantri; Telangana says market value. The Income-tax Act calls all of them the stamp duty value and hangs real consequences on it. Why the two values rarely match The benchmark is committee-set and revised occasionally; the market moves with demand, supply and sentiment — sometimes daily. A slow official floor under live weather: the drift between them is not a flaw, it is the design. What matters is reading the SIZE and DIRECTION of the gap. How stamp duty gets calculated On the HIGHER figure, always. Market above benchmark (the usual case in premium pockets — official rates there can run 30–50% below street prices): duty follows your real price. Benchmark above your price (stagnant pockets, or a genuine bargain): duty follows the benchmark anyway — you pay tax on value that may not exist. A deed declared below benchmark can still be presented, but assessment proceeds on the notified value under the state’s law. The income-tax traps on big gaps Seller side — Section 50C: sell below the benchmark and your capital gains are computed AS IF you sold at the benchmark. Buyer side — Section 56(2)(x): buy meaningfully below it (beyond the tolerance band) and the shortfall is taxed as YOUR income. Registrar side — Section 47A-type scrutiny: under-declaration invites reference to valuation anyway. The “saving” from a low declared price returns as somebody’s tax notice — usually both somebodies’. Definition — Tolerance band: a small statutory cushion (commonly 10%) between declared price and benchmark within which the deeming provisions stay quiet. Near the line, the band decides everything — know the current figure. Example: Benchmark ₹1 crore, agreed price ₹80 lakh. Duty: charged on ₹1 crore. Seller’s capital gains: computed on ₹1 crore. Buyer: ₹20 lakh (beyond tolerance) taxable as income from other sources. One “bargain”, three tax events. Circle rate vs market value, side by side Aspect Circle / guidance value Market value Set by State government / registration department Negotiation between buyer and seller Moves Periodically — yearly or slower Constantly, with demand and sentiment Purpose Minimum benchmark for duty and registration The actual transaction price Registration below it Duty still assessed on at least the notified value — Decides duty when It is the higher figure It is the higher figure One date-rule worth gold Where the agreement and registration straddle a benchmark revision, the AGREEMENT date’s value can govern the deal — but only if part of the consideration moved by cheque/draft/electronic transfer on or before that date. A cash token preserves nothing; one small bank-routed payment can save the entire revision delta. Pre-negotiation checklist ☐ Applicable benchmark pulled from the official portal BEFORE agreeing a price. ☐ Compared against the asking price — the higher figure is your duty base; budget it now. ☐ The tolerance band checked when the price sits near the benchmark. ☐ Bank-routed token on the agreement date when a revision looms. ☐ Lawyer or registered valuer consulted when the numbers refuse to reconcile. Quick answers (FAQ) Can I register below circle rate? Present the deed, yes; escape assessment on the notified value, no. Why do the values diverge so much in some areas? Slow official revisions under a fast market — the gap is a growth signal as much as a tax nuisance. What if I sell below circle rate? Section 50C computes your gains at the benchmark anyway — price that in before agreeing. Bottom line Two prices, one rule: duty follows the higher. Check the benchmark before negotiating — at the registrar’s desk it is a surprise; at the negotiating table it is leverage. For you: Keep the two-column sheet per pipeline village — benchmark | evidenced street price. It tells you where revisions will strike next, where duty friction is cheapest today, and which corridors’ registered comparables are honest. And use the agreement-date lock deliberately around revisions — legitimately saved duty is margin. Original Deccan Ledger lesson; full source article on 1acre.in (links above). 2026-09-11|ls-jda: Joint Development Agreement: how builder and owner shares work Land School — an original Deccan Ledger lesson · source & further reading: Joint Development Agreement: How Builder and Owner Shares Work in India — 1acre.in Key Highlights A JDA trades the owner’s land for a share of what the builder makes of it — neither pays the other upfront. Three sharing structures — area, revenue, profit — each with a different risk profile. Owners typically end with 30–50% of the developed property, set by location and leverage. Courts will not enforce an UNREGISTERED JDA. Registration is existential, not optional. Section 45(5A) defers the owner’s capital gains to the completion-certificate year, not the signing year. Most JDA disasters are builder-selection disasters — vet the builder harder than the draft. What a JDA actually is A structured trade: the owner contributes land — granting development RIGHTS, retaining ownership until later conveyances — and the developer builds at his own cost, returning a slice of the outcome as units or revenue. The owner unlocks idle land without selling; the developer gets prime land without buying. Four laws touch it at once — Contract Act, Transfer of Property Act, Registration Act, RERA — and the Registration Act point is decisive: skip registration and the agreement has no legal teeth at all. The three sharing structures Area sharing (commonest in residential): the built area — carpet, built-up or super built-up, whichever the agreement DEFINES upfront — divides by ratio; 40:60 on 100 flats leaves the owner 40 units to hold, rent or sell, keeping some shelter from a shaky market. Revenue sharing : the developer sells everything and remits the owner’s percentage — cash rather than keys, common in hot urban markets — where the drafting MUST nail gross vs net vs actually-collected, because loose words here breed most fights. Profit sharing : splits what remains after all costs; aligns incentives in theory, but a developer who inflates costs quietly shrinks the owner’s cut — workable only with real audit rights. Definition — Carpet / built-up / super built-up: three ways to measure the same building — usable floor, plus walls, plus common areas. A ratio without a named measure is not a ratio; it is a future argument. Typical ratios and what moves them Location Typical owner share Why Prime Tier-1 corridors 40–50% Scarce, expensive land = owner leverage City periphery 35–45% Land value still strong, competition higher Tier-2 cities 30–40% Land less scarce; builder carries more sales risk Tier-3 / rural fringe 25–35% Developer shoulders nearly all risk Large parcels (5 acres+) swing ratios back toward the owner; higher FSI, residential use, and proximity to existing infrastructure all push the owner’s share up. The professional way to argue any ratio: reverse-engineer it from GDV — owner share ≈ land value ÷ (land value + all-in build cost + builder margin) — then fight over the inputs, not the emotion. How the process runs Negotiate model and ratio → lawyer drafts (sharing clause, timelines, a registered GPA scoped strictly to what the project needs) → REGISTER with the Sub-Registrar → approvals and RERA registration → construction → handover of units or revenue at completion. A mid-sized residential project: three to five years end to end. Red flags in the draft No registration — worthless in court. A bare percentage with no named units, floors or defined revenue base — the single biggest fight-starter. A loosely-drafted GPA handing the developer more authority than the project needs — hard to claw back. No penalty clause — delays go unremedied. No REVERSION clause — a defaulting builder means litigation instead of an automatic handback of development rights. Definition — Reversion clause: the provision that returns development rights to the owner automatically on defined defaults — the difference between a bad year and a decade in court. Insist on it; a builder who resists it is telling you why. Area vs revenue sharing — choosing Area sharing suits owners planning to hold or rent, and shields them somewhat from market swings. Revenue sharing suits owners wanting liquidity who trust the builder’s sales machine. In either: define the measure, the base, and the audit rights in the first schedule — not in a WhatsApp message. Tax implications Section 45(5A) : individual and HUF owners under a REGISTERED JDA pay capital gains in the completion-certificate year, not the signing year — fixing the old horror of owing tax before receiving a single flat. Section 194-IC : cash paid alongside the property share draws 10% TDS. The builder’s own share is stock-in-trade — business income when sold. GST : applies on units sold BEFORE the completion certificate; sales after it are immovable-property sales, GST-exempt — a timing lever both sides should understand. Is the model reliable? The structure holds; the BUILDER is the risk. A developer running out of money leaves a half-built project and a stuck owner. RERA registration, delivery record and financial health, checked before signing, prevent most of what goes wrong later. Before signing — checklist ☐ Builder’s RERA status, delivery record, financial standing verified. ☐ Ratio names exact units / a defined revenue base — never a bare percentage. ☐ GPA scoped tightly to the project. ☐ Penalty clause on missed milestones. ☐ Reversion clause that functions automatically. ☐ Property lawyer AND tax advisor before signature — 45(5A), GST and TDS shape what actually lands in your pocket. Quick answers (FAQ) Is JDA registration mandatory? For enforceability, yes — an unregistered JDA cannot be defended in court. Can the owner cancel on default? With a reversion clause, rights return automatically; without one, litigation. When does the owner pay capital gains? Completion-certificate year, under 45(5A), for registered JDAs. Bottom line A JDA unlocks land value without a sale — and succeeds or fails on two things: the builder’s track record, and drafting that contemplates failure calmly. Registration, a precise sharing clause, and a working reversion clause are the owner’s armour. For you: Your home ground. Walk into every ratio negotiation with the GDV maths done — the side that computed the pie controls the split. Prefer area-sharing when you believe in the corridor more than the counterparty, revenue-sharing when the sales machine is the asset. And the two clauses that keep JDs out of courtrooms: registration immediately, reversion always. Original Deccan Ledger lesson; full source article on 1acre.in (links above). Sridhar Babu or KTR could not be found despite real effort and are flagged as open gaps, not filled with invented detail The story, explained from zero — fact by fact F1 · What CURE-2026 is and what it replaces Telangana has introduced a Bill to replace the legal framework governing Hyderabad’s municipal administration since the 1955-era GHMC Act — a law written for a city of roughly 15 lakh people that now governs a metro region of about 1.3 crore. Plain English: the rulebook for who runs Hyderabad’s roads, drains, building permissions and property tax has not been rewritten from scratch in seven decades, even though the city has grown nearly ninefold in that time. Numbers: reported as roughly 43 chapters and nine schedules in the draft — a genuinely large piece of legislation, not a narrow amendment. F2 · The Bill was introduced, not passed On the Assembly’s final sitting day, Legislative Affairs Minister D. Sridhar Babu moved the motion to introduce CURE-2026; the motion carried and the Bill had its first reading. Plain English: this is step one of a multi-step legislative process — introduction, not law. A Bill can still change substantially, get sent to a Select Committee for closer study, or stall entirely before it is finally passed. Mechanics: no report found confirms whether CURE-2026 was referred to a Select Committee, unlike the separately controversial Hate Speech and Hate Crimes Bill, which was referred to one in March 2026. That asymmetry — one contentious bill gets extra scrutiny, this one (as far as could be confirmed) does not — is worth watching, though its absence from search results is not proof it didn’t happen. F3 · The new governance structure sits above, not instead of, the existing corporations A CURE Apex Governance Council, chaired by the Chief Minister and including a minister and a Principal Secretary as convenor, is reported to sit at the top, with a CURE Executive Committee below it made up of Commissioners, Police Commissioners and Collectors. GHMC, Cyberabad Municipal Corporation and Malkajgiri Municipal Corporation keep their own elected mayors and corporators underneath. Plain English: the three corporations don’t disappear, but a new layer of state-appointed officials above them would set shared policy — including, crucially, the property-tax and building-permission rules all three now have to follow. Mechanics: critics point out that neither the Apex Council nor the Executive Committee, as reported, includes a single elected mayor, corporator, MLA or MP — every seat on both bodies is either a minister or a bureaucrat. Incentives: a body with no elected member and no mandated meeting frequency (per the critical reporting) can move faster than a body that has to answer to local voters — useful for pushing through unpopular reforms like a tax overhaul, and exactly what critics say is the constitutional problem. F4 · The property-tax switch is the Bill’s single biggest change Property tax would move from the current Annual Rental Value method, frozen since the year 2000, to a Capital Value method pegged to the government’s own registration/market value — a change Deccan Chronicle’s own headline states could roughly double the bill. Plain English: the old system taxed a property on what it could theoretically rent for, using a formula nobody has updated in over 25 years; the new one taxes it on what it is actually worth today, which for most Hyderabad property is a far bigger number. Numbers: one single-sourced figure (not independently corroborated, treat with caution) puts residential rates at 0.10–0.50% of capital value and commercial rates at 0.20–2%. No outlet offers a more precise overall multiplier than “roughly double” — that phrase is the ceiling of what could be confirmed. The tax base for new construction would apply immediately; for existing buildings, reporting says it will be phased in gradually, though no specific schedule was found. F5 · A cluster of other reforms rides along in the same Bill Beyond the tax switch, CURE-2026 reportedly abolishes octroi and dog tax, introduces a self-assessment property-tax mechanism with a new property identity code, sets up a “deemed approval” system for building permissions that auto-escalates a stalled application and can approve it by default after a Commissioner ignores a 7-day notice (with exclusions for lake, FTL, buffer-zone, government or 22A-listed land), moves unauthorised-construction enforcement toward graded civil penalties with power to seal a structure after 24 hours’ notice, bans unauthorised construction-and-demolition waste dumping across the region, and adds a single trade licence, night-time economy zones and a Gender Inclusion Cell. Plain English: this is a genuinely wide-ranging governance bill, not a narrow tax amendment — the deemed-approval building-permission clause in particular is a direct, practical change for anyone who has ever waited months for a GHMC-style approval to move. Mechanics: the deemed-approval exclusions matter as much as the mechanism itself — any parcel touching a lake, its FTL, a buffer zone, government land or the 22A prohibited list gets none of the automatic-approval benefit, meaning the fastest new process explicitly does not apply to exactly the riskiest categories of land. Numbers: no fine amounts for unauthorised-construction penalties were found in any source — a genuine reporting gap, not a fact this paper is choosing to omit. Resident welfare associations submitted more than 3,000 representations and sought more time; the government did not grant an extension. Plain English: the public did get a formal chance to object, and did so in large numbers — but the government moved ahead on its own schedule rather than the objectors’ preferred one. Incentives: refusing an extension after a large volume of objections signals the government prioritised keeping to its legislative timeline over accommodating stakeholder concerns — a choice that will likely shape how contested the Bill’s next stage becomes. Plain English: real, on-record opposition exists, but it came before introduction (on the draft) or from outside the chamber — not as floor resistance during the actual 11 September introduction, because the BRS bench that would normally lead that fight was absent. Numbers: no direct, CURE-specific quote from KTR was found despite his well-documented “₹5 lakh crore scam” language on the related HILTP policy — that phrase is confirmed for HILTP, not for CURE, and should not be conflated. Plain English: this is not just a tax fight — a specific, legally-grounded objection exists that the new top-tier governance bodies violate India’s own constitutional guarantee of elected local self-government. Mechanics: the 74th Constitutional Amendment (1992) is the specific provision requiring elected urban local bodies; a governance layer above them with zero elected members is the exact structure that Amendment was designed to prevent state governments from quietly recreating. 2026-09-12|ls-ulpin: ULPIN: what the 'Aadhaar for land' means for buyers Land School — an original Deccan Ledger lesson · source & further reading: ULPIN: What the “Aadhaar for Land” Means for Buyers — 1acre.in Key Highlights ULPIN is a 14-digit code for every surveyed parcel, generated from its exact geo-coordinates. The Aadhaar comparison is fair: one permanent identity per parcel, whoever owns it. It attacks a real problem — the same plot carrying unlinked identifiers across departments. Coverage varies hugely by state: some are at 100%, others far behind; nationally roughly half of parcels are covered. It speeds verification and blocks multi-selling fraud where implemented — but it never replaces legal due diligence. What ULPIN actually is ULPIN — Unique Land Parcel Identification Number, officially Bhu-Aadhaar — is a 14-digit code assigned to each parcel under the Digital India Land Records Modernization Programme, built from the parcel’s records of rights and its geo-coordinates. Like citizen Aadhaar, the point is one verifiable identity that stays consistent across every department, bank and registration office. The problem it solves India has over 600 million parcels, and historically each state tracked them its own way — survey numbers, khasra numbers, patta numbers, tax accounts — none linked automatically. The same land wearing four numbers in four registers is exactly the confusion fraudsters exploited: multi-selling the same plot under its different identities. One coordinate-based ID across all registers removes that whole class of fraud. What ULPIN does — and does not — replace Identifier What it tracks Key limitation ULPIN / Bhu-Aadhaar Geo-coordinate identity of the parcel Does NOT confirm ownership or title cleanliness Survey number State reference for a plot within a village Can repeat across regions; not geo-referenced Khasra number Agricultural plot ID in northern states State-specific; no national linkage without ULPIN Patta / khatauni Revenue record of occupancy / tax liability A tax record — not proof of clean title Sale deed The legal transfer document Says nothing about whether the chain behind it is complete ULPIN does not retire the identifiers you know; it sits above them as the connector — once the linkage for a given parcel is actually done. How far the rollout has reached Uneven, and that unevenness decides its usefulness for YOUR parcel. Andhra Pradesh finished first at full coverage (60+ million parcels); Karnataka, Odisha, Telangana, Madhya Pradesh and Chhattisgarh sit in the 60–90% band; some large states lag far behind. Nationally, roughly half of parcels carry a ULPIN. No ULPIN on your parcel = none of the benefits yet — the traditional checks carry the full weight. What it means practically for a buyer Where implemented, states link the ULPIN to the working records — pattas, extracts, deeds, tax records — creating one auditable trail. Mutations update under the ULPIN, so buyers and lenders read CURRENT status rather than chasing offices. A mortgage or dispute linked to the ID surfaces without hand-cross-referencing registries. Example: The old scam ULPIN kills: sell the plot once under its survey number, once under an old revenue identifier — two “different” properties on paper, one piece of earth. With one coordinate-derived ID stamped on every record, the second sale collides with the first instantly. What ULPIN still does not solve It confirms WHICH parcel — never WHOSE. It cannot verify the seller’s title, and cannot reach back into unregistered history. And within even high-coverage states, parcels miss IDs where surveys are incomplete or boundaries disputed. Treat it as a checksum on identity that narrows your work — the title chain, EC and litigation checks remain the work itself. Definition — Bhoodhar: Telangana’s own parcel-ID under the same national idea, assigned village by village through the ongoing resurvey — quote it in documents once your village is covered. Pre-purchase checklist ☐ Check whether your state/district has completed the rollout. ☐ Where a ULPIN exists, cross-verify it against survey number, owner name and description. ☐ Use linked mutation/encumbrance data as an accelerant — never as a substitute for the title search. ☐ Where none exists, run the full traditional drill. ☐ Lawyer on anything beyond a routine purchase. Quick answers (FAQ) Is ULPIN mandatory for buying? No — it is infrastructure, arriving parcel by parcel. Does it replace the survey number? No; it bridges identifiers under one framework. Can it prevent fraud completely? It removes identity-based fraud; title fraud remains your due diligence. Does having one mean the title is verified? No — identity yes, ownership no. Bottom line ULPIN is plumbing, not paint: when it works, deals simply stop failing for identity reasons. Use it, quote it, and keep doing the ownership homework it was never designed to do. For you: Habit for the transition years: verify every pipeline parcel on the current portal, and the moment a Bhoodhar exists write it into your agreements beside the survey number. If two documents show different parcel IDs for “the same” land — that mismatch IS the due-diligence finding. Original Deccan Ledger lesson; full source article on 1acre.in (links above). 2026-09-12|ls-ceiling: Agricultural land ceiling limits by state: how much you can own Land School — an original Deccan Ledger lesson · source & further reading: Agricultural Land Ceiling Limits by State: How Much You Can Own — 1acre.in Key Highlights Ceiling laws cap the agricultural land any person or family may hold — and they are still enforced today. No national number exists: land is a state subject, and limits run from ~7.5 acres to over 50 by state. Many states measure in STANDARD acres — irrigated land counts for more ceiling than dry land. The FAMILY often matters more than the individual: several acts aggregate the household’s holdings. Exceed the cap — even unintentionally — and the state can take the excess as surplus. What ceiling laws actually do Born of the post-independence land-reform agenda, ceiling acts cap agricultural holdings and redistribute the surplus to the landless — an answer to a world where a large landlord held roughly 45 times a marginal farmer’s land. Every state had passed one by the early 1960s, tightened again around 1971. They never expired: exceeding the ceiling remains a live legal problem, not a historical footnote. Why there is no single national limit Land is a state subject, so each state wrote its own act with its own numbers. Kerala’s figure tells you nothing about Telangana’s. The only safe move before a large purchase is a state-specific check of the CURRENT limit — amendments happen, and working from an outdated figure is working from the wrong law. The standard acre — the concept that trips buyers A stated ceiling does not always mean physical acres. A standard acre weights land by productivity and irrigation: under Madhya Pradesh’s act, for instance, one double-cropped irrigated acre equals 1.5 single-crop irrigated acres, or three dry acres. So a “30 standard acre” ceiling could allow far more physical dry land — or far less irrigated land — than the headline number suggests. Definition — Standard acre: a productivity-weighted unit for measuring ceiling compliance. Always ask of any ceiling figure: standard or physical? And of any parcel: what irrigation class does the record show? How family-unit calculation changes your real limit In several states the ceiling applies to the HOUSEHOLD as a unit — everyone’s holdings aggregate against one shared cap, with shares proportioned across members. A common exception: major (adult) sons in some states count as independent holders, subject to filing declarations. The classic ambush: a joint family where each member holds comfortably under the limit individually — but the family total quietly crossed it, discovered during inheritance or partition. Example: A family holding 20 irrigated acres buys 15 more “dry” acres — but 6 turn out irrigation-classified in the record. Converted to standard acres, the household crosses the cap, and the excess is exposed to surplus proceedings. The fix — splitting across eligible holders/entities — costs nothing at agreement stage and is miserable after registration. Red flags Combined family holdings crossing the cap even though no individual does; land in OTHER states not factored (some acts count out-of-state land in the calculation even though only in-state land can be declared surplus); relying on a pre-amendment ceiling figure; and misclassified irrigation status flipping the standard-acre conversion entirely. Individual-basis vs family-basis states Aspect Individual basis Family basis What is capped What one person holds What the whole household holds combined Source The same state ceiling act — differing in how it defines the holding unit Same Practical effect Each person’s limit stands alone All members aggregate against one shared limit Diligence needed Your own holdings The household’s TOTAL in-state holdings, before your share Who actually needs to worry For most buyers of 1–10 acres, this is genuinely a non-issue. It bites in two places: buyers already holding substantial land approaching the cap, and joint families whose aggregate has never been totalled. If either describes the deal, run the numbers before the agreement. What happens if you exceed the ceiling A notice arrives requiring declaration of total holdings and a choice of which land to retain within the cap. The excess vests in the state, compensation is paid — typically below market — and the land is redistributed to landless labourers. An active mechanism, not a museum piece. Pre-purchase checklist ☐ The CURRENT ceiling for the exact state — never borrowed from elsewhere. ☐ The family’s total existing holdings, not just yours. ☐ The parcel’s irrigation classification confirmed (it drives the conversion). ☐ A revenue lawyer’s calculation when buying as a joint family or near the limit. ☐ Figures verified with the local revenue department. Quick answers (FAQ) Is the ceiling per person or per family? Depends on the state’s act — several aggregate the household. Do these laws still apply? Fully. Does irrigated land have a lower effective ceiling? Yes — through the standard-acre conversion. What if I inherit my way over the cap? The surplus machinery applies to inherited excess too — total the family holdings at every succession. Bottom line No single number answers “how much can I own” — the state, the household structure, and the irrigation class together decide. Run the family-level calculation BEFORE a large purchase, and the ceiling stays a footnote instead of a surplus notice.
