2026-09-13|ls-disputes-check: How to check land disputes and litigation before buying Land School — an original Deccan Ledger lesson · source & further reading: How to check land disputes and litigation before buying — 1acre.in Key Highlights A clean-looking sale deed proves little — sellers rarely volunteer pending cases. The Encumbrance Certificate, pulled for 15–30 years, is the first filter for hidden loans and old claims. eCourts and the NJDG let you search pending cases free — but a wrong spelling can hide the case. Lis pendens binds a new buyer to a pending case’s outcome even if nobody told them it existed. Revenue-court disputes and old village claims are often NOT online — a physical visit still counts. What checking for disputes actually means There is a difference between a title that LOOKS fine and one that has been CHECKED. Land carries history the deed never shows: an old inheritance quarrel, a boundary shifted after a family split, a loan never cleared. A litigation check confirms — through independent sources, never the seller’s word — that none of this is unresolved. Two different searches get confused: the EC tracks registered financial claims; a court search tracks live litigation. A property can be clean on one and dirty on the other. What a proper check covers Encumbrance history — loans, mortgages, claims, from the SRO. Court cases — anything involving the owner or the property, via eCourts and the NJDG. Ownership and survey records — mutation entries cross-checked against the deed. Unrecorded local disputes — boundary and revenue matters not yet digital. The neighbours — who usually know about a fight before any court does. Why the check must happen before you pay anything Land fights make up a striking share of India’s pending civil cases, tracing to a few causes: contested inheritance, forged papers, unclear titles, encroachment. A seller with a pending case usually will not mention it. The check matters at three moments: before the offer, before any advance, and before registration — each later stage makes a discovered defect more expensive. Definition — Lis pendens: “suit pending”. Once litigation over land is on foot, whoever buys the land inherits the case’s outcome — knowledge or ignorance makes no difference. The law assumes you searched. Start with the Encumbrance Certificate Ask for at least 15 years, ideally 30 — a spotless five-year EC says nothing about a fifteen-year-old dispute that never resolved. Read it for court attachments, unreleased liens, and windows where entries abruptly stop; a gap is a question, not a quirk. Then search eCourts and the NJDG Both portals cover District and High Courts, searchable by party name, case number or type — free. Search the owner’s name in every reasonable variation (initials, spellings), the FAMILY’S names, and past owners’ names from the chain. A nil result under one spelling proves only that spelling. Example: A buyer near Shamshabad stopped at a clean EC. The seller’s sister’s partition suit was two minutes away on eCourts — under HER name. The court notice arrived after his registration; lis pendens did the rest. Red flags — what they usually mean, what to do Red flag What it usually means What to do EC entries suddenly stop A dispute or transaction may have been kept off the record Ask the SRO for a written explanation of the gap eCourts returns nothing at all The case may sit under a name variant Re-search with initials and past owners’ names Seller resists the full-period EC Possibly avoiding an older entry Insist on the 15–30 year window — non-negotiable Neighbours mention a fight the seller did not Local knowledge runs ahead of filings Visit the tahsildar; investigate before any advance Title changed hands fast and often Rapid resales can be laundering a defect Trace and check each prior owner in the chain The physical checks documents cannot replace Revenue-court records — at the tahsildar or sub-divisional office — are mostly not digitised; someone must go and look. Neighbours help more than expected. For anything beyond a small purchase, a lawyer running the full search is cheap against the alternative. Pre-purchase checklist ☐ EC for 15–30 years. ☐ eCourts + NJDG searched under every reasonable name variation. ☐ Ownership and survey details cross-checked on the state portal. ☐ SRO and revenue office visited for what is not online. ☐ Neighbours asked about disputes and boundaries. ☐ Lawyer’s full search before any advance. Quick answers (FAQ) Can I search property litigation online free? Yes — eCourts and NJDG. Do all disputes show there? No — revenue matters and fresh village fights often exist offline first. What if I unknowingly buy disputed land? Lis pendens binds you to the outcome; your recourse is against the seller — which is why the check precedes the money. How far back should the EC go? 30 years where possible; 15 as the floor. Bottom line Disputes rarely announce themselves; they sit in old entries and filings the seller has no reason to mention. A few hours across the EC, eCourts and one village visit cost almost nothing against untangling a case later. For you: Fixed habit for your pipeline: fifteen minutes on eCourts — seller, family, survey number — before any serious conversation. The suit that kills a JD is usually a brother or an uncle, not the man across the table. Original Deccan Ledger lesson; full source article on 1acre.in (links above). 2026-09-13|ls-rera-plots: RERA for plotted developments: what plot buyers must verify Land School — an original Deccan Ledger lesson · source & further reading: RERA for Plotted Developments: What Plot Buyers Must Verify — 1acre.in Key Highlights RERA is not an apartment law — plotted layouts fall inside it once they cross a size or amenity threshold. The commonly cited trigger: land above 500 sq m OR more than 8 plots (states vary slightly). A simple one-off land transfer between individuals, with no promised infrastructure, generally stays outside RERA. “RERA approved” is marketing language with no legal meaning — only registration on the state portal counts. Verification is minutes, free, and done by you — and can save years of dispute. What RERA for plotted development is The 2016 Act defines a “real estate project” broadly enough to cover developing land into plots for sale. Gated-plot communities, farm-plot schemes and ordinary layouts sit under the same registration, disclosure and escrow regime as towers. Four terms that get blurred: RERA registration (a verifiable number), “RERA approved” (a phrase with no defined status), NA permission (a separate land-use approval), and the Occupancy Certificate (local compliance — not a substitute for RERA’s protections). Untangling these is step one, because sellers use them interchangeably on purpose. What registration discloses The project’s portal page shows: the sanctioned layout (plots, roads, common areas); the land title behind it; the registration number that must match brochures and agreements exactly; the promised amenities the developer is now BOUND to deliver; the disclosed timeline; and the escrow confirmation that buyer money is ring-fenced for this project’s development. Definition — Escrow: a dedicated account where buyer payments must be spent on this project. It is what stops your road money funding somebody’s next launch. When registration becomes mandatory At the MARKETING stage — before the first sale agreement — once the layout crosses the threshold. And note the second trigger: promising shared infrastructure (roads, park, clubhouse, security) pulls a project into RERA REGARDLESS of size. The escrow protects instalments before delivery; registration also opens the authority’s complaint machinery to buyers after purchase. When a plotted sale is legitimately exempt A one-off land transfer between individuals with no promised development generally stays outside. Some states treat layouts where NA permission preceded the sale agreement as demarcated land sales. Agricultural land stays exempt while there is no active plan to convert and market it as a housing project. The rule for buyers: an exemption CLAIMED must be an exemption DOCUMENTED — ask what specifically justifies it, in writing. How to verify in minutes Check the triggers (size, plot count, promised amenities). Search the state portal by project name, promoter name or number. A genuine listing shows plans, approvals, title, timelines. Cross-check the number character-for-character against brochure and draft agreement — a mismatch, or no listing, is your answer. Red flags — and the checks that answer them Red flag What it usually means What to check Number does not match the portal Unregistered project — or someone else’s number Search the exact number on the official state portal yourself No mention of escrow Payments may not be ring-fenced Demand the escrow disclosure in the project details or agreement Exemption claimed, nothing shown Informal justification, not a legal one Request the NA permission or the exempting provision in writing “RERA approved” with no number Loose marketing, possibly zero compliance Ask for the number; verify independently Brochure amenities missing from the disclosure The promises may not be binding Compare brochure against the registered disclosure line by line RERA registered vs OC vs marketing claims Term What it actually confirms Where to verify RERA registered Formal registration, unique number, legal accountability State RERA portal “RERA approved” Nothing defined — a phrase No register exists; demand the number Occupancy Certificate Local safety/infrastructure compliance Municipal / planning authority RERA matters BEFORE you sign and pay; the OC matters near handover; the marketing phrase is always a claim to verify, never evidence. Example: The Amber Homes case near Hyderabad: an HMDA-approved layout never registered with RERA. A buyer paid over ₹1 crore for 1,000 sq yds, got half registered, and the regulator’s cease-and-desist arrived after the money. Approved layout, illegal selling — the two locks are different locks. Pre-purchase checklist ☐ Project found on the state portal by name or number. ☐ Number matches brochure and agreement exactly. ☐ Exemption claims backed by NA permission or the exempting clause, in writing. ☐ Promised amenities present in the registered disclosure. ☐ OC never treated as equivalent to RERA registration. ☐ Lawyer consulted when the status looks unclear. Quick answers (FAQ) Does RERA apply to all plot purchases? No — plain person-to-person land transfers without promised development are outside. Can a developer sell plots without registration? Not once the thresholds or amenity promises apply — that selling is illegal, with penalties. What if I buy into an unregistered project? You lose the escrow protection and the authority’s machinery; remedies shrink to ordinary contract suits. Bottom line Registration is not a formality a plot developer may skip. Once the threshold or an amenity promise is crossed, the number on the portal — not the phrase on the hoarding — is what protects a buyer. Verify it yourself, before signing, every time. For you: Your sequence as a developer is fixed: title → layout approval → RERA → marketing. And your fastest filter of other people’s ventures: “tell me the RERA number — I’ll look it up while we talk.” The reaction is the answer. Glossary — every term, simply Section 22-A (Registration Act, 1908) The specific legal clause letting a Sub-Registrar refuse to register a document at all — not just delay it — if the property falls in a defined prohibited category. Example: a family with a perfectly genuine, decades-old patta discovers they cannot sell because their survey number sits on this list. Sub-Registrar The local government officer who formally registers property-sale documents, making a transaction legally recognised. Example: it is this officer's desk where a 22A-listed sale gets turned away, whatever the buyer and seller have already agreed. Short discussion (legislative) A scheduled House debate slot set aside for one named issue, letting a minister answer at length on the record, but without the binding vote or extended formal notice a full motion would carry. Example: today’s dedicated debate titled “Issues related to Section 22A of Registration Act.” Prohibited list (22A list) A district-wise register of survey numbers where the Sub-Registrar must refuse registration, meant to cover only government, assigned, endowment/Waqf, ceiling-surplus and genuinely disputed land — but in practice also trapping ordinary private plots wrongly recorded on it. TM-15 A specific data-correction module in Telangana’s land-records system, used to fix wrongly recorded 22A entries. Example: about 23,000 of the 47,440 acres the minister says were freed came through this exact channel. Dharani vs Bhu Bharati Dharani was the BRS government’s land-records digitisation portal, launched around 2020; Bhu Bharati is the current Congress government’s replacement system. Errors carried over from Dharani are the government’s own repeated explanation for why so much private land ended up wrongly listed. High Court judge-led probe An inquiry where a sitting High Court judge, rather than a police officer or bureaucrat, investigates facts and can recommend action — carrying real independent weight since the judge sits outside the executive branch being investigated, though such a probe cannot itself prosecute anyone; that would require a separate criminal case. Doubtful transactions Political shorthand for property transactions opposition parties allege were improperly permitted or improperly blocked — a deliberately broad term used here to justify a wide-ranging probe rather than a narrow, specific complaint. Endowment / Waqf land Property permanently dedicated for a religious purpose — Hindu temple endowment land under one legal regime, Muslim Waqf land under a separate central Act — both categories legitimately sit on the 22A list, but their records are often old and hard to correct quickly. Ceiling-surplus land Land a now-repealed Urban Land Ceiling law once required a large landholder to surrender to the government above a fixed cap — some parcels genuinely exempted from that surrender decades ago were still wrongly re-listed for want of the exemption being entered in the record. The backstory — how we got here Date Event September 1999 Section 22-A first added to the Registration Act via Andhra Pradesh Amendment Act 4 of 1999, barring registration of anything “opposed to public policy.” 2005 The Andhra Pradesh High Court strikes down the “public policy” wording as unconstitutionally vague. 19 June 2007 Andhra Pradesh Amendment Act 19 of 2007 re-enacts Section 22-A retrospectively, replacing vague wording with defined prohibited categories — the version still in force. 2 June 2014 Telangana is carved out as a separate state and carries the 2007 Section 22-A framework into its own law. ~2020 The BRS government launches Dharani, digitising Telangana’s land records statewide and, per the current government’s account, carrying forward or introducing fresh 22A-listing errors in the process. 7 December 2023 Congress takes office; the prohibited list stands at 1,02,52,690 acres statewide, the baseline the minister now measures every reduction against. The deeper pattern is a land-records crisis that has now outlasted three distinct digitisation efforts (the original manual system, Dharani, and now Bhu Bharati) and two changes of government, without any single administration fully owning a fix. A first-time reader sees today’s headline as one more political spat over acreage; a ten-year follower of Telangana land administration recognises a structural problem — a prohibited-list mechanism designed for a handful of genuinely disputed categories, bolted onto records digitised in successive rushed phases, each phase inheriting and sometimes compounding the last one’s errors. The politics changes color from BRS to Congress to whatever comes next; the underlying data-quality problem does not resolve itself just because responsibility for it changes hands. BJP gets to occupy the opposition’s loudest seat on this issue while BRS’s MLAs remain suspended, and its High Court judge-probe demand — spanning both rival parties — is a harder, more credible-sounding ask than a simple resignation call. 2026-09-14|ls-gpa-risk: Power of attorney for property: why a GPA sale is risky Land School — an original Deccan Ledger lesson · source & further reading: Power of attorney for property: why a GPA sale is risky — 1acre.in Key Highlights A PoA creates an AGENCY: someone may act on the owner’s behalf. It transfers no ownership, ever. Suraj Lamp v. State of Haryana (Supreme Court, 2011): only a registered sale deed conveys immovable property. A 2025 Supreme Court ruling repeated it: a GPA — even paired with an agreement to sell — does not create title. Genuine GPAs remain perfectly valid for MANAGEMENT — the classic case being NRIs and family members handling property from afar. A deal where the GPA is the transaction itself is a deal to pause and lawyer-check. What a power of attorney for property is One person — the principal — signs a document authorising another — the agent (attorney holder) — to act for them on a specific property: collect rent, pay dues, sign routine paperwork, represent them before authorities when they cannot be present. The land stays the principal’s throughout. Definition — Principal / agent: the owner giving the authority, and the person receiving it. Every power the agent has flows from the principal — and stops when the principal cancels it or dies. What a legitimate GPA typically covers A clean GPA spells out a limited, specific set of powers, never a vague catch-all. Read it for five things: scope — does it name the property, survey number, and the exact permitted actions? Sale authorisation — explicit words allowing price negotiation, deed execution and receiving payment (general “manage my affairs” language is NOT enough to sell); duration — open-ended, or tied to one period or transaction? Registration details — which SRO registered the GPA itself, and its number; revocation clause — how the principal can cancel it. When a GPA is genuinely needed Owners cannot attend every signature and filing. Legitimate uses cluster at three stages: pre-purchase — an NRI authorising a relative to negotiate while abroad; registration — an owner who cannot travel authorising someone to complete SRO formalities; post-purchase — ongoing management, rent, taxes, maintenance. The problem begins the moment a GPA is used INSTEAD of a sale deed — as a way to skip stamp duty and keep the deal off the record. Example: The old “GPA sale”: seller hands over a GPA + agreement to sell, buyer pays full price, both save duty, nothing registers as a transfer. Cheap and invisible — until an heir, a creditor or the seller himself reappears. Everything that made it cheap made it worthless. Red flags in GPA-based deals — severity and checks Issue Severity What to check No legal title transfer behind the deal High Confirm a registered sale deed exists or will be executed — never just a GPA Same GPA used for multiple sales High Search the SRO records for earlier transactions on the property GPA revoked without notice High Verify directly with the principal that it is still active Vague or expired authority Medium Read for explicit sale/price/execution powers and the validity period Principal dead or incapacitated High Confirm the principal’s current status before relying on the holder Unregistered / notarised-only GPA Medium Insist on a GPA registered at the SRO for anything consequential Power of attorney vs registered sale deed Aspect Power of attorney Registered sale deed Purpose Authorises someone to ACT for the owner Legally transfers ownership Where issued SRO (or notarised for limited non-transfer uses) SRO only Validity Until revoked, expired, or the principal dies Permanent, until a future lawful transfer Typical use Management, remote representation, execution help Actual sale, purchase or gift Cost Duty on the GPA itself — small, varies by state Full stamp duty + registration on the transaction value A GPA is right when someone must act for an owner. A registered deed is the ONLY right instrument when ownership itself must move. Treating the two as interchangeable is where most GPA disputes are born. Is a PoA reliable? Only as reliable as its registration and the principal’s continuing authority. The classic failures: relying on an old GPA nobody confirmed was unrevoked; accepting a notarised-only document where registration was required; assuming a GPA survives the principal’s death (it does not — agency ends at death, with a narrow exception where the agent holds a genuine interest in the property). After Suraj Lamp, several states issued circulars tightening registration practice — another reason to verify at the SRO rather than trust the paper shown. Definition — Agency coupled with interest: the narrow exception where the agent has a real stake in the property itself — such authority can survive revocation and death. It is the legitimate backbone of a builder’s PoA inside a registered JDA. Pre-purchase checklist ☐ GPA registered at the SRO — note the number. ☐ It explicitly authorises sale, price negotiation and deed execution. ☐ The principal personally confirms it is unrevoked (a video call is cheap). ☐ The principal was alive and competent when it was signed — and is alive now. ☐ The actual transfer happens by registered sale deed, with the principal as vendor. ☐ A property lawyer reads any deal where a GPA carries real weight. Quick answers (FAQ) Is a GPA sale legal in India? As a transfer of ownership — no. Since Suraj Lamp (2011), only a registered deed conveys property. Can a GPA holder sell on the owner’s behalf? Yes — IF the GPA expressly authorises sale, and the deed is registered naming the principal as seller. The holder signs FOR the owner; he never becomes the owner. What happens to a GPA when the principal dies? It dies too. Anything signed after is void — except the narrow coupled-with-interest case. Does a PoA transfer ownership? Never, however it is worded. How do I verify a GPA before a purchase? Registration at the SRO, express powers in the text, principal alive and confirming — the three checks that cover almost everything. Bottom line A power of attorney is a genuinely useful management tool that was never designed to replace a sale deed. Buyers who keep that line bright — and verify registration and current validity before relying on one — avoid nearly all the GPA grief that ends up in court. For you: In your JD work, PoAs are daily equipment — landowners grant you development authority, NRI owners send registration authority. Draft them task-scoped and registered; and when one appears on the OTHER side of the table, run the three checks before the price conversation. The process in order Eligibility → verification file → agreement (price, advance, timelines) → registered deed at the SRO with duty and fees → mutation so the record names you. Each step gates the next; hurrying the order is how buyers finance other people’s mistakes. Glossary — every term, simply Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023 India’s new criminal code, which replaced the colonial-era Indian Penal Code (IPC) from 1 July 2024 with renumbered and in places rewritten offences. Example: what used to be charged under IPC sections is now charged under differently numbered BNS sections, which is why recent Indian FIRs cite BNS rather than IPC. BNS Section 132 Covers assault or use of criminal force against a public servant to deter them from doing their duty. Example: the charge used here against KTR’s aides for allegedly obstructing police at the Assembly gate. BNS Section 352 Covers intentional insult meant to provoke a breach of peace — roughly, saying or doing something deliberately designed to make someone lose their temper and cause a public disturbance. BNS Section 351 (criminal intimidation) Covers threatening someone with harm to themselves, their reputation, their property, or someone they care about, in order to frighten them or force them to act a certain way; sub-section (2) covers a more serious form of the same offence. “No coercive steps” court order A specific, limited form of protection a court can grant while a criminal investigation continues: police may keep investigating and can question the person, but may not arrest them or take similarly forceful action, unless and until the court says otherwise. Example: the order the Telangana High Court gave KTR’s two aides on 9 September. Notice vs. FIR vs. arrest Three different, increasingly serious stages in Indian criminal procedure: a notice merely calls someone in for questioning; an FIR (First Information Report) is the formal record that a cognisable offence is being investigated; an arrest physically takes someone into custody. Being served a notice, as Mahesh and Mahender Reddy were, does not by itself mean arrest is coming or even likely. Adjournment motion A formal procedural tool letting a legislator force the House to stop its scheduled business and debate one specific, urgent matter instead — used here by BRS to put its manhandling allegation formally on record. MLA vs. MLC An MLA (Member of the Legislative Assembly) sits in a state’s directly-elected lower house; an MLC (Member of the Legislative Council) sits in the upper house, in states that have one, typically reaching it via indirect election or nomination rather than a direct public vote in a constituency. Legislative Council Chairman vs. Assembly Speaker Two separate presiding officers for a state’s two legislative houses — the Chairman runs the Council (upper house), the Speaker runs the Assembly (lower house) — each with independent authority to discipline members of their own house. Task force (police) A specialised, often plainclothes police unit typically used for raids, surveillance or high-risk operations rather than routine beat policing — the specific unit Harish Rao alleged, without independent confirmation available to this paper, was used to carry out today’s alleged attack. 2026-09-15|ls-rfctlarr: Land acquisition by government: compensation rules under the RFCTLARR Act Land School — an original Deccan Ledger lesson · source & further reading: Land Acquisition by Government: Compensation Rules Under RFCTLARR Act — 1acre.in Key Highlights The RFCTLARR Act 2013 (in force 1 Jan 2014) replaced the colonial 1894 acquisition law. Compensation is a FORMULA: market value × rural/urban multiplier, then DOUBLED by a mandatory 100% solatium. Rural land multiplies 1.0–2.0 by distance from the urban centre (some states go higher); urban land sits at 1×. Crops, trees, wells, structures, severance damage and relocation costs are valued and ADDED. R&R benefits — housing, allowances, sometimes jobs or annuities — run alongside the cheque. An award that looks short can be formally challenged — and often is, successfully. What acquisition under RFCTLARR means The state’s power to compulsorily take private land for a public purpose against compensation fixed by law — fundamentally different from a voluntary sale. The 2013 Act was written to make the process humane, participative and transparent after 120 years of complaints about the 1894 law’s arbitrary payouts. It is the law behind every highway, ring road and industrial corridor — including the RRR’s. How compensation is calculated Step 1 — market value (Section 26): the Collector uses registered sale deeds of similar land from the prior three years, taking the HIGHEST of: the top comparable deed, the average of the top half of nearby deeds, or any consented negotiated amount. Step 2 — the multiplier: urban ×1; rural on a sliding 1.0–2.0 scale rising with distance from the urban centre — some states push rural factors higher still. Step 3 — solatium: 100% added on top, doubling the result. Step 4 — additions: structures, wells, trees, standing crops, severance and relocation. Definition — Solatium: a statutory 100% top-up recognising the sale was FORCED. On ₹50 lakh of assessed value it adds another ₹50 lakh — a real break from the 1894 law’s 30% cap. Definition — Severance: when a road takes a strip and leaves your remaining field cut off or oddly shaped, the damage to the REMAINDER is separately compensable — the head owners most often forget to claim. The multiplier bands at a glance Where the land sits Multiplier What that means with solatium Urban land 1.0× (some states allow more) ≈ 2× market value all-in Rural, near the urban centre 1.0–1.5× ≈ 2–3× market value Rural, far from the urban centre Up to 2.0× (higher in some states) ≈ 4× market value — and beyond where states enhance The 12% clock On top of everything, the Collector adds 12% per annum on market value, running from the Social Impact Assessment notification date until the award or possession — whichever comes first. A slow acquisition literally accrues interest for the owner; a mis-tracked SIA date silently underpays it. Rehabilitation and resettlement The Act’s Second Schedule adds a structured R&R package beyond cash: housing, transport and resettlement allowances, and in defined cases employment or annuity support — aimed at restoring livelihoods, not just replacing land value. Crucially it reaches beyond owners: agricultural labourers who worked the acquired fields can qualify without owning an inch. Consent rules for private and PPP projects Where private companies acquire for a public purpose: consent of at least 80% of affected families (70% for public-private partnerships), preceded by a Social Impact Assessment. Emergencies — disasters, critical defence — can invoke the fast-track and skip the SIA. Definition — Social Impact Assessment (SIA): the mandatory study of who is affected and how, done before ordinary acquisitions proceed. Its notification date also starts the 12% clock — a date worth recording the day it appears. Common mistakes in awards The urban multiplier applied to land that should be rural (understating badly); wells, trees and boundary structures skipped because they need a separate survey; the 12% amount miscalculated off the wrong SIA date; and livelihood-dependent families never told they qualify for R&R. None are exotic — all are line-checkable. How to challenge an award An undervalued award is not final because the Collector signed it: apply for a reference to the LARR Authority within the time limit, and appeal onward to the High Court if needed. Most successful challenges trace to exactly the mistakes above — wrong multiplier, missed assets, miscalculated solatium or interest. Check every line before accepting; enhancement is common enough to be a strategy. Example: A Shadnagar-belt farmer’s award used three-year-old registered deeds from a corridor where real prices had doubled — and applied a 1.2 multiplier where distance justified 1.8. Documented recent comparables plus the correct band, argued at reference, materially enhanced the award. The formula is fair; the INPUTS are where owners win or lose. Bottom line The framework is fair on paper; implementation slips are where money leaks — a wrong multiplier here, a missed well there, an SIA that should have happened and did not. Line-by-line checking before acceptance is not distrust; it is how the Act was designed to be used. For you: In the RRR belt every landowner conversation reaches “what if the road takes it?” The developer who can sketch this formula on a napkin — deeds-based value × multiplier + solatium + structures + 12% clock — becomes the most credible person the family has met. And for the land bank: parcels NEAR an alignment appreciate; parcels ON it get the formula — which pays better where registration culture is honest. 2026-09-15|ls-circle-vs-market: Circle rate vs market value vs guidance value: what decides stamp duty Land School — an original Deccan Ledger lesson · source & further reading: Circle Rate vs Market Value vs Guidance Value: What Decides Stamp Duty — 1acre.in Key Highlights Circle rate, guidance value, ready-reckoner rate, jantri — one government benchmark under four names. Market value is what buyer and seller actually agree — moving daily, unlike the fixed benchmark. Stamp duty is ALWAYS charged on the higher of the two. Declaring low never helps. In hot localities the official rate can lag the street by 30–50%; in dead pockets it can sit ABOVE the market. A big gap between price and benchmark triggers income-tax consequences for BOTH sides. What the three names actually mean All one thing: the minimum property value per unit area set by the state for an area — the government’s floor for duty purposes even when the declared price is lower. Delhi and UP say circle rate; Karnataka and Tamil Nadu say guidance value; Maharashtra says ready reckoner; Gujarat says jantri; Telangana says market value. The Income-tax Act calls all of them the stamp duty value and hangs real consequences on it. Why the two values rarely match The benchmark is committee-set and revised occasionally; the market moves with demand, supply and sentiment — sometimes daily. A slow official floor under live weather: the drift between them is not a flaw, it is the design. What matters is reading the SIZE and DIRECTION of the gap. How stamp duty gets calculated On the HIGHER figure, always. Market above benchmark (the usual case in premium pockets — official rates there can run 30–50% below street prices): duty follows your real price. Benchmark above your price (stagnant pockets, or a genuine bargain): duty follows the benchmark anyway — you pay tax on value that may not exist. A deed declared below benchmark can still be presented, but assessment proceeds on the notified value under the state’s law. The income-tax traps on big gaps Seller side — Section 50C: sell below the benchmark and your capital gains are computed AS IF you sold at the benchmark. Buyer side — Section 56(2)(x): buy meaningfully below it (beyond the tolerance band) and the shortfall is taxed as YOUR income. Registrar side — Section 47A-type scrutiny: under-declaration invites reference to valuation anyway. The “saving” from a low declared price returns as somebody’s tax notice — usually both somebodies’. Definition — Tolerance band: a small statutory cushion (commonly 10%) between declared price and benchmark within which the deeming provisions stay quiet. Near the line, the band decides everything — know the current figure. Example: Benchmark ₹1 crore, agreed price ₹80 lakh. Duty: charged on ₹1 crore. Seller’s capital gains: computed on ₹1 crore. Buyer: ₹20 lakh (beyond tolerance) taxable as income from other sources. One “bargain”, three tax events. A cash token preserves nothing; one small bank-routed payment can save the entire revision delta. Pre-negotiation checklist ☐ Applicable benchmark pulled from the official portal BEFORE agreeing a price. ☐ Compared against the asking price — the higher figure is your duty base; budget it now. ☐ The tolerance band checked when the price sits near the benchmark. ☐ Bank-routed token on the agreement date when a revision looms. ☐ Lawyer or registered valuer consulted when the numbers refuse to reconcile. Quick answers (FAQ) Can I register below circle rate? Present the deed, yes; escape assessment on the notified value, no. Why do the values diverge so much in some areas? Slow official revisions under a fast market — the gap is a growth signal as much as a tax nuisance. What if I sell below circle rate? Section 50C computes your gains at the benchmark anyway — price that in before agreeing. Bottom line Two prices, one rule: duty follows the higher. Check the benchmark before negotiating — at the registrar’s desk it is a surprise; at the negotiating table it is leverage. S5 · He briefed Prince Rahim on the 30,000-acre Bharat Future City project, noting that global companies including Amazon have already begun operations there The Chief Minister described Telangana’s Bharat Future City megaproject to the Prince, citing Amazon’s presence as evidence of real, already-arrived investment rather than a plan on paper. Plain English: This is the CM pivoting, in the same meeting, from a heritage-and-culture ask to an investment-and-industry pitch — using a concrete, already-operating anchor tenant (Amazon) as proof the project is real. Numbers: 30,000 acres; Amazon Web Services broke ground on a 202-acre hyperscale data centre there on 15 July 2026, tied to a reported ₹60,000 crore regional AWS commitment — the single most concrete, verifiable anchor-investment fact in this entire story. Plain English: The CM is not just asking for one-off help — he is trying to fold the Aga Khan relationship into the state’s biggest annual investment showcase, twelve weeks out. Mechanics: The first edition of this summit (December 2025) reportedly drew ₹5.75 lakh crore in prospective investment commitments — a scale that makes an invitation to a globally recognised figure like the Aga Khan a genuine reputational asset for the event’s second edition, not just a courtesy. Backstory: a former Telugu Desam Party leader who defected to Congress; ended the decade-long BRS/KCR government on taking office. Why in this story: personally hosted and drove both the heritage ask and the Future City pitch; both Musi Riverfront and Bharat Future City fall inside his own Municipal Administration & Urban Development portfolio, alongside General Administration and Law & Order, which is why he is personally hands-on with both projects rather than delegating to a minister. Power map: heads the state government; answers politically to the Congress high command in Delhi; his main rival is the opposition BRS. Source: cross-checked across multiple outlets on his 7 December 2023 swearing-in and portfolio allocation. Prince Rahim Aga Khan V What: the 5th Aga Khan and 50th hereditary Imam of the Nizari Ismaili Muslims, head of the Aga Khan Development Network (AKDN). Backstory: born 12 October 1971 in Geneva; studied comparative literature at Brown University and completed an executive programme at IESE Business School, Barcelona (2006); worked across AKDN’s Asia and Africa programmes and sat on several of its agency boards before becoming Aga Khan. His father, Aga Khan IV (Karim al-Husseini, the 49th Imam), died on 4 February 2025 in Lisbon; Prince Rahim was named successor in his father’s will, unsealed 5 February 2025 and confirmed publicly around 6 February 2025 — meaning he has held this role for barely seven months at the time of this meeting. He has direct prior hands-on experience with Indian heritage work: he co-inaugurated a new sunken site museum at Delhi’s Humayun’s Tomb on 29 July 2024, before becoming Aga Khan. Why in this story: the global figure whose network’s cooperation Telangana is actively courting for two live projects. Power map: leads AKDN’s network of development, culture and economic agencies worldwide; not a head of state or government, so his cooperation is philanthropic and institutional rather than a binding treaty commitment. Aga Khan Development Network (AKDN) & Aga Khan Trust for Culture (AKTC) What: AKDN is a network of private, non-denominational development agencies working in health, education, culture, rural development and economic development, mainly across Asia and Africa; AKTC is its heritage-and-culture-focused agency. Why in this story: the institutional body Telangana is asking to restore City College and Osmania Hospital. Backstory: AKTC’s flagship India project is the Humayun’s Tomb–Sunder Nursery–Nizamuddin Basti conservation and urban-renewal effort in Delhi, running since 2007 in partnership with the Archaeological Survey of India, restoring 60-plus monuments (about 20 of them sitting inside a UNESCO World Heritage site) and creating a 36-hectare public park now drawing 3 million-plus visitors a year — described as India’s first privately funded restoration of a World Heritage Site. In Hyderabad specifically, AKTC has restored the Qutb Shahi Tombs since 2013 in partnership with the Telangana government, with 80-plus monuments restored across at least two completed phases, a first phase publicly unveiled 10 March 2020, and ongoing oversight by AKTC CEO Ratish Nanda — though this relationship has not been friction-free, with reported litigation around a Qutb Shahi Tombs museum case that AKTC’s CEO has publicly called “abuse of judicial system.” Power map: AKDN/AKTC typically partners with national or state heritage and public-works departments, combining its own private funding with government land access and regulatory cooperation. Source: AKTC’s Delhi and Hyderabad project histories cross-checked across multiple independent outlets and aggregator summaries; primary AKDN sources were not directly fetchable this session. Why in this story: the megaproject the CM pitched to Prince Rahim as evidence of Telangana’s investment momentum. Numbers worth flagging: this paper found materially inconsistent acreage figures across otherwise credible outlets — a 30,000-acre core, a separately reported 13,500-acre “nucleus,” and a much larger roughly 1.9 lakh-acre wider planning footprint (about 765 sq km) — which should be checked against a primary government order before being treated as one settled number. Why in this story: this is the concrete compensation mechanism underneath the CM’s Amazon-anchored investment pitch, and the same 60:40-style ratio this paper has flagged before as Telangana’s emerging default alternative to forced cash acquisition. Source: cross-checked across Telangana Today, Deccan Herald, Hyderabad Mail and Telangana Jagruthi. Chandrashekar Rao, to lead Musi river rejuvenation; the project as currently scoped by the Congress government covers a 55km stretch from Gandipet to Gowrelly across 46 villages in three districts, with a proposed 50-metre buffer zone on both banks. Numbers worth flagging: reported budget figures span a wide, apparently non-contradictory but poorly reconciled range — ₹375 crore released for the wider Musi Development Project, ₹1,500 crore allocated in each of FY2024-25 and FY2025-26, a Phase-1 cost of ₹5,812.4 crore backed partly by a ₹4,100 crore Asian Development Bank loan, and an overall blueprint cited at ₹6,500–7,000 crore, against one outlet’s much larger ₹58,000 crore figure for the full multi-decade redevelopment — almost certainly different phases and time horizons rather than a genuine contradiction, but not clearly labelled as such in the coverage. Political history: KCR’s original 2017 direction was explicitly to rejuvenate the river without displacing bank-dwelling residents, a notably different posture from the current government’s buffer-zone-and-restoration approach. Power map: MRDCL remains the operative vehicle under the current Congress government, now with the CM personally driving the heritage-diplomacy angle. Source: cross-checked across Telangana Today, ThePrint, Deccan Chronicle and the live musi.telangana.gov.in government portal reference found in search results. City College, Hyderabad What: a heritage-listed government college on a 16-acre Musi-riverbank campus. Backstory: origins trace to an 1865 city school set up under the 6th Nizam, Mir Mahboob Ali Khan; formally established as Government City College in 1919 under the 7th Nizam, Osman Ali Khan; built in Indo-Saracenic style by Chief Engineer Nawab Khan Bahadur Mirza Akbar Baig, blending Ajanta/Ellora-style pillar-and-lintel elements, with a stone ground floor specifically built for flood resilience given its riverside site; carries a Grade-II heritage listing and sits adjacent to the Telangana High Court. Source: cross-checked across Telangana Today, Siasat and Munsif Daily coverage of the building’s centenary and World Monuments Watch listing. Osmania General Hospital (OGH) What: a heritage-listed government hospital built in 1919 under the 7th Nizam, Mir Osman Ali Khan; reported to be the first hospital in India to use chloroform and among India’s first super-speciality hospitals; carries a Grade II-B heritage listing under HMDA’s own heritage regulations. Why in this story: the second named building the CM wants restored, and the more politically loaded of the two — after Telangana’s 2014 formation, then-CM KCR visited OGH in 2015, after which a demolition proposal followed for a new 35.76-lakh-sq-ft hospital building, triggering years of sustained heritage-activist opposition; an independent structural committee later found the heritage block structurally stable and safe. The most recent reported government position is that the heritage in-patient block will be restored rather than demolished — making the CM’s ask to AKDN a visible signal that this reversal is now real policy, not just a paused controversy. Power map: sits under the state Health Department for operations, but its heritage-block fate has been a state-government political decision rather than a purely medical or engineering one. Source: cross-checked across The Quint, The News Minute, Siasat and Gulf News coverage spanning 2015 through the most recent restoration-not-demolition reporting. Organisers: coordinated by the state Industries Department, TGIIC (Telangana Industrial Infrastructure Corporation) and an “Invest Telangana” unit, under the Chief Secretary’s direct coordination. Power map: explicitly tied to the state’s longer-term “Telangana Rising 2047” economic vision. Source: cross-checked across Siasat, Newkerala, Indtoday, Telangana Today, Tribune India and PCCRealty-indexed coverage of both editions. Why in this story: the single most concrete, independently verifiable anchor-investment fact the CM could point to when pitching Future City to Prince Rahim — proof of committed capital rather than only a masterplan. Source: cross-checked across multiple outlets reporting the July 2026 groundbreaking. Publication bias notes ANI is a wire service whose India-politics copy frequently reproduces official government readouts close to verbatim, including for chief-ministerial engagements like this one — useful for speed and reach, but structurally more likely to carry only the government side of a story, exactly what happened here. Siasat and Munsif Daily are Hyderabad-based, Muslim-community-oriented outlets with a natural, non-partisan interest in Islamic-heritage and Ismaili-community stories, which likely explains their fuller pickup of the Aga Khan angle specifically. Telangana Today and Deccan Chronicle are mainstream regional dailies without a strong partisan lean on this particular story. The punjabkesari/TheHawk/Bhaskar Live cluster appears to share a single wire source for the Governor-meeting and reception details not found elsewhere, so this paper treats that cluster as one corroborating source, not several independent ones. Glossary — every term, simply AKDN (Aga Khan Development Network) A global network of private, non-religious-in-operation development agencies — covering health, education, culture and economic development — funded and led by the Aga Khan, the hereditary spiritual leader of the Shia Ismaili Muslim community. Example: it runs hospitals, schools and heritage-restoration projects across dozens of countries, including India. AKTC (Aga Khan Trust for Culture) AKDN’s specific heritage-and-culture-restoration arm. Example: it is the body that has been physically restoring Hyderabad’s Qutb Shahi Tombs since 2013 and Delhi’s Humayun’s Tomb complex since 2007. Ismaili Imam The hereditary spiritual leader of the Shia Ismaili Muslim community worldwide, a title passed down through a specific family line; Prince Rahim is the 50th person to hold this title, following his father Aga Khan IV’s death in February 2025. Example: unlike an elected religious post, this leadership passes by inheritance, decided by the previous Imam’s will. Future City Development Authority (FCDA) A dedicated Telangana government body created just to plan and approve development inside the 30,000-acre Bharat Future City area, similar in concept to how HMDA plans greater Hyderabad. Example: instead of a builder near Future City applying to HMDA for approval, they now apply to FCDA. Land pooling A land-assembly method where the government “pools” raw land from many owners, develops it with roads and infrastructure, then returns a share of the now-more-valuable developed plots back to the original owners instead of paying only cash. Example: at Bharat Future City, farmers reportedly get back 50–60% of their land as developed plots, plus cash, rather than being paid once in cash for raw farmland. RFCTLARR Section 10A exemption A provision letting the state exempt certain acquisitions — ones it judges urgent public-purpose projects — from some of the standard consent and Social Impact Assessment safeguards under India’s main land-acquisition law. Example: the Musi Riverfront project has been granted this exemption, which is part of why some affected landowners went to the High Court. Grade-II / Grade II-B heritage listing A tiered classification Indian heritage regulations use to rank how strictly a building must be protected — Grade-I is the strictest (virtually no alteration allowed), with Grade-II and its sub-grades allowing more flexibility for interior change while still protecting the exterior and structure. Example: both City College and Osmania Hospital carry Grade-II-level listings, which is why demolishing either draws automatic heritage scrutiny. World Monuments Watch A biennial list published by the New York-based World Monuments Fund, an independent international body, naming heritage sites worldwide it judges at risk and worth global attention — distinct from and independent of any Indian government body. Example: the Musi River Historic Buildings group, including City College and Osmania Hospital, made the 2025 list. Hyperscale data centre A very large, purpose-built facility housing thousands of servers for cloud computing, needing enormous amounts of electricity and water for cooling. Example: Amazon’s 202-acre data centre at Bharat Future City is exactly this kind of facility. MoU (Memorandum of Understanding) A signed statement of intent between two parties (here, a government and an investor) to pursue a project together — a serious signal of interest, but not yet a binding, funded contract. Example: the ₹5.75 lakh crore figure from the 2025 Telangana Global Summit is mostly MoU commitments, not money already spent. Buffer zone (river) A protective strip of land along a riverbank kept largely free of construction, to protect the river’s flow, flood path and water quality. Example: the Musi project proposes a 50-metre buffer zone on both banks along its 55km stretch. Night economy / night tourism Deliberately extending a district’s commercial and cultural activity into the evening and night hours — longer restaurant and market hours, lighting, cultural events and safety infrastructure — to generate additional economic activity from the same physical space. Example: the CM’s plan for evening activity along the restored Musi riverbank. SPV (Special Purpose Vehicle) A dedicated company or corporation set up by a government (or private group) to run one specific project, keeping its finances and management separate from the rest of the administration. Example: MRDCL is the SPV set up solely to run the Musi rejuvenation project. GSDP (Gross State Domestic Product) The total value of all goods and services produced within a state in a year — a state’s own version of a country’s GDP, used to measure its economic size and growth. Example: Telangana’s Global Summit is explicitly framed as a tool to grow the state’s GSDP by attracting outside investment. Both need external validation to be credible: Future City needs anchor investors like Amazon; Musi needs a credible international heritage partner like AKTC, which is precisely why a freshly-installed Aga Khan — only seven months into the role, still building his own diplomatic relationships — was a well-timed guest to pitch both to in one sitting. What a ten-year follower of Hyderabad heritage politics knows that a first-time reader doesn’t: the Osmania Hospital ask is not a neutral heritage gesture — it is a quiet, deliberate reversal of a demolition plan that consumed years of activist energy and bad press for the previous BRS government, now being turned into a positive international-partnership story by the party that inherited the controversy. And the Aga Khan relationship itself is not new diplomacy either — it is the state cashing in a decade-old, already-proven partnership (Qutb Shahi Tombs) to ask for a bigger favour. So what — stakes and consequences Who wins if this goes well: the Telangana government gains a credible, non-partisan international heritage validator for its Musi-corridor ambitions, plus another prestige name attached to December’s investment summit; Hyderabad’s heritage and tourism sector gains two more professionally restored landmark buildings; farmers under the Future City land-pooling scheme win if the promised 50–60% developed-plot return actually materialises at the values described. Who is at risk: farmers still contesting Future City’s greenfield-road acquisition in court, and Musi-area landowners contesting acquisition under the RFCTLARR Section 10A exemption — neither dispute is resolved by this meeting, and both continue in parallel to the diplomacy. Watch: (1) whether AKDN/AKTC formally commits to City College and Osmania Hospital restoration in the coming months — likely, given the decade-long Qutb Shahi precedent, but not yet confirmed by AKDN itself; (2) whether the December 7–9 Global Summit matches or exceeds 2025’s ₹5.75 lakh crore commitment figure — likely to be presented as a success regardless, so check the fine print on MoU-versus-actual-spend; (3) whether the Musi Section 10A High Court dispute reaches a substantive ruling before the summit — timing uncertain; (4) whether Future City’s land-pooling friction (the 43-day protests, the four-village court stays) escalates further or quietly resolves as more farmers receive their promised developed plots — a genuine open question given the CM’s own admission that timing “may be delayed.” What this means for you: for Hyderabad/Telangana real estate specifically — Bharat Future City’s land-pooling ratio (50–60% developed plots back to the original owner, plus cash reportedly up to ₹1.24 crore/acre near the Outer Ring Road) is a template worth studying closely, since it is Telangana’s clear preferred mechanism now for large land assemblies, and the same anchor-investment-reprices-everything-nearby effect this paper has flagged before at Kokapet will likely play out along the Srisailam Highway/Nagarjunasagar Road corridor as Future City matures. For business and investment more broadly — a government credibly restoring rather than demolishing its own heritage assets is a genuine, if slow-moving, positive signal for long-term city branding and heritage-adjacent property values near the Musi, distinct from and complementary to the industrial land story unfolding 40km south. The beginner mistake here is reading this purely as a ceremonial photo opportunity between a Chief Minister and a foreign royal. The sharper, expert read: this is Telangana using one afternoon and one well-timed, still-new international relationship to advance two of its largest active land stories at once — a heritage-restoration pitch that quietly closes out a decade-old demolition controversy, and an investment pitch for its biggest new land bank, both timed roughly twelve weeks ahead of the state’s marquee investment event. The 20% that gives you 100% — your keep-forever map Telangana is running two enormous, simultaneous land projects: a brand-new 30,000-acre city south of Hyderabad built on land-pooling and anchored by Amazon, and a heritage-led revival of the old city’s Musi riverfront anchored by two century-old Nizam-era buildings. To make both credible, the Chief Minister is courting outside validators — a hyperscale tech investor for one, a global heritage philanthropy network for the other — and he did both in a single meeting with a newly-installed Aga Khan, timed ahead of December’s investment summit. Neither project is free of friction: Future City still faces farmer litigation over its land-pooling acquisition, and Musi still faces a High Court dispute over its RFCTLARR exemption. For a Hyderabad land developer, both frontiers are worth tracking at once — the industrial-land frontier moving south along Future City’s highway corridors, and the heritage-value frontier reviving old-city land near a restored Musi. Track “anchor validators,” not just anchor investors — a credible non-political heritage or philanthropic partner can legitimise a government’s land story just as much as a corporate investment can. 2. A quiet demolish-to-restore reversal on one heritage asset is a leading indicator worth watching for similar assets nearby — policy shifts often move building by building before they become a stated rule. 3. Land-pooling ratios (roughly 50–60% developed plots back to the owner) are becoming Telangana’s default alternative to cash-only acquisition — learn the ratio now, because it will keep recurring in future mega-projects. 4. Big diplomatic or investment meetings are timed deliberately ahead of marquee events — read the calendar backwards from a known summit date to spot the sales pitches building up to it. 5. When official coverage of a diplomatic meeting is entirely one-sided, with no quote or statement from the visiting party, treat the whole readout as government messaging to be verified later, not as an agreed joint statement. 2026-09-16|ls-lal-dora: Lal Dora and Abadi Deh land: what buyers should know before investing Land School — an original Deccan Ledger lesson · source & further reading: Lal Dora and Abadi Deh Land: What Buyers Should Know Before Investing — 1acre.in Key Highlights Lal Dora and Abadi Deh both mean the village habitation area — terminology and legal treatment vary by state. These pockets historically grew OUTSIDE municipal building bylaws; newer planning rules and regularisation schemes may now overlay them. The trade-off is stark: big discounts in central locations, against unclear title history and limited legal protection. Buying, selling and registering IS possible — but only under conditions most casual buyers never check. The honest test of the paper: would a bank lend against it? What Lal Dora and Abadi Deh actually mean Around 1908, colonial revenue officers drew a literal red line — lal dora — on village maps, separating the lived-in area from the surrounding farmland, and revenue departments were told to maintain that distinction ever after. Abadi or Abadi Deh is the same zone described from the revenue-record side: the village habitation area itself. Whatever a document calls it, both point at one category — village residential space running on a different rulebook from both farmland and planned urban colonies. Why these areas sit outside normal property rules The defining feature: lal dora areas were historically EXEMPT from building and zoning regulations — houses rose for generations without permits or codes. So a decades-old house inside the line is not automatically an illegal structure; it operates under a genuinely different, older framework. That is meaningfully different from unauthorised construction in a regular colony — even though the two can look identical from the street. The real trade-off As cities swallowed villages, these pockets became affordable islands beside prime urban zones — Delhi’s Chhatarpur and Munirka belts are the famous examples; Hyderabad’s old village cores inside GHMC are the local cousins. The attraction is price and position. The pitfalls run equally deep: ownership is typically NOT formally documented, structures lack sanction, and the legal safeguards a normal buyer expects — clean registration, bank finance, municipal recourse — thin out or vanish. Example: Two plots on the same road: the titled one at ₹60,000/sq yd, the abadi one at ₹35,000. The ₹25,000 gap is the market pricing three questions — can ownership be proven, can a plan be sanctioned, can your eventual buyer get a loan? The discount is not a bargain; it is a price tag on missing paper. Can you actually buy, sell and register this land? Yes — conditionally, not like a standard transaction. The seller needs verifiable proof of ownership through inheritance records, mutation, or prior registered transfers; some jurisdictions require approval from the tahsildar, SDM or municipal authority before the sale; and the property must be free of litigation and encroachment claims. Registration follows the same conditional path — possible under the state’s village-land policies, never automatic. In practice, sales within the family or village move smoothly; sales to outside third parties — especially where urban expansion looms — draw far more scrutiny. Red flags Broken ownership chains — generations of informal transfers leave gaps that surface exactly when you try to resell. No approved building plans — any construction dispute loses its normal municipal resolution path. Thin municipal services — affecting livability and resale both. Survey-scheme errors — where new village-survey programmes (like SVAMITVA property cards) apply, an uncorrected draft entry can complicate mutation, inheritance and sale. Definition — SVAMITVA: a central scheme using drone surveys to map village habitation areas and issue property cards — the first formal ownership paper many abadi properties have ever had. Where it has run, the card is a key verification document; where the draft entry is wrong, fixing it comes before buying. Lal Dora property vs regular freehold Aspect Lal Dora / Abadi property Regular freehold property What it is Long-standing village habitation under revenue records Formally registered under standard municipal and land law Source of ownership Possession + informal transfer history; revenue records A clear registered title chain via the SRO Building rules Historic exemption; newer overlays vary Full sanction regime applies Best suited to Buyers prioritising low entry cost and location over certainty Buyers prioritising finance-ability and resale liquidity True cost Cheap upfront; hidden cost in blocked loans and resale friction Full market price; fewer downstream complications Is it a reliable investment? The structural limit: banks lend against clear title, and lal dora properties usually cannot show one — so most lenders decline. That constraint follows the property forever: your future buyer faces the same wall, which caps resale liquidity. The bull case some investors run — regularisation catching up and prices converging with authorised areas — is a bet on future POLICY, not a guaranteed outcome. Price it as speculation, because that is what it is. Verification checklist ☐ Obtain the Lal Dora / Abadi certificate from the revenue department — remembering it is NOT a title deed. ☐ Trace the ownership chain as far as records go; hunt for gaps and rival claims. ☐ Check whether an active regularisation scheme covers the property. ☐ Search for litigation and encroachment complaints. ☐ Verify the SVAMITVA/property-card entry on the official portal where the survey has run. Quick answers (FAQ) Is buying lal dora property legal? Yes, under conditions — verified ownership, sometimes official approval, no disputes. Can I get a home loan on it? Usually not — the missing standard records stop most lenders. Can it be registered like regular property? Conditionally, under state village-land policies — not automatically. What is the lal dora certificate? A revenue-department confirmation of the property’s location and the holder’s connection to it — useful, but never equivalent to title. Bottom line Real affordability, real location advantage, real documentation gap — all three at once. Verifying the certificate, the chain, and the regularisation status before buying is what separates a calculated bet from an avoidable dispute. For you: When assembling land near old village cores, map the red line FIRST: a parcel straddling it carries two legal regimes in one deal, and your clean layout can inherit one permanently unclear corner. 2026-09-16|ls-plot-safe: How to check if a plot is legally safe to buy Land School — an original Deccan Ledger lesson · source & further reading: How to Check If a Plot Is Legally Safe to Buy in India — 1acre.in Key Highlights With plots, nobody upstream has checked anything — legal verification is entirely your job. The 30-year title chain proves a seller CAN sell; the latest deed alone proves little. An EC only catches REGISTERED transactions — deposit-of-deeds mortgages and court cases need separate searches. ULPIN, the 14-digit parcel ID, catches an altered survey number. The whole drill costs a few thousand rupees; a disputed title costs years. Why verification matters MORE for plots Buy a flat and a builder, a lender and usually a RERA registration have each done a slice of checking before you arrived. Buy a plot and NONE of that happened. Vacant land also carries a messier past — split among siblings after a death, handed around inside a family, converted from farmland years ago with paperwork that never caught up. Every one of those moments is a place a defect could have entered the record and stayed. Verification is finding them BEFORE you pay. Start with the title chain, not the latest deed A sale deed tells you who holds the land — nothing about whether the person BEFORE them had any right to hand it over, and that gap is where most disputes begin. Ask for the Mother Deed, then trace every sale, gift, partition and inheritance forward. Thirty years is the working standard — your bank will stop at a 13-year EC, but that is a LENDING threshold, not a title standard. Inheritance deserves special attention: in ancestral property every coparcener holds a share and ALL must sign; a guardian selling a minor’s share needs court permission; one absent signature can unwind a sale a decade later. The EC catches less than you think Owning land and being FREE to sell it are separate things. Pull the EC yourself from the sub-registrar for the full 30 years — in most southern states a clean result returns as Form 16, while Form 15 lists whatever is registered against the property. Now the part sellers rarely volunteer: the EC shows only REGISTERED transactions. A mortgage created by depositing title deeds with a bank often never reaches the register; neither will an unregistered sale agreement, an oral family partition, or unpaid dues. So run two more searches: the e-courts portal for litigation on the survey number, and the state land-records portal for the latest revenue record — comparing owner name, survey number, extent and classification against the deed. Any mismatch: investigate before proceeding. Definition — Equitable mortgage (deposit of title deeds): a loan secured by simply handing the original deeds to the bank — legally valid, and frequently invisible on the EC. It is why “show me the ORIGINALS” is a due-diligence question, not rudeness: a seller without originals may have a banker holding them. Zoning, conversion and RERA: what you can actually build Start with the master plan — how is the parcel classified? Farmland once? Ask for the conversion ORDER and the fee receipt; a seller’s assurance is not a document. Then RERA: larger plotted developments generally must register, and an unregistered one becomes a problem YOU inherit. Then who may buy at all — agricultural-land eligibility varies by state. And layout approval sits with the planning authority — verified separately, on its portal, by its LP number. Legal checks vs physical checks Check What it proves Where you get it 30-year title chain The seller’s right to sell Sub-registrar copies + your advocate EC (30 years) Registered loans/claims Sub-registrar / online e-courts search Pending litigation ecourts portal, by survey number/parties Revenue record State’s view of owner + classification State land-records portal (Dharani in TG) Licensed survey Ground matches paper Surveyor on site ULPIN check Parcel identity not altered State records where rolled out Walk the boundary before you pay A licensed surveyor measures the plot against the deed AND the revenue record — paper and ground drift apart more often than buyers expect. Where your state has rolled it out, check ULPIN — the 14-digit parcel ID under the national land-records programme, sometimes called Bhu-Aadhaar — which nails the parcel’s identity against an altered or misquoted survey number. Warning signs of a risky purchase Survey numbers that DISAGREE across deed, revenue record and EC. A PoA sale where the PoA is unregistered or does not explicitly authorise sale. A seller who produces photocopies every time and originals never. Land on a prohibited-property list — the Sub-Registrar will refuse it until the restriction resolves. And resistance to a NEWSPAPER NOTICE: publishing one inviting objections before closing is ordinary practice — a seller who argues against it is telling you something. Example: The newspaper notice is the cheapest trap-detector in the kit: ₹3,000, one column, fifteen days. A silent fortnight closes the deal with confidence; a phone call from an unknown “co-owner” just saved you the whole purchase price. Quick answers (FAQ) How far back should the chain go? 30 years. Does the EC show every loan? No — registered ones only; deposit-of-deeds mortgages hide. Do all plots need RERA? Larger plotted developments generally yes; small ones may be exempt — check the threshold. Is patta proof of ownership? Supporting evidence only. Do I need a lawyer for a small plot? Yes — defect risk does not scale down with plot size; a small plot with a bad title is 100% bad. Bottom line Chain, EC, courts, record, zoning, survey — six checks, each catching what the others miss, none substituting for the rest. A few thousand rupees of verification against years of litigation: the cheapest insurance in real estate. For you: This lesson is the customer’s-eye view of everything your school has covered — use it as your master checklist template. Better: run the six checks on your OWN ventures and publish the results as a buyer pack. In a market where verification is “entirely the buyer’s job”, the developer who does the job FOR the buyer owns the trust premium. Glossary — every term, simply Section 22A (prohibited list) A legal power letting a government Sub-Registrar refuse to register a sale, gift or transfer of certain categories of land — meant to stop illegal sale of government, temple/Wakf, or ceiling-surplus land. Example: if your survey number is on this list, you cannot register a sale deed for it at all, even if you genuinely own it, until it is cleared. Poramboke land Government-owned land set aside for common or public use — grazing grounds, roads, drains, village ponds — that was never meant to be privately owned. Example: a portion of poramboke land wrongly enclosed by a private fence decades ago can never be legally sold, regardless of how long someone has possessed it. Assigned land Government land formally handed over to a specific landless or poor beneficiary (often SC/ST) under conditions that typically prohibit resale. Example: a farmer given five acres of assigned land in the 1970s land-reform era technically still cannot legally sell it today in most cases, even if buyers are willing. Ceiling-surplus land Land a landowner was made to give up because they held more than the legal maximum (“ceiling”) allowed under land-reform law, which the government then redistributes or retains. Example: this is one of the categories Section 22A protects from unauthorised resale. Patta land Privately owned land with a formal government ownership record (a patta, or title document) in the current owner’s name — the category the 22A crisis wrongly swept up thousands of examples of. Example: a family that has held clean, registered patta land for generations found itself unable to register a sale simply because its survey number matched one on the prohibited list. Survey number A unique identifying number assigned to a specific parcel of land in government revenue records, used to track ownership, classification and boundaries. Example: the 22A crisis often happened because an entire survey number was blanket-marked prohibited, even when only part of it was genuinely government land and the rest was legitimately private. Dharani The BRS government’s land-records and registration portal (2020–2025), replaced by Bhu Bharati. Example: the flawed 22A tagging at the root of this crisis originated on Dharani and carried over when records migrated to the new system. Bhu Bharati Telangana’s current land-records and registration portal, launched by the Congress government in 2025. Example: this is the system property owners check today to see if their land is flagged prohibited. IGRS (Inspector General of Registration & Stamps) The state body overseeing property registration and stamp duty collection through local Sub-Registrar Offices, and which maintains its own separate list of urban 22A-prohibited properties. Example: a property can show as clear on Bhu Bharati but still be blocked at the Sub-Registrar’s office because of a mismatched IGRS entry. HMDA / DTCP layout approval Formal permission from the Hyderabad Metropolitan Development Authority (for Hyderabad-area land) or the Directorate of Town and Country Planning (for land elsewhere in the state) confirming a subdivided plotted layout meets planning rules. Example: a layout can be HMDA-approved for years and still have individual plot registrations blocked today if its survey number got wrongly caught in the 22A sweep. Regularisation A formal government process that legalises land use, construction or a layout that was never originally approved, usually against payment of a fee or penalty. Example: GO 118 and GO 59 are both regularisation routes, for different categories of land occupation. Simultaneous registration-and-regularisation A proposed process change letting a property owner register their sale deed and regularise their unauthorised land status in one combined step, instead of finishing regularisation first and registering only afterward. Example: today this is two sequential queues; the promised system would merge them into one. GO 118 A specific Telangana government order regularising long-standing, low- and middle-income family land occupations across 44 identified colonies, 36 of them in the LB Nagar constituency. Example: a family that has lived in one of these colonies for decades without full paperwork can apply under GO 118 to formalise their status. GO 59 A separate regularisation order letting non-BPL (above-poverty-line) occupants of certain government land regularise their holding by paying its market value. Example: roughly 1.22 lakh applications under this route are currently pending clearance. Urban Land Ceiling (ULC) An older category of law that capped how much urban land any one person or entity could hold, with surplus land liable to government acquisition; though the central ULC Act was repealed nationally years ago, land still nominally affected by old ULC proceedings remains a live administrative category in some states. Example: the CM’s promised new “ULC lands policy” is meant to finally resolve leftover cases like this. Special Investigation Team (SIT) A team specially constituted, usually from police or investigative officers, to look into one particular case with focused attention rather than as part of a general caseload. Example: some outlets described the KCR-farmhouse probe as an SIT; others described a Collector-led fact-finding team instead — this paper could not confirm which is accurate. Fact-finding team A less formal administrative inquiry, typically led by a district-level revenue official like a Collector, to establish facts before any formal legal or investigative action is taken. Example: the alternative description used for the same 30-day Erravelli probe in some coverage.
