Kishan Reddy (BJP) demands a judicial inquiry ~30 Aug–Sep 2026 Ponguleti claims 98% of booked-slot registrations cleared 7–11 Sep 2026 Harish Rao presses the issue in the Assembly; seeks Ponguleti’s resignation (11 Sep) 12 Sep 2026 Ponguleti gives Assembly figures: 1.0205 crore acres listed, down from 1.0253 crore in Dec 2023 15 Sep 2026 KTR, in Delhi, demands a judicial probe and alleges a 30% delisting “commission” racket 16 Sep 2026 CM announces the committee, new policies, and orders the KCR-family land probe — today’s story The deeper forces underneath this single Assembly sitting: Telangana has spent two land-record migrations in five years (Dharani in 2020, Bhu Bharati in 2025) trying to digitise and clean up a records system that is, underneath the software, still built on decades of overlapping, sometimes contradictory paper-era entries. Each migration inherits the last one’s errors and adds new administrative friction of its own — the 22A crisis is best understood not as one government’s mistake but as the latest surfacing of a much older, structural problem: India’s land records have never been fully clean, and every attempt to modernise them exposes another layer of the mess rather than erasing it. What a ten-year follower of Telangana land politics knows that a first-time reader doesn’t: this is not the first time a Telangana government has announced a “high-level committee” to fix a land-records crisis — Ponguleti’s own 18 August committee was the first attempt this year alone, and it did not stop the crisis from reaching the Assembly floor a month later. The pattern of announcing committees, toll-free numbers and clearance percentages, without a single named, dated, independently-auditable outcome, is itself a recurring feature of how this particular crisis has been managed so far — worth remembering when judging whether this newest committee will be different. So what — stakes and consequences Who wins if this goes well: any owner of genuinely clean patta land currently frozen by a wrongly-tagged survey number gets a faster, simpler path back to registrability; developers sitting on HMDA/DTCP-approved layouts with stuck registrations get relief within the promised week; families in GO 118 and GO 59 backlogs finally see movement on years-old applications. Who is at risk either way: genuinely disputed government, assigned or ceiling-surplus land stays permanently prohibited under this framework, so anyone hoping a general amnesty might quietly cover a genuinely encroached parcel will be disappointed; and the KCR family, regardless of the probe’s eventual finding, faces a public 30-day process that is itself politically costly no matter the outcome. Watch: (1) whether the promised authorised-layout guidelines actually land within the stated week (by roughly 23 September) — the single most concrete, date-checkable promise in this story; (2) whether the new high-level committee gets named members and a public first meeting, or remains an announcement without an institution behind it, as happened with Ponguleti’s August committee; (3) whether the 30-day KCR-family land probe (due mid-October) produces a public report, and whether its findings on the 388-acre and 439-acre figures hold up; (4) whether Kavitha’s specific rebuttal on her 37.26-acre allegation is ever formally tested against records. What this means for you: for Hyderabad/Telangana real estate specifically — if you or anyone you deal with has a plot inside an HMDA/DTCP-approved layout that has been stuck in the 22A freeze, the next ten days are worth watching closely for the promised guidelines; more broadly, this crisis is a reminder that even long-registered, seemingly clean patta land is not immune to a records-migration error, so keeping your own EC, revenue record and Bhu Bharati status cross-checked and current is now a genuinely higher-value habit than it was two years ago. For business and investment more broadly — a state government publicly ordering a probe into the opposition leader’s own family land, on the same day it promises regulatory relief to ordinary owners, is a useful real-time example of how directly land administration and political combat intertwine in Telangana; expect land-policy announcements to keep arriving bundled with political messaging rather than as clean, standalone regulatory news. The beginner mistake here is treating the committee-and-guidelines announcement as good news already delivered. The sharper, expert read: this is the government’s third or fourth distinct promise on this crisis since August (the toll-free line, the first committee, the 98%-clearance claim, and now this), and the single most testable of today’s promises — guidelines within a week — had not materialised as of this research. Track the date, not the announcement. The 20% that gives you 100% — your keep-forever map Telangana’s two land-record digitisation efforts in five years (Dharani, then Bhu Bharati) each inherited and carried forward the last system’s errors, and this year that surfaced as a Section 22A crisis wrongly freezing thousands of clean private plots alongside legitimately prohibited government, forest and assigned land. On 16 September, under mounting opposition pressure, the CM announced a new committee, a simultaneous registration-regularisation system, and authorised-layout guidelines within a week — while, in the same sitting, ordering a 30-day probe into whether the opposition leader’s own family holds undisclosed government land. Neither promise is yet delivered; both are dates worth marking on a calendar rather than news to file away as resolved. Dharani (2020) tags survey numbers prohibited, sometimes wrongly, sometimes whole-number-blanket -> migrates into Bhu Bharati (2025) as-is -> Aug 2026: crisis goes public, thousands of clean patta owners locked out of registration -> Ponguleti apologises, first committee, toll-free line (18 Aug) -- doesn't stop the political fight -> BRS presses in Assembly (7-12 Sep), KTR escalates nationally (15 Sep, "30% commission") -> 16 Sep: CM announces NEW committee + regularisation policy + guidelines "within a week" -> in the SAME speech, CM orders 30-day probe into KCR family land (388 / 439 acres) -> land-policy relief and political land-combat now bundled in one news cycle -> for a developer: watch the ~23 Sep guideline date, not the announcement itself Five transferable lessons: 1. A records-migration inherits its predecessor’s errors by default — whenever a government announces a new digital land or registration system, treat the transition period itself, not just the old system, as a fresh source of risk. 2. Track dated, testable promises separately from announcements — “a committee will be formed” and “guidelines will be issued within a week” are different categories of claim, and only the second has a date you can actually hold the government to. 3. When two very different numbers describe what sounds like the same thing (388 acres vs 439 acres here), check whether they are actually measuring different scopes before assuming a contradiction. 4. Political land disputes and land-policy relief often arrive in the same news cycle by design — a government fighting a regulatory-failure story finds it useful to simultaneously go on the offensive elsewhere; read both halves, but don’t let the political half distract from the regulatory half that actually affects your transactions. 5. Repeated committees on the same unresolved problem (this is at least the second in a month) are themselves a signal — track whether a new committee gets named members and a public output, or simply becomes the next in a series of announcements without institutional follow-through. 2026-09-17|ls-agri-to-resi: How to convert agricultural land to residential property Land School — an original Deccan Ledger lesson · source & further reading: How to Convert Agricultural Land to Residential Property in India — 1acre.in Key Highlights Agricultural land must usually be CONVERTED before residential construction is legal on it. Approval depends on the master plan, zoning and state land-use law — not on willingness to pay. Green belts, protected agricultural zones, forests and environmentally restricted land often cannot be converted at any price. The order comes from the competent planning or revenue authority, with documents and a site inspection. Buying land “already converted”? Verify the order is VALID and unexpired — a lapsed conversion reverts the land to agricultural. Agricultural vs residential land: the real difference Agricultural land is meant for farming, and its registration, taxation and transfer rules all follow from that purpose. Converted land costs more per square yard — but it carries the legal standing you need to build, raise a home loan, or sell to someone who will. The premium is not decoration; it is the difference between a plot and a field. What the law actually requires Start with the MASTER PLAN, not the application form — this is where most people get the sequence backwards. Formal conversion approval from the competent planning or revenue authority is required before agricultural land can legally host residential construction, and that approval must align with the master plan zone, the zoning classification, and the state’s land-revenue statutes. Two hard truths follow: where the plan already designates the land residential, conversion is not discretionary — it should be granted; where the plan marks the zone green belt, forest or agriculture-protection, conversion is simply NOT AVAILABLE. No fee fixes a blocking zone. Definition — Master plan: the government’s long-term land-use map for a region — which areas are residential, commercial, industrial, green. In conversion matters it outranks everything: the plan decides what is possible; the application only executes it. Documents you will need ☐ Title deed and the 30-year chain of title. ☐ Updated land-record extract — registered deed, 7/12, patta, or your state’s equivalent (pattadar passbook in Telangana). ☐ Survey sketch, master plan extract, and an EC. ☐ NOCs from agriculture, town planning, forest or water-resources departments where applicable. Getting the file right the FIRST time saves months of back-and-forth. The step-by-step process 1) Pull the master plan extract; confirm the zone permits residential use. 2) File the application with the revenue or planning authority for your state and zone. 3) Pay the conversion fee — assessed on area, location and proposed use. 4) Site inspection: an official verifies the land matches the application. 5) Receive the conversion order; the land record is updated. 6) READ THE CONDITIONS on pages two and three — they decide whether the order stays alive. 7) Apply for building-plan sanction from the local body before any construction starts — conversion permits the USE; the sanction permits the BUILDING. Common challenges The zone itself blocking the change — no application can convert green-belt, forest or protection-zone land. Delays or rejection from incomplete files, missing NOCs, or mismatches found at inspection. And the quiet one: conversion orders that LAPSE because construction timelines or conditions went unmet — leaving the land agricultural despite a framed approval on the wall. Example: A buyer pays a premium for a “converted” plot with a 2019 order. Condition 4 on page two required construction to commence within three years; nothing was built. The order lapsed in 2022 — the parcel is agricultural again, and the premium bought paper. One reading of the conditions would have repriced the deal. Best practices before you start Master plan zone first; then road access, water and soil. A short consultation with a local surveyor costs less than discovering a blocking issue after the fee is paid. And engage someone who knows THAT district’s revenue office — procedures genuinely differ between neighbouring districts. Quick answers (FAQ) Is conversion mandatory before building a house? Generally yes — building on unconverted agricultural land invites demolition and denies you sanction, loans and clean resale. Who approves? The competent revenue or planning authority (RDO/Collector-side in Telangana, with HMDA/DTCP layers for layouts). Can any land be converted if I pay? No — the zone decides; money cannot move a green belt. Does an order expire? Yes — it is conditional and time-bound; verify validity when buying “converted” land. Can NRIs apply? For land they lawfully hold (e.g. inherited) — subject to the same zoning rules. If I skip conversion? Unauthorised use: penalties, demolition risk, no sanction, and a discount when you sell. Bottom line Conversion is a sequence, not a fee: zone first, statute second, payment last — and the order you receive is a living document with conditions and an expiry. Read it like a contract, because it is one. For you: This is the machinery of your margin: farmland in, NA/DTCP-approved plots out. Your edge is the SEQUENCE discipline — verify the master-plan zone before the land is even priced, and when buying “converted” parcels from others, audit the order’s conditions and dates like a bank would. Against apartments, gold or index funds, farmland trades liquidity for tangibility and long-horizon stability. Who may buy still depends on the state — some restrict to agriculturists, others are open. Water, title and zoning decide value over a decade — not any brochure’s return chart. Why farmland near cities became an investment category Buying farmland used to mean buying agriculture. Near an expanding city it increasingly means buying the city’s own future: infrastructure, road connectivity, industrial corridors and outward urban growth pull nearby rural land up with them. This is precisely Hyderabad’s ORR story — and the bet now being placed along the RRR belt. What returns to realistically expect Two separate engines. Appreciation — corridor-driven, the reliable thesis in genuine growth belts, though wildly location-dependent. Crop income — the unreliable bonus: pitches built on projected yields have a long history of underdelivering. The safe frame: appreciation is the thesis, crop income the tip — never the reverse. Example: A managed-farmland brochure promises 12% yearly “returns” — quietly built as 4% “guaranteed” farm income + 8% assumed appreciation. The farm income needs rain, labour, prices and an honest operator, every year. Strip it out and ask: is the land, at this price, in this corridor, a good buy on appreciation alone? If not, the crops will not save it. Who can legally buy farmland State law decides: some states restrict purchases to registered farmers or those meeting background/income tests; others — Telangana among them — are open to any buyer. Exemptions and family-eligibility routes exist where restrictions apply. The three ways to hold it Freehold — full control, but labour, crop planning and selling produce are your problem; suits owners with farming knowledge or a trusted local partner. Fractional — a small group pools funds for a bigger parcel, sharing cost and risk, at the price of needing agreement among partners. Fully managed — an operator runs everything for a fee and remits revenue; convenient, but you are underwriting the OPERATOR as much as the land. Whichever model: the land’s own title must be registered in identifiable names, not lost inside a scheme. What to check before you commit Papers and position outrank projections. Water : a cheap plot with no reliable source is not a bargain, it is a liability — borewells genuinely run dry in rocky belts, and waterless land carries a different risk profile at any price. Then the full drill : title deed and chain, EC, survey boundaries, land classification, zoning status. Access : legal road access, not a neighbour’s goodwill. Definition — Water security: year-round availability from borewell, canal or tank — checked in summer, not monsoon. It is the single physical factor that most separates farmland that holds value from farmland that stalls. Red flags Ownership disputes and murky chains; wrong survey boundaries; missing ECs; classification problems; water scarcity; zoning restrictions the seller forgot to mention; and — the soft one — return projections that only work if everything goes right. Any one of these changes the price; several together change the decision. How farmland compares with other assets Asset Typical return profile Liquidity Best suited for Managed farmland Varies — appreciation + uncertain crop income Low Long-term diversification, not quick gains Urban apartment ~6–9% (rent + appreciation) Medium Income plus moderate growth Gold ETF ~6–8% High Liquid store of value Index fund ~10–14%, volatile High (daily) Long-term growth, risk-tolerant money Farmland does not compete on liquidity or explosive upside. It competes on stability, inflation resistance, and being a real thing you can stand on, gift, and pass down. Is it reliable? The structure is sound — patient holders in genuine corridors have done very well. Failures follow one pattern: an unchecked title, an unreliable water source, or crop income that never arrived. None of these are hidden risks; all are checkable before the advance. Checking them is standard practice, not paranoia. Pre-purchase checklist ☐ Eligibility under the state’s purchase rules. ☐ Title deed + ownership history verified. ☐ Fresh EC. ☐ Survey boundaries and extent confirmed on the ground. ☐ Classification and zoning verified. ☐ Year-round water availability checked. ☐ Road connectivity and access assessed. ☐ Holding model chosen deliberately (freehold / fractional / managed). ☐ Crop projections discounted; appreciation case evaluated on its own. Quick answers (FAQ) Is farmland near a city a good investment now? In real corridors, at farmland-honest prices, on an appreciation thesis — yes, as patient money. Managed vs unmanaged? Managed buys convenience and adds operator risk; unmanaged buys control and adds workload. Bottom line Buy the corridor, not the crop chart. Water, title and zoning decide the decade; the brochure decides nothing. Glossary Assigned land — Land the government formally handed to a specific (usually landless or poor) beneficiary under conditions, typically banning resale. Example: a Dalit family given assigned land decades ago cannot legally sell it to a private buyer even today, no matter how much the land has appreciated. Patta land — Privately owned land with a formal government-recorded title. Example: a plot with a clean pattadar passbook in the owner’s name that can be freely sold, mortgaged or inherited. Government land — Land the state owns outright, with no private title ever validly issued over it. Example: a stretch of forest or grazing land that appears in revenue records as belonging to the government, not any individual. Fact-finding team (Collector-led) — A team of revenue officials a District Collector assembles to physically verify facts on the ground — here, whether specific survey numbers inside a property are government, assigned or patta land. Unlike a police investigation, it has no power to arrest; it only produces a report for the government to act on. Survey number — The unique identifying number revenue records assign to each demarcated parcel of land, going back generations. Example: when officials say “388 acres across specific survey numbers,” they mean specific, individually numbered parcels, not a rough estimate of total area. Election affidavit — A sworn, legally binding declaration every Indian election candidate must file listing their assets, liabilities and criminal cases; making a false declaration is a punishable offence. Example: Kavitha anchoring her defence to what her affidavits state is a bet that those sworn numbers will hold up. CBI (Central Bureau of Investigation) — India’s premier federal investigating agency, distinct from a state police force, typically brought in for politically sensitive or interstate cases via a court order or government reference. Example: Kavitha wants the CBI, not Telangana’s own state police or revenue department, to check the CM’s claims — because the CBI is not under the state government’s day-to-day control. Court-monitored audit — A financial or asset review conducted under a High Court or Supreme Court’s active oversight, rather than by a government department alone. Example: KTR’s offer of a court-monitored 1954–2026 audit would mean judges, not Revanth Reddy’s own officials, ultimately vouch for the process’s fairness. Gajwel constituency — The Telangana Assembly seat KCR has represented for years, located in Siddipet district; Erravelli falls within it. Example: a probe into land inside a rival’s own home constituency carries an extra political charge beyond an ordinary land dispute elsewhere. 2026-09-18|ls-patta-vs-deed: The real difference between patta, sale deed, and title deed Land School — an original Deccan Ledger lesson · source & further reading: The Real Difference Between Patta, Sale Deed, and Title Deed — 1acre.in Key Highlights Patta vs sale deed = tax record vs transfer of ownership. Only one moves title. A patta SUPPORTS an ownership claim; it does not create one — no court treats it as proof of title. “Title deed” is not a document at all — it is the category term for the registered instruments behind your ownership chain. When patta and deed disagree, the registered deed generally prevails — but the mismatch still blocks resale and loans until mutation fixes it. Revenue records wear different names across states; the administrative job is the same. Why the difference matters Three documents, three different questions. A patta answers: whose name does the revenue department hold against this survey number? A sale deed answers: did a legal transfer occur? A title deed answers: is the ownership chain behind that transfer clean? Confusing them is not a vocabulary slip — it decides which paper a buyer trusts when the papers conflict. What a patta records — and does not Issued by the revenue department, not a court: landholder’s name, extent, survey number. Its function is administrative — tax assessment and revenue tracking. Real uses: banks ask for it before lending against land; it supports a possession claim in a dispute; it confirms the parcel exists in state records under a stated name. What it does NOT do is create ownership — courts have consistently held revenue records are evidence of possession, not conclusive proof of title. (Telangana’s pattadar passbook, Maharashtra’s 7/12, Karnataka’s RTC — different names, same administrative job.) Why the registered sale deed carries the most weight The deed is the instrument that MOVES ownership; registration is what gives it force. Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act: any sale of immovable property worth ₹100 or more requires a registered instrument — which, at that threshold, means EVERY land sale in India; the folk belief that registration only applies above some higher value is simply wrong. Section 17 of the Registration Act makes the registration compulsory; and Section 49 delivers the consequence — an unregistered document that required registration cannot even be received as evidence of the transaction. Registration also feeds the public record every future EC draws from: the paper trail exists because the statute compels it. “Title deed” is a category, not a certificate No office in India issues a document titled “title deed”. The term describes whichever registered instruments TOGETHER establish you hold the property free of competing claims: your registered sale deed plus the deeds behind it — earlier sales, partitions, gifts — back to the Mother Deed that first established ownership. When a bank asks for “title documents”, it wants that SET. And a title deed’s strength is borrowed: exactly as strong as the registered instruments standing behind it, and no stronger. Definition — Mother Deed: the earliest traceable document that established ownership of the parcel — the root of the chain. Every later deed inherits its validity from this root; a defect there flows down through everything. The three compared Aspect Patta / revenue record Sale deed Title deed Issued by Revenue department Executed by parties, registered at SRO Not issued — the chain of registered instruments Function Tax + revenue tracking Transfers ownership Establishes the clean chain Legal weight Evidence of possession The operative instrument As strong as the deeds composing it Buyer’s use Cross-check + loan requirement The document you actually acquire by What your advocate traces 30 years back When patta and deed disagree The registered deed generally prevails — ownership does not wait for the revenue record to catch up. But the mismatch still does practical damage: a patta in the previous owner’s name stalls your RESALE (the next buyer’s advocate flags it), stalls a LOAN (the bank matches patta name against deed), and can send tax demands to the wrong person for years. The correction is MUTATION: file with the revenue authority, attaching the registered deed, EC, identity proof and the previous revenue record. Fix it because it blocks your next transaction — not because your ownership depends on it. Example: A buyer holds a clean 2021 registered deed but never mutated; the passbook still names the seller. In 2025 the resale buyer’s bank refuses sanction on the name mismatch, and the deal waits months for a mutation that would have taken weeks back in 2021. The deed was always enough for OWNERSHIP — never enough for the next transaction. Your document checklist ☐ Start with the registered sale deed — the heaviest of the three. ☐ Trace the chain behind it to the Mother Deed, watching for gaps. ☐ Compare patta vs deed on name, extent, survey number. ☐ File mutation if the revenue record lags. ☐ Pull a separate EC for hidden loans and claims. Quick answers (FAQ) Does a patta prove ownership? No — it supports possession; the registered deed chain proves title. Is a title deed the same as a sale deed? The sale deed is usually its main component; the title deed is the whole chain. Can I sell if the patta still shows the previous owner? Legally the deed lets you — practically, mutate first or watch buyers walk. Can an EC replace a patta? No — they answer different questions (registered transactions vs revenue holding); a full check uses both. Bottom line Deed for ownership, patta for the record, chain for confidence — verify all three and make them agree before money moves. Where they disagree, the deed wins the law and the mismatch loses you the deal. For you: Use the three-question frame in every negotiation: whose name does Dharani hold (patta)? did a registered transfer occur (deed)? is the chain clean to the root (title)? A seller strong on one and vague on the others has told you where to dig. And keep your own ventures’ trinity aligned — deed, passbook, mutation — plot by plot; it is what “clear-title developer” means in practice. 2026-09-18|ls-na-conversion: Converting agricultural land to non-agricultural (NA) use: the complete guide Land School — an original Deccan Ledger lesson · source & further reading: Converting Agricultural Land to Non-Agricultural (NA) Use: A Complete Guide — 1acre.in Key Highlights Conversion is the legal reclassification of agricultural land for residential, commercial or industrial use. Every parcel defaults to agricultural in the records — whatever is actually standing on it. The process rhymes everywhere: verify classification → apply → inspection → fee → conversion order. Fees vary dramatically by state — usually a percentage of guideline value, sometimes flat per-square-metre rates. Building without conversion is illegal, unfinanceable, and demolishable — not a technicality. What land conversion actually means A parcel’s legal identity lives in its revenue-record classification, and agricultural is the default until someone formally changes it. The change goes by different names — NA order , land use change , DC conversion (after the District Collector who typically grants it) — but the idea is identical everywhere: the official status must match the intended use BEFORE that use becomes legal. Why conversion is mandatory before non-farm use Two reasons, both flowing from how land is legally treated. First, classification: agricultural is the default, and only conversion changes it. Second, tax: agricultural land is largely tax-exempt, while residential, commercial and industrial uses carry their own tax treatment — so the state insists the record match the reality. A house already standing on farmland changes nothing in the record; the mismatch IS the legal exposure — blocking finance, complicating sale, inviting demolition. The step-by-step process 1. Verify the current classification in the revenue records. 2. Apply to the tahsildar/revenue officer — with land extent, current and previous owners, and the proposed use — seeking the conversion NOC. 3. An inspection report goes to the sanctioning authority. 4. On clearance, a fee assessment order issues. 5. Pay, and the authority issues the formal Conversion / NA Order — the document that changes the classification and specifies the permitted use. Then the record itself updates. Definition — Conversion order: a dated, numbered, conditional government order — the parcel’s promotion certificate from farm to buildable. When buying “converted” land, verify the ORDER; brochures do not convert land. How fees are calculated Structures differ too much across states for one estimate: most charge a percentage of guideline value / circle rate / jantri; some use flat per-square-metre rates. The practical consequence: because fees key off CURRENT guideline values, the same conversion costs more after every revision in an appreciating area — timing conversions before revisions is real money on a large layout. Red flags Building without NA permission : illegal, and demolition is a standard outcome, not a rare one — however long the structure has stood. An unconverted plot with a house on it is unfinanceable, unsellable with clean title for its actual use, and permanently exposed. “Deemed conversion” states : some treat unauthorised use as converted but stack a penalty ON TOP of the normal fee — skipping the process buys a fine, not a saving. No-go zones : several states bar conversion outright in restricted belts — coastal regulation zones, railway/highway corridors, protected forest. Example: The colony test: fifty houses on unconverted farmland is not fifty exceptions — it is fifty legal problems holding hands. No sanctioned plans possible, no loans against the houses, demolition legally on the table for each. NA conversion vs layout approval Aspect NA conversion Layout approval Purpose Changes the land’s CLASSIFICATION from agricultural Authorises SUBDIVIDING land into plots with roads and drainage Authority Collector / tahsildar (revenue side) Town planning / development authority (HMDA, DTCP) Applies to The land as a whole The specific subdivision plan submitted Needed for Any non-farm construction Developing or selling individual plots Fees Percentage of guideline value or flat rate Typically per plot or per acre developed A residential layout needs BOTH, in order: convert the land first, then obtain layout approval to subdivide and sell legally. Pre-application checklist ☐ Exact current classification verified; master plan permits the intended use (green belt/forest/protection zones cannot convert). ☐ Title deed, land records, survey map and tax receipts assembled in advance. ☐ The state’s specific fee structure and authority confirmed. ☐ Conversion time and cost priced into any purchase of unconverted land. ☐ The numbers actually run before deciding to convert ahead of a sale. Quick answers (FAQ) Can I sell agricultural land without converting? Yes — as agricultural land, at agricultural prices, to eligible buyers. Conversion is about USE, not sale. What if I build without it? Illegal construction: demolition exposure, no finance, no clean resale. Is NA conversion the same as layout approval? No — see the table; a plotted venture needs both. How long does it take? State-dependent — weeks to months; the master-plan check FIRST is what prevents dead applications. Bottom line Conversion is a formality with real teeth: skipped, it blocks finance and invites demolition; done in the right order — zoning first, then papers, then fee, then order — it is predictable machinery. Read the order’s condition pages; that is where the surprises live. For you: For a plotting developer conversion IS the product: your margin lives between farmland price and legally-buildable price, and the order manufactures the difference. Zoning → restrictions → title → conversion → layout — the sequence, every time. Original Deccan Ledger lesson; full source article on 1acre.in (links above). This deep dive is about the second one. Mechanics: a Chief Minister’s spoken assurance on the floor of the Assembly is not itself a law or order — it has to be turned into a Government Order before it has legal force, which is exactly the gap this story tracks being closed. Numbers: the two threads share one thing — both were given roughly a month-long clock, though as F3 shows, only one of the two initially got a firm deadline. Plain English: “22-A mess” is not one problem — it is at least twelve different kinds of land, each needing its own fix, lumped under one prohibited list. Mechanics: separating disputes into named categories (Assigned Land, Indiramma, Secunderabad leasehold, Bhoodan, and so on) lets the government apply a different legal test to each, instead of one blunt rule for every prohibited survey number. Numbers: twelve categories, one 30-day sub-deadline (Secunderabad leasehold only) inside the wider announcement. F3 · The critical framing: a promise without a deadline Telangana Today’s own headline on that 16 September announcement was pointed: “Revanth promises solution, but offers no immediate relief to 22-A land victims.” The report notes the CM announced a high-powered committee, new regularisation policies, e-KYC and newspaper-notice procedures with a proposed 15-day objection window before any land is newly added to the prohibited list, and fresh policies for ULC lands, unauthorised layouts, HMDA/GHMC/DTCP layouts, Singareni lands and GO 59/GO 118 applications — but fixed a hard 30-day deadline only for the Erravelli/KCR-family land inquiry, giving no firm timeframe for when the 22-A committee itself would report. Plain English: the government promised a lot on 22-A, but the only part with an actual date attached, on 16 September, was the probe into a political rival’s land — not the relief for ordinary owners. Incentives: a dated deadline is politically riskier (it can be measured and missed publicly) than an open-ended promise, which is precisely why governments tend to date the things they most want credit for finishing on time. Example: before buying any plot in Telangana, a buyer’s lawyer checks this list by survey number, the same way they’d check for an existing loan against the property. Buying from abroad is an information problem: due diligence must happen BEFORE the wire, not after. Who counts as an NRI here The definitions run through FEMA, 1999. An NRI is an Indian citizen living abroad — Indian passport overseas. An OCI is a foreign citizen of Indian origin — foreign passport, Indian roots. For property purchases the two follow essentially identical rules, so everything below applies to both. What NRIs can and cannot buy Freely: apartments, villas, houses, offices, shops — residential and commercial, any number, no RBI approval. Never: agricultural land, farmhouses, plantation property — a national ban, whatever the buyer’s income or country, and it covers every route: sale deed, agreement to sell, or any indirect structure trying to dress the purchase up. Why the farmland ban exists The restriction lives in FEMA’s capital-account framework — today the Non-debt Instruments Rules, 2019 plus the RBI Master Direction, not one neat section. The policy logic: farmland touches food security, and offshore money flooding in could distort prices and displace the people who actually work the land. RBI approval technically exists but is granted rarely, for genuine agricultural or public-interest cases — it is not an investment route. And breaking the rule is not a slap on the wrist: the transaction can be VOIDED, the Enforcement Directorate can step in, and penalties can reach three times the value. The three exceptions Inheritance — the common path: an NRI can inherit farmland from a resident Indian (or from another NRI with RBI clearance), and can later sell it — but only to a resident Indian. Gift from a specified relative — allowed if the giver is a RESIDENT Indian who qualifies as a specified relative under FEMA; NRI-to-NRI farmland gifting is barred. Prior ownership — farmland you owned while resident stays yours after your status changes; the ban bites only on NEW acquisitions. In all three cases, sending the eventual sale money abroad is not automatic — RBI guidance and tax compliance govern it. Repatriation — getting money out later From an NRO account, up to USD 1 million per financial year can go abroad, subject to tax compliance. Yes, but only to a resident Indian. What if an NRI buys farmland in breach? Transaction voidable, ED proceedings, penalty up to 3× the value. It can never hand over ownership. Suraj Lamp (Supreme Court, 2011) settled it: a PoA is not a title-transfer instrument; Shakeel Ahmed (2023) confirmed old GPA chains get no pass. A PoA normally DIES with the principal (Section 201) — except where the agent holds a real interest in the property (Section 202). Registration is mandatory whenever a PoA creates an interest in land, is marked irrevocable, or empowers sale/gift/transfer. Stamp duty turns on the relationship: close family pay nominal rates; unrelated buyers/developers face conveyance-level charges. What a PoA actually does for land One person — the principal — authorises another — the agent — to act on their behalf: signing agreements, handling Sub-Registrar paperwork, managing tenants, negotiating a sale. Representative authority only. The persistent confusion is treating a PoA as a stand-in for a sale — it is not and cannot be: under Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, only a REGISTERED SALE DEED transfers title to immovable property. GPA vs SPA: picking the instrument A General PoA grants sweeping authority — suited to an NRI overseeing property across years and distance, but broad authority is hard to police, and if the agent oversteps, the very breadth makes the overstep harder to prove. A Special PoA is built for ONE job and expires when it is done. For land, advocates lean SPA: narrow scope, less room for misuse, cleaner record. What the Supreme Court has said Suraj Lamp (2011) : the “GPA sale” — the once-common practice of selling property via GPA + agreement + will, skipping the sale deed and its stamp duty — transfers NO title. Shakeel Ahmed (2023) : confirmed the principle applies to old chains too — decades-old GPA transactions do not ripen into ownership with time. If your seller’s ownership story runs through a GPA instead of a registered deed, there is no ownership in the story. Example: A Shamshabad plot is offered cheap: the “owner” bought it in 2008 “on GPA” from the recorded owner and has possession ever since. Under Suraj Lamp he owns nothing — only the recorded owner (or their heirs) can convey. The fix, if everyone is alive and willing: a proper registered sale deed from the true owner now, with duty paid. Without that, the plot is unbuyable at any discount. The five classic PoA risks 1) Revoked but presented as valid — an unregistered cancellation shows no outward sign, so a revoked PoA can still deceive a third party. 2) Death of the principal — agency ends automatically under Section 201; anything signed after is void — except the narrow Section 202 case where the agent holds a genuine interest in the property itself. 3) Tangled chains of sub-authority — each PoA granting power to the next makes true ownership harder to trace; buyers inherit disputes they never saw. 4) Self-dealing — an agent selling to HIMSELF is valid only if the PoA explicitly permits it; otherwise a breach of fiduciary duty. 5) Missing registration — where a PoA permits sale, gift or transfer, registration at the sub-registrar is not optional; skipping it guts the document’s standing. Definition — Section 202 (Contract Act): the exception that makes a PoA survive the principal’s death: when the agent has a real INTEREST in the property (say, money already advanced against it), the authority is coupled with that interest and does not lapse. Everything else dies with the principal. Registration, stamp duty, validity Registration is mandatory when the PoA creates an interest in land, is marked irrevocable, or empowers sale/gift/transfer; a PoA limited to rent collection follows lighter rules. Stamp duty follows the relationship : close family typically nominal; an unrelated buyer or developer holding a sale-empowering PoA can face conveyance-level duty — precisely to kill the GPA-sale dodge. NRIs : execute before the Indian mission (or apostille in Hague-convention countries) and stamp within three months of the document reaching India. How to verify a land PoA before acting on it ☐ The PoA names the exact survey number, the exact act, and a duration. ☐ Registered, where the sale/irrevocable/interest test applies. ☐ A revocation clause built in from day one. ☐ The principal INDEPENDENTLY confirmed as owner — in the state land record, not the PoA’s own recitals. ☐ The principal confirmed ALIVE (for a Section 201 document, this is not a formality). ☐ EC pulled — showing any PoA, mortgage or transaction already registered against the parcel. ☐ The land itself transferable — no assigned/prohibited/acquisition taint, because no PoA overrides a land-law restriction. Quick answers (FAQ) Can a PoA be used to SELL land? An agent under a valid, registered, sale-empowering PoA can EXECUTE a sale deed for the owner — but the PoA itself never makes anyone an owner. Does calling it “irrevocable” make it irrevocable? No — the label doesn’t; only a genuine Section 202 interest does. What if the principal dies? Authority ends; post-death signatures are void (Section 202 excepted). Stamp duty? Relationship-dependent — nominal for close family, conveyance-level for unrelated sale-empowered holders. Bottom line A PoA is a tool for ACTING at a distance, not for owning. Verify the principal, the registration, the scope and the land’s own transferability — and treat any ownership chain that runs through a GPA as a chain with a missing link. For you: Two rules for your desk. Buying: any parcel whose chain contains a “GPA sale” is unpriced risk — either the true owner signs a fresh registered deed or you pass. Structuring your own JDs: the development GPA you take from landowners should be SPECIAL, scoped to the project, registered, with the JDA’s reversion clause mirrored in it — broad GPAs frighten landowners and courts alike. 2026-09-20|ls-ulpin: ULPIN: what the 'Aadhaar for land' means for buyers Land School — an original Deccan Ledger lesson · source & further reading: ULPIN: What the “Aadhaar for Land” Means for Buyers — 1acre.in Key Highlights ULPIN is a 14-digit code for every surveyed parcel, generated from its exact geo-coordinates. The Aadhaar comparison is fair: one permanent identity per parcel, whoever owns it. It attacks a real problem — the same plot carrying unlinked identifiers across departments. Coverage varies hugely by state: some are at 100%, others far behind; nationally roughly half of parcels are covered. It speeds verification and blocks multi-selling fraud where implemented — but it never replaces legal due diligence. What ULPIN actually is ULPIN — Unique Land Parcel Identification Number, officially Bhu-Aadhaar — is a 14-digit code assigned to each parcel under the Digital India Land Records Modernization Programme, built from the parcel’s records of rights and its geo-coordinates. Like citizen Aadhaar, the point is one verifiable identity that stays consistent across every department, bank and registration office. The problem it solves India has over 600 million parcels, and historically each state tracked them its own way — survey numbers, khasra numbers, patta numbers, tax accounts — none linked automatically. The same land wearing four numbers in four registers is exactly the confusion fraudsters exploited: multi-selling the same plot under its different identities. One coordinate-based ID across all registers removes that whole class of fraud. What ULPIN does — and does not — replace Identifier What it tracks Key limitation ULPIN / Bhu-Aadhaar Geo-coordinate identity of the parcel Does NOT confirm ownership or title cleanliness Survey number State reference for a plot within a village Can repeat across regions; not geo-referenced Khasra number Agricultural plot ID in northern states State-specific; no national linkage without ULPIN Patta / khatauni Revenue record of occupancy / tax liability A tax record — not proof of clean title Sale deed The legal transfer document Says nothing about whether the chain behind it is complete ULPIN does not retire the identifiers you know; it sits above them as the connector — once the linkage for a given parcel is actually done. How far the rollout has reached Uneven, and that unevenness decides its usefulness for YOUR parcel. Andhra Pradesh finished first at full coverage (60+ million parcels); Karnataka, Odisha, Telangana, Madhya Pradesh and Chhattisgarh sit in the 60–90% band; some large states lag far behind. Nationally, roughly half of parcels carry a ULPIN. No ULPIN on your parcel = none of the benefits yet — the traditional checks carry the full weight. What it means practically for a buyer Where implemented, states link the ULPIN to the working records — pattas, extracts, deeds, tax records — creating one auditable trail. Mutations update under the ULPIN, so buyers and lenders read CURRENT status rather than chasing offices. A mortgage or dispute linked to the ID surfaces without hand-cross-referencing registries. Example: The old scam ULPIN kills: sell the plot once under its survey number, once under an old revenue identifier — two “different” properties on paper, one piece of earth. With one coordinate-derived ID stamped on every record, the second sale collides with the first instantly. What ULPIN still does not solve It confirms WHICH parcel — never WHOSE. It cannot verify the seller’s title, and cannot reach back into unregistered history. And within even high-coverage states, parcels miss IDs where surveys are incomplete or boundaries disputed. Treat it as a checksum on identity that narrows your work — the title chain, EC and litigation checks remain the work itself. Definition — Bhoodhar: Telangana’s own parcel-ID under the same national idea, assigned village by village through the ongoing resurvey — quote it in documents once your village is covered. Pre-purchase checklist ☐ Check whether your state/district has completed the rollout. ☐ Where a ULPIN exists, cross-verify it against survey number, owner name and description. ☐ Use linked mutation/encumbrance data as an accelerant — never as a substitute for the title search. ☐ Where none exists, run the full traditional drill. ☐ Lawyer on anything beyond a routine purchase. Quick answers (FAQ) Is ULPIN mandatory for buying? No — it is infrastructure, arriving parcel by parcel. Does it replace the survey number? No; it bridges identifiers under one framework. Can it prevent fraud completely? It removes identity-based fraud; title fraud remains your due diligence. Does having one mean the title is verified? No — identity yes, ownership no. Bottom line ULPIN is plumbing, not paint: when it works, deals simply stop failing for identity reasons. Use it, quote it, and keep doing the ownership homework it was never designed to do. For you: Habit for the transition years: verify every pipeline parcel on the current portal, and the moment a Bhoodhar exists write it into your agreements beside the survey number. If two documents show different parcel IDs for “the same” land — that mismatch IS the due-diligence finding. Original Deccan Ledger lesson; full source article on 1acre.in (links above). 2026-09-20|ls-jda: Joint Development Agreement: how builder and owner shares work Land School — an original Deccan Ledger lesson · source & further reading: Joint Development Agreement: How Builder and Owner Shares Work in India — 1acre.in Key Highlights A JDA trades the owner’s land for a share of what the builder makes of it — neither pays the other upfront. Three sharing structures — area, revenue, profit — each with a different risk profile. Owners typically end with 30–50% of the developed property, set by location and leverage. Courts will not enforce an UNREGISTERED JDA. Registration is existential, not optional. Section 45(5A) defers the owner’s capital gains to the completion-certificate year, not the signing year. Most JDA disasters are builder-selection disasters — vet the builder harder than the draft. What a JDA actually is A structured trade: the owner contributes land — granting development RIGHTS, retaining ownership until later conveyances — and the developer builds at his own cost, returning a slice of the outcome as units or revenue. The owner unlocks idle land without selling; the developer gets prime land without buying. Four laws touch it at once — Contract Act, Transfer of Property Act, Registration Act, RERA — and the Registration Act point is decisive: skip registration and the agreement has no legal teeth at all. The three sharing structures Area sharing (commonest in residential): the built area — carpet, built-up or super built-up, whichever the agreement DEFINES upfront — divides by ratio; 40:60 on 100 flats leaves the owner 40 units to hold, rent or sell, keeping some shelter from a shaky market. Revenue sharing : the developer sells everything and remits the owner’s percentage — cash rather than keys, common in hot urban markets — where the drafting MUST nail gross vs net vs actually-collected, because loose words here breed most fights. Profit sharing : splits what remains after all costs; aligns incentives in theory, but a developer who inflates costs quietly shrinks the owner’s cut — workable only with real audit rights. Definition — Carpet / built-up / super built-up: three ways to measure the same building — usable floor, plus walls, plus common areas. A ratio without a named measure is not a ratio; it is a future argument. Typical ratios and what moves them Location Typical owner share Why Prime Tier-1 corridors 40–50% Scarce, expensive land = owner leverage City periphery 35–45% Land value still strong, competition higher Tier-2 cities 30–40% Land less scarce; builder carries more sales risk Tier-3 / rural fringe 25–35% Developer shoulders nearly all risk Large parcels (5 acres+) swing ratios back toward the owner; higher FSI, residential use, and proximity to existing infrastructure all push the owner’s share up. The professional way to argue any ratio: reverse-engineer it from GDV — owner share ≈ land value ÷ (land value + all-in build cost + builder margin) — then fight over the inputs, not the emotion. How the process runs Negotiate model and ratio → lawyer drafts (sharing clause, timelines, a registered GPA scoped strictly to what the project needs) → REGISTER with the Sub-Registrar → approvals and RERA registration → construction → handover of units or revenue at completion. A mid-sized residential project: three to five years end to end. Red flags in the draft No registration — worthless in court. A bare percentage with no named units, floors or defined revenue base — the single biggest fight-starter. A loosely-drafted GPA handing the developer more authority than the project needs — hard to claw back. No penalty clause — delays go unremedied. No REVERSION clause — a defaulting builder means litigation instead of an automatic handback of development rights. Definition — Reversion clause: the provision that returns development rights to the owner automatically on defined defaults — the difference between a bad year and a decade in court. Insist on it; a builder who resists it is telling you why. Area vs revenue sharing — choosing Area sharing suits owners planning to hold or rent, and shields them somewhat from market swings. Revenue sharing suits owners wanting liquidity who trust the builder’s sales machine. In either: define the measure, the base, and the audit rights in the first schedule — not in a WhatsApp message. Tax implications Section 45(5A) : individual and HUF owners under a REGISTERED JDA pay capital gains in the completion-certificate year, not the signing year — fixing the old horror of owing tax before receiving a single flat. Section 194-IC : cash paid alongside the property share draws 10% TDS. The builder’s own share is stock-in-trade — business income when sold. GST : applies on units sold BEFORE the completion certificate; sales after it are immovable-property sales, GST-exempt — a timing lever both sides should understand. Is the model reliable? The structure holds; the BUILDER is the risk. A developer running out of money leaves a half-built project and a stuck owner. RERA registration, delivery record and financial health, checked before signing, prevent most of what goes wrong later. Before signing — checklist ☐ Builder’s RERA status, delivery record, financial standing verified. ☐ Ratio names exact units / a defined revenue base — never a bare percentage. ☐ GPA scoped tightly to the project. ☐ Penalty clause on missed milestones. ☐ Reversion clause that functions automatically. ☐ Property lawyer AND tax advisor before signature — 45(5A), GST and TDS shape what actually lands in your pocket. Quick answers (FAQ) Is JDA registration mandatory? For enforceability, yes — an unregistered JDA cannot be defended in court. Can the owner cancel on default? With a reversion clause, rights return automatically; without one, litigation. When does the owner pay capital gains? Completion-certificate year, under 45(5A), for registered JDAs. Bottom line A JDA unlocks land value without a sale — and succeeds or fails on two things: the builder’s track record, and drafting that contemplates failure calmly. Registration, a precise sharing clause, and a working reversion clause are the owner’s armour. For you: Your home ground. Walk into every ratio negotiation with the GDV maths done — the side that computed the pie controls the split. Prefer area-sharing when you believe in the corridor more than the counterparty, revenue-sharing when the sales machine is the asset. And the two clauses that keep JDs out of courtrooms: registration immediately, reversion always. Original Deccan Ledger lesson; full source article on 1acre.in (links above). No Congress-aligned outlet’s account was distinctly identifiable in this sweep; if one surfaces in future coverage it should be flagged with equal rigour. 📚 Glossary — every term, simply Inam land “Inam” is Persian/Urdu for “gift” or “grant.” Under Hyderabad State’s rulers, land was routinely granted, tax-free or low-tax, to individuals or institutions for service, religious, or charitable reasons — a village headman, a temple, a soldier’s family. Example: imagine a Nizam-era equivalent of a government granting a plot to a war veteran instead of a pension — that plot became “Inam land,” owned differently from ordinary taxed farmland. The Andhra Pradesh (Telangana Area) Abolition of Inams Act, 1955 The law that formally ended this whole category: from its effective date, every Inam grant was cancelled and the land vested back in the government. People actually living on and farming the land at that time could apply to convert their Inam holding into an ordinary “ryotwari” (regular, taxed) title — but only through a formal re-grant process, not automatically. Example: a family that had farmed Inam land for generations in 1955 had to go and get an Occupancy Rights Certificate (below); a family that didn’t — or whose paperwork was lost — is, legally, still sitting on government land today, seven decades later. ORC — Occupancy Rights Certificate The specific document that converts a former Inam occupant into a lawful ryotwari owner. Telangana’s 1975 Inams rules fixed 1 November 1973 as the cut-off date for who counted as the rightful occupant entitled to one. Without an ORC on record, an “Inam” parcel’s private ownership claim rests on much weaker ground — exactly the gap this week’s allegation is pointing at. The Telangana (formerly Andhra Pradesh) Land Reforms (Ceiling on Agricultural Holdings) Act, 1973 A land-reform law capping how much agricultural land any one family could legally own, with the exact limit depending on land quality — roughly 10–18 acres for the best irrigated land, up to 27 acres for lower-grade single-crop land, and more for dry or hilly land. Anything above the ceiling was, in principle, supposed to be surrendered to the government for redistribution. Example: this is the law implicitly behind Revanth Reddy’s “above the legally allowed limit” framing of the KCR family’s 439.30 acres — almost any single family holding several hundred acres is, on the face of it, holding far more than this ceiling ever permitted, unless it is split across many separate legal owners or exempted categories. Benami transaction / Benamidar / Beneficial owner Under the Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Act, 1988 (amended 2016), a benami transaction is one where a property is bought and paid for by one person (the “beneficial owner”) but held in another person’s name (the “benamidar”) specifically to hide who really owns it. Example: if it were proven that Jagadish Reddy’s wife holds title to land her husband actually controls and benefited from acquiring through his office, that arrangement itself — regardless of the Inam-land question — could separately be examined as a possible benami transaction. Penalty: confiscation of the property by the central government, plus criminal liability for both parties. Election affidavit Every candidate for the Assembly or Parliament in India must file a sworn affidavit with the Election Commission before every election, declaring assets, liabilities, education and criminal cases. These are public documents, freely searchable (via sites like myneta.info), and this week’s campaign is using successive affidavits from the same politician, filed years apart, as a rough measure of how fast their declared wealth grew. Full Tank Level (FTL) & buffer zone The maximum water level a reservoir or lake reaches when full; Telangana law generally bars construction within the FTL itself and imposes buffer-zone restrictions in a ring around it. Harish Rao’s counter-allegation — that some Congress leaders’ own houses sit within an FTL — uses the identical legal category GO 111 relies on, just applied to a different, smaller waterbody. Fact-finding team / inquiry committee An administrative, not judicial, body appointed by the government to gather facts and report back within a set deadline — it has no power to punish on its own; its report simply feeds into whatever the government decides to do next (a formal order, a court case, or nothing). EAGLE wing Telangana Police’s dedicated Enforcement Against Ganja, Liquor and Extremism / narcotics-enforcement wing — the unit Congress cited as having raided the Moinabad farmhouse in March 2026, cited here only as reported context, not independently re-verified today. MLA vs MLC vs MP vs Whip An MLA sits in the state Legislative Assembly, directly elected from a constituency; an MLC sits in the state Legislative Council, usually elected indirectly or nominated; an MP sits in Parliament, either the Lok Sabha (directly elected) or Rajya Sabha (indirectly elected). A “Whip” is a senior party post responsible for ensuring party members vote/attend as instructed — a Government Whip specifically manages this for the ruling party. 🕑 The backstory — how we got here Date Event 1955 Abolition of Inams Act vests all Inam land in the Telangana-area government; occupants must apply for re-grant. 1973 Land Reforms (Ceiling on Agricultural Holdings) Act sets per-family land ceilings, roughly 10–27 acres depending on land quality. 1975 Telangana Inams Rules fix 1 November 1973 as the cut-off for who could claim an Occupancy Rights Certificate. 1996 GO 111 restricts development in the Osman Sagar/Himayat Sagar 10-km catchment. 2014 Telangana state formed; KCR becomes first Chief Minister. 2020 KCR’s BRS government moves toward repealing GO 111. Dec 2023 Congress wins the Assembly election; Revanth Reddy becomes Chief Minister; GO 111 repeal paused. Nationally, land-ceiling laws from the 1970s are notorious for having recovered only a small fraction of the “surplus” land they identified, precisely because family-splitting, benami holding and decades of litigation routinely outlasted the enforcement machinery. What a ten-year follower of Telangana politics knows that a first-time reader doesn’t: “farmhouse culture” allegations against the state’s political elite are cyclical, not new — similar claims circulated before the 2023 election too, and rarely survive to an actual land-recovery order once the news cycle moves on. The genuinely new element this week is the specific, document-anchored technique — matching successive election affidavits against each other, year by year — rather than a general corruption claim. ⚖️ So what — stakes and consequences Congress wins the news cycle regardless of the legal outcome: four straight days of coverage, a clear anti-corruption narrative, and a stated plan to keep expanding statewide. BRS’s named leaders lose reputationally the moment their farmhouse is toured, whatever a court or revenue inquiry eventually finds — allegation itself is costly in a state where land wealth is a recurring public preoccupation. The Congress government also carries real risk: if 30 days pass and none of the four probes produces a formal order, BJP’s “WWE” framing and BRS’s “good friends, nothing will happen” cynicism both get vindicated. What this means for you: For Hyderabad/Telangana real estate — any large parcel anywhere in the state with an “Inam,” “assigned,” or ceiling-surplus history is now politically radioactive to touch until this campaign settles; if you are underwriting a JD on land with any such history in its record, add an explicit ORC/re-grant and ceiling-clearance check to your diligence checklist now, not after a deal is signed. Beginner mistake vs. the sharper read: the beginner dismisses this as “just politics, nothing to do with my deals.” The sharper read treats it as a leading indicator of exactly which categories of land title — Inam, assigned, ceiling-surplus, catchment-zone — the revenue department’s attention (and therefore its scrutiny of ordinary buyers’ paperwork too) is about to fall on next. 🎯 The 20% that gives you 100% — your keep-forever map Since 16 September, Congress has toured four BRS leaders’ farmhouses on four straight days, escalating the legal theory each time — undeclared wealth, then a catchment-zone violation, then today, land whose title itself traces back to a 1955 law that never finished being applied. No formal order has yet been issued against anyone named. The campaign is explicitly planned to expand statewide. And underneath the politics sits a genuinely useful lesson: in Telangana, a piece of land’s legal history rarely ends with the seller’s sale deed — it can reach back through a ceiling declaration, an Inam re-grant, or a catchment order from decades before anyone alive today bought it. 1955 Inams Abolition Act -> land not re-granted via ORC stays LEGALLY GOVERNMENT LAND -> decades pass, land quietly resold/inherited as if private -> 2026: political campaign singles out a large landholding -> journalists check the paper trail (affidavits, survey numbers) -> allegation: "this Inam/ceiling-surplus land is still government land" -> TWO POSSIBLE PATHS: (a) revenue dept confirms -> reclaim + redistribute order -> owner litigates -> years of court delay (Telangana precedent) (b) revenue dept finds clean re-grant/ORC on file -> claim dies, land stays private MEANWHILE: every OTHER Inam/ceiling-surplus parcel in the state becomes harder to clear, finance or register until the political heat cools Five transferable lessons for a plotting developer: 1. “Inam” on an old record is not a historical footnote — check specifically for the Occupancy Rights Certificate proving the 1955 abolition was formally cleared for that exact parcel. 2. A ceiling-law “surplus” flag from the 1970s can resurface on land that has since changed hands many times, because ceiling declarations were never systematically cross-linked to later sale deeds. 3. Treat political attention itself as a due-diligence signal: when a land category becomes a news cycle, expect slower approvals and sharper scrutiny on anything resembling it for months afterward, whether or not you are personally involved. 4. Election affidavits are free, public, and dated — use them the way this campaign is using them, as a wealth-growth cross-check on any politically connected seller or JD partner. 5. A benami risk doesn’t require a hidden scheme to be real in the public’s eyes — a lease or a family-member registration with a perfectly legitimate commercial logic can still trigger scrutiny purely from appearances, so document the business reasoning behind any such arrangement in writing from day one. TG-RERA (Telangana Real Estate Regulatory Authority) — the state regulator that heard the case and passed the order. 🧠 Learn the concepts (from zero) RERA registration — the gate before any money changes hands Section 3 of the RERA Act says a promoter cannot advertise, market, book, sell or even accept an advance for a project until it is registered with the state authority. The idea: buyers should only ever be dealing with a project the regulator has already vetted (title, sanctioned plan, escrow account for construction funds), never a promise on paper. Section 59 — the penalty for jumping the gate A promoter who sells, offers to sell, or otherwise transacts on an unregistered project can be fined up to 10% of the project’s estimated cost — and for repeat violations, faces imprisonment. Here, the ₹32.17 lakh penalty is TG-RERA quantifying exactly that violation for one flat’s advance payment, years after the fact. 2026-09-21|ls-stamp-duty: How to calculate stamp duty and registration charges on land Land School — an original Deccan Ledger lesson · source & further reading: How to Calculate Stamp Duty and Registration Charges on Land — 1acre.in Key Highlights Stamp duty is a STATE tax on the transfer; registration charges are a separate fee for recording it. Both are generally payable before the sale deed can register. Rates vary by state, property type, buyer category and value — property is a state subject. The base is generally the HIGHER of the sale price and the guideline/stamp-duty value. Online calculators estimate the bill in advance — with current-year rates only. The two levies, separated Stamp duty : a statutory tax on the property transaction itself — the state’s cut for recognising the transfer. Registration charges : the fee for recording the deed in official records. Different levies, different lines on the challan; both generally must be paid before the Sub-Registrar registers your deed. Budget them together: in Telangana the combined package on a sale deed runs about 7.5% of the value. Understanding stamp duty Each state’s own stamp law governs — which is why rates, concessions and even calculation methods differ across borders. The two planning variables: the STATE-SPECIFIC RATE (the biggest number in your closing costs), and POTENTIAL EXEMPTIONS — many states discount duty for women buyers or first-time purchasers. Verify the current rate and valuation rules before finalising any purchase; budgets built on last year’s percentages miss. Registration charges explained Payable for entering the sale deed into the official record — the act that makes your ownership publicly traceable and your deed retrievable as a certified copy forever. Rates vary by state and can carry minimum or maximum limits (some states cap registration fees in absolute rupees; others charge a flat percentage — Telangana’s is 0.5%). The calculation, step by step The maths is simple once the base is fixed. 1) Determine the transaction value — the actual agreed price. 2) Check the guideline / stamp-duty value for the survey number. 3) The BASE is the higher of the two. 4) Apply the state’s duty rate. 5) Add registration charges. 6) Add any state surcharge or cess. The declared price never beats the guideline floor: under-declare and the department simply computes on its own benchmark. Example: Telangana example: plot agreed at ₹80 lakh, guideline value ₹90 lakh. Base = ₹90 lakh. At ~7.5% combined, the SRO bill is ≈ ₹6.75 lakh — on the guideline figure, not the price. A buyer who budgeted 7.5% of ₹80 lakh is ₹75,000 short at the counter. Using a calculator effectively State portals and property sites host duty calculators: feed location and value, get the estimate instantly. Two disciplines: confirm the calculator uses THIS year’s rates (states tweak percentages in budget sessions), and use it comparatively — running the same investment across district or state lines can reveal lakhs of difference in friction cost alone. Exemptions and reductions State-dependent concessions exist for women purchasers, affordable-housing projects, specified FAMILY transfers (gift/settlement deeds between close relatives often carry nominal duty), and other notified categories. Always check eligibility before registration — concessions are claimed at the counter, not refunded after. Why rates vary regionally Property is a state subject: each government prescribes its own rates and concessions, tuned to its revenue needs, property type (commercial vs residential) and urban demand. The practical rule: never carry one state’s percentage in your head into another state’s deal — verify with the registration department that will actually stamp your deed. Key takeaways for buyers ☐ Calculate duty BEFORE signing the agreement. ☐ Verify the guideline value for the exact survey number. ☐ Put registration charges in the budget line, not the surprise line. ☐ Check concession eligibility (women buyers, family transfers). ☐ Verify ownership documents before registration — duty paid on a bad title is money on a bad title. Quick answers (FAQ) Calculated on sale price or guideline value? The higher of the two. Same across states? No — rates, fees and concessions all differ. First-time buyer discounts? In some states; check the current notification. Documents needed to pay and register? The deed, identity/PAN, the challan or e-stamp, and the property’s record extracts. Why estimate in advance? Because 6–8% of a land deal is lakhs — a closing-day shortfall can cost you the slot and, with a hard deadline in the agreement, the advance. Bottom line Duty and registration are the certain, calculable part of a land deal — the only closing surprise they ever produce is the one a five-minute advance calculation would have removed. For you: Quote plot prices to your buyers as “all-in at registration” maths — price + ~7.5% + mutation — in the first meeting. Transparency about the state’s cut builds the trust that closes files. On your own acquisitions, model duty into land cost per acre from day one: on a ₹10 Cr assembly it is ₹75 lakh of real money, not a rounding error.
