2026-09-21|ls-sale-deed: The Sale Deed: what it is, how registration works, and why it matters Land School — an original Deccan Ledger lesson · source & further reading: Sale Deed: What It Is, How Registration Works, and Why It Matters for Land Buyers — 1acre.in Key Highlights The sale deed — not the agreement to sell — is the document that legally transfers ownership (Section 54, Transfer of Property Act, 1882). Registering it at the Sub-Registrar’s office is compulsory (Registration Act, 1908). No registration, no transfer. An agreement to sell only gives you the right to DEMAND a future sale. It moves no ownership. The Supreme Court said it again as recently as 2025: unregistered papers cannot stand in for a registered deed. A buyer who has paid fully and moved in — but holds no registered deed — is still legally exposed. What a sale deed is The sale deed is the legal instrument that actually moves ownership of immovable property from seller to buyer. It works under Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, and it comes alive only when it is signed AND registered under the Registration Act, 1908. Three words get mixed up constantly, and the mix-up is expensive. An agreement to sell is a contract (under the Indian Contract Act, 1872) fixing price, payment schedule and possession date — a binding promise, but only a promise. The sale deed is the transfer document that follows once the promise’s conditions are met. And “registry” , the word everyone uses loosely, is not a third document at all — it is the ACT of registering the sale deed. Only the registered sale deed changes whose name the law recognises. Definition — Sub-Registrar Office (SRO): the government office where property documents are recorded. The moment the deed is registered at this counter is the moment ownership legally changes hands. What a sale deed covers A properly drafted deed is the complete record of the transaction. It contains: Party details — full names, addresses and ID of buyer and seller. Property description — survey number, boundaries, area and location exactly as the revenue records show them. Sale consideration — the price and how it was paid. Possession clause — when and how possession passes. Title and indemnity clause — the seller’s written confirmation that the title is clean and free of encumbrances, and his liability if that turns out false. Registration particulars — stamp duty paid, registration number and SRO details, which anchor the deal in the public record. Definition — Indemnity clause: the seller’s promise inside the deed to compensate you if the title is defective. If trouble ever comes, this clause is what your lawyer sues on — read it before signing, not after. Why a sale deed is required Indian law treats REGISTRATION — not payment, not possession — as the trigger for ownership. Without the registered deed, your claim rests only on contract, which is a far weaker seat in any dispute. It matters at three stages. Before buying: part of due diligence is confirming the SELLER’S own deed was properly registered — his weakness becomes yours. At registration: the deed formally transfers ownership. After buying: the registered deed is what you use for mutation, for a loan against the property, and for reselling later. Example: Ravi pays ₹80 lakh, takes possession, builds a compound wall, and holds a signed agreement to sell. Years later the seller’s heirs register a sale deed for the same plot to someone else. The registered deed wins; Ravi’s money and wall buy him a court case, not a plot. How the registration process works, step by step 1. Buyer and seller sign the agreement to sell — price, payment schedule, timelines. 2. The buyer uses this window for due diligence: title documents, Encumbrance Certificate, tax records. 3. The deed is drafted and stamp duty calculated — a state-set percentage of the HIGHER of the official value and the deal price. 4. Both parties appear before the Sub-Registrar with two witnesses: signatures, biometric verification, registration fee. 5. The office checks and registers the deed; the buyer receives the certified registered copy. Timeline: typically a few days to a few weeks, depending on the state and how ready the papers are. Cost: stamp duty plus a registration fee — the fee is a smaller percentage on top of the duty. Definition — Stamp duty: the state’s tax on the transaction, paid before registration. In Telangana the working total for a sale deed is about 7.5% including transfer duty and registration; it varies by state (roughly 4–8% across India). Regulatory red flags — and what to check for each Risk What it means What to check Unregistered sale deed Ownership never legally moved, even if possession changed hands Ask for the registered copy bearing the SRO stamp and registration number Under-valued stamp duty A deed declared below the circle rate can be penalised or challenged Compare the declared value against the state’s current circle/market value Missing Encumbrance Certificate The property may carry undisclosed loans or claims Demand an EC covering at least 13–30 years Seller delaying execution You stay stuck at a contractual claim instead of ownership Write a hard registration deadline into the agreement itself Forged or altered documents The deed may collapse as evidence of title Verify authenticity directly at the Sub-Registrar’s office (certified copies) Sale deed vs agreement to sell — the key differences Aspect Agreement to sell Sale deed Purpose Records the terms of an INTENDED sale Legally transfers ownership Where it happens Signed between buyer and seller Registered at the Sub-Registrar’s office Legal force Enforceable as a contract Conclusive evidence of title once registered Typical use Fixes price, payment schedule, possession date The formal transfer of property rights Cost Nominal stamping Full stamp duty — roughly 4–8% of value by state Use the agreement during negotiation and due diligence, when both sides need something binding before completion. The moment you want actual enforceable ownership rather than a promise — you need the deed. Is a sale deed always reliable? It carries strong weight — under conditions. It must be REGISTERED (an unregistered deed transfers nothing, whatever it says). Stamp duty must be correctly paid (under-stamped deeds face penalties and can be refused as evidence). And the seller’s own CHAIN must be clean — every earlier deed in the property’s history properly registered — because a break anywhere upstream weakens your title downstream. Example: Simple memory test: if the dispute went to court tomorrow and each side placed its papers on the table, which paper wins? The registered one, standing on a registered chain. Always be the person holding that paper. Pre-purchase checklist ☐ The agreement to sell states price, payment schedule and possession date clearly. ☐ The seller’s title verified — EC plus his prior registered deeds. ☐ Possession or full payment is never treated as ownership. ☐ The deed is executed and registered as soon as conditions are met. ☐ No long, open-ended gap between agreement and registration. ☐ A property lawyer is called the moment a seller resists or delays registration. Quick answers (FAQ) Is registering a sale deed mandatory? Yes — without registration the transfer simply has not happened in law. Can possession alone prove ownership? No. Possession supports other evidence but cannot substitute for a registered deed. What if the seller refuses to execute the deed after the agreement? The agreement gives you the right to sue for “specific performance” — a court can compel the sale. Slow, but real; the deadline clause in your agreement is what makes it strong. Does an unregistered agreement have ANY value? As a contract, yes — you can sue on it. As ownership, none. What should I verify before registering? The seller’s chain, the EC, the survey-number match across all records, and the current circle value your duty will be computed on. Bottom line The sale deed is what actually places property in your name; the agreement to sell only holds your place in the queue. Treat registration as the finish line — never as a formality to get to later. For you: In your plotting business this cuts both ways: never leave your own purchases parked on agreements, and never let your plot buyers sit on them either — their limbo matures into your dispute. The date that matters in every deal file is the SRO appointment. This is an original Deccan Ledger lesson; full source article: 1acre.in (link above). Numbers: 700+ acres total holding alleged; 388 acres 5 guntas specifically disputed. A gunta is a small revenue-survey unit of area — roughly 101 square yards, so 40 guntas make one acre; “5 guntas” on top of 388 acres is simply the precise remainder in the survey record, the kind of exact fractional figure that only comes from an actual land-records document, not a rough estimate. Glossary — every term, simply Assigned land Government-owned land formally allotted (“assigned”) to a landless poor family, usually Dalit or otherwise disadvantaged, for their own cultivation — but ownership never fully transfers to them the way an ordinary sale deed would. Example: the Erravalli families here. Gairan / Lavani (Lavani Patta) Local Telangana revenue terms for the same broad idea: government land set aside for community use or allotted to landless agricultural labourers and, in some cases, ex-servicemen. A “Lavani patta” holder can farm the land and even pass it to their children, but cannot legally sell it — the government remains the ultimate owner. Example: this is the legal category the 388 disputed acres most likely falls under. Patta A formal, government-issued document recording who holds rights over a specific piece of land. A patta is not automatically the same as full private ownership — an assigned-land patta comes with the transfer restrictions above, while an ordinary revenue patta on privately-owned land does not. Gunta A small unit of land area used in Indian revenue records, especially in the Deccan region: 40 guntas make one acre, so one gunta is roughly 101 square yards. Seeing a figure like “388 acres 5 guntas” in a report is a strong sign the number comes from an actual survey record, not a rounded estimate. Survey number The unique identifying number Indian revenue departments assign to a specific parcel of land within a village, used in every land record from tax rolls to court cases. One survey number can span village or even mandal boundaries, as Survey No. 325 does here. Mandal An administrative sub-division of an Indian district, sitting between the village and the district in Telangana’s revenue hierarchy — Markook mandal here sits inside Siddipet district. DGPS (Differential Global Positioning System) A satellite-based land-surveying method accurate to within a few centimetres, far sharper than the older manual chain-and-compass surveys most Indian village land records were originally drawn up with. Resurveying old land with DGPS often reveals boundary mismatches against decades-old paper records — not necessarily because anyone did anything wrong, but because the old records were never that precise to begin with. Revenue Divisional Officer (RDO) A mid-level Telangana revenue official overseeing a group of mandals (a “revenue division”), positioned between village-level staff and the District Collector — the office that directs affected landholders to appear and produce documents, as Gajwel’s RDO did here. District Collector The senior-most administrative officer of a Telangana district, ultimately responsible for how land disputes like this one are resolved once the RDO-level document review is complete. 30-day fact-finding probe An administrative inquiry ordered by the Chief Minister and carried out by Revenue Department officials — it establishes facts and can recommend action, but it is not a court proceeding and carries no independent power to punish anyone; whatever it finds still has to go through a separate legal process to actually change who holds the land. Special Investigation Team (SIT) vs. judicial inquiry An SIT is a team of police/administrative officers set up to investigate a specific matter — it reports to the government that created it. A judicial inquiry, led by a sitting judge, is seen as more independent because judges don’t report to the executive government the way an SIT effectively does — which is exactly why KTR demanded the latter instead of the former. Recovery and redistribution The two-step process this story turns on: first the government establishes (“recovers”) which land is genuinely its own to reclaim, then it hands that land out (“redistributes”) to intended beneficiaries. The entire controversy here is about how carelessly or carefully step one is done, since step two only helps people if step one doesn’t also catch innocent long-term holders in its net. Dalit The modern, widely-used term (replacing “Scheduled Caste” in everyday and political language, though SC remains the constitutional/legal term) for communities historically subjected to caste-based discrimination and untouchability in India, who receive specific constitutional protections and welfare schemes such as Dalit Bandhu. The backstory — how we got here When What ~1966 (roughly “60 years ago” per farmers’ own account) Government assigns land in and around Erravalli, including the tract now numbered Survey No. 325, to landless Dalit families for cultivation. 1977 Telangana Assigned Lands (Prohibition of Transfers) Act enacted, formally barring assigned land from being sold or transferred and empowering the government to reclaim illegally-transferred assigned land. 2001–2014 KCR builds the Telangana statehood movement from Gajwel; Erravalli farmhouse develops over this period into both a working farm and a de facto party power centre. 2014–2023 KCR serves three terms as Telangana’s first Chief Minister; Erravalli is developed as a model village with pucca housing under his personal attention. Dec 2023 Congress wins the Assembly election; Revanth Reddy becomes Chief Minister, ending a decade of BRS rule. 2025–2026 Section 22-A prohibited-land-list crisis emerges statewide, entangling large numbers of ordinary patta-holders; becomes a recurring Assembly and media flashpoint. 16 Sep 2026 During a Section 22-A Assembly debate, Revanth Reddy alleges KCR’s Erravalli farmhouse sits on 388 acres of government land and orders a 30-day probe. 17–20 Sep 2026 DGPS survey of Survey No. 325 conducted over three days amid farmer protests; over 50 police deployed. ~19 Sep 2026 Revenue Department serves notices on 120+ farmers, demanding proof of ownership/cultivation rights. 21 Sep 2026 Farmers appear before RDO Chandrakala with documents; district administration begins scrutinising replies, continuing into 22 September. The deeper forces at work here run well beyond one farmhouse. Telangana’s assigned-land system was built on 1970s-era paper records that were never comprehensively digitised or resurveyed for fifty years — so almost any large, politically powerful landholding built up over decades near a village with an active assignment history carries some risk of exactly this kind of dispute, whether or not there was ever any actual wrongdoing. Layer onto that a bitter, personal BRS–Congress rivalry between two Telangana politicians (Revanth Reddy spent years as an opposition leader attacking KCR before becoming CM) and an approaching cycle of long-delayed local body elections, and a technical land-records question becomes a headline political weapon almost overnight. What a ten-year Telangana-watcher knows that a first-time reader doesn’t: this is not the first time a Chief Minister has ordered a land probe into a rival’s farmhouse (BRS itself, in office, faced and made similar allegations against opponents over the past decade), and such probes historically move fast in their survey/notice phase, then slow to a crawl once they reach the stage of actually taking land away from anyone with real political backing — the practical risk almost always ends up falling hardest on whichever party in the dispute has the least power to resist, which in this specific case looks like the ordinary Dalit cultivators, not KCR’s own household. So what — stakes and consequences If the process is run fairly, the Dalit farmers who already hold this land keep it (their occupation for six decades is itself powerful evidence of a valid original assignment), and whatever land, if any, has genuinely been absorbed into the farmhouse compound gets identified and recovered. If it is run carelessly or with political intent, the opposite happens: politically powerless farmers lose long-held land to a paperwork technicality while the politically powerful farmhouse owner, protected by resources, lawyers and public attention, keeps whatever he actually holds. Watch: (1) whether the 30-day probe deadline (mid-October 2026) produces a public report at all, or quietly lapses — moderate likelihood of a delayed or partial report, based on how similar past probes have played out; (2) whether any of the 120+ notified farmers are actually stripped of land they can’t document to the government’s satisfaction — a real risk given how thin 60-year-old paper trails typically are, though the Minister’s public assurance makes an immediate, visible eviction less likely in the short term; (3) whether KTR’s demand for a judge-led inquiry covering both families gets anywhere — historically, such demands from an opposition party rarely succeed in getting the ruling party to submit its own family to the same process; (4) whether this becomes a template applied to other BRS-linked farmhouses beyond Erravalli and Shamshabad, given the pattern this week already suggests it will. What this means for you: For Hyderabad/Telangana real estate specifically — if you are assembling land near any village with a documented history of government land assignment (common across the Siddipet, Medak, Sangareddy and outer-Hyderabad belt), assume the paper trail on any individual parcel may be thinner than it looks, and that a sudden political trigger (not necessarily anything you did) can put an entire survey number under scrutiny overnight, freezing everyone holding land in it regardless of how they came to hold it. For business and investment generally — this is a clean example of how a high-profile political fight, fought in the name of protecting a vulnerable group, can end up imposing its heaviest real-world cost on that exact group, simply because they have the least capacity to produce documentation or resist a process on short notice; the same dynamic shows up whenever a well-intentioned regulatory clean-up sweeps too broadly and catches the smallest, least-resourced parties in its net. The beginner’s read on this story is: “the government caught a corrupt politician stealing 388 acres of Dalit land.” The sharper, expert read is: “the government announced a politically convenient headline before finishing the actual paperwork, and the people bearing the immediate real-world cost of that headline are not the politician it was aimed at, but the ordinary families the announcement claimed to be helping.” Both readings can be true at once — KCR’s family may indeed hold land it shouldn’t, and the farmers may still be the ones who suffer first while that gets sorted out. The 20% that gives you 100% — your keep-forever map A Chief Minister announced, mid-debate, that his predecessor’s farmhouse sits on 388 acres of government land meant for Dalit families, and ordered a 30-day probe with the outcome (half-acre pattas to 800 families) already named. Revenue officials then DGPS-surveyed the disputed tract over three days, amid farmer protests, and served notices on 120-plus farmers who say they, not the farmhouse owner, have actually held and cultivated this land for sixty years. The farmers appeared with their documents on 21 September; officials are now deciding, case by case, whose paperwork holds up. The BRS response has been to demand equal, judge-led scrutiny of the ruling family too, rather than to directly dispute the acreage. The genuinely important open question is not whether KCR’s farmhouse is too big — it’s whether the process meant to fix that ends up costing the powerless farmers around it more than it costs him. 2026-09-22|ls-boundary: How to resolve land boundary disputes using survey records Land School — an original Deccan Ledger lesson · source & further reading: How to Resolve Land Boundary Disputes Using Survey Records — 1acre.in Key Highlights Most boundary fights trace to outdated surveys, vague old deeds, or inherited land split informally without fresh measurement. Cadastral maps and Field Measurement Books carry more weight in these disputes than any other evidence. A fresh official survey from the revenue department is the FIRST move, not the last resort. Twelve years of open hostile possession can ripen into adverse possession — delay has a price in land, not just time. Digitisation is real but uneven: ~95% of RoRs computerised, ~68% of maps, geo-referencing at ~49%. Why these disputes keep happening Outdated or inconsistent records; ambiguous boundary descriptions in older sale deeds; inherited property subdivided informally without fresh surveys; delayed mutation. Many records originate in the colonial era, and though the national modernisation drive (DILRMP) has digitised much, progress is uneven — leaving some areas running on decades-old measurements while land prices around them multiplied. Survey records: where every resolution starts Two records outrank everything else. The cadastral map — the official parcel map identifying each survey number and its neighbours. The Field Measurement Book (FMB) — the recorded measurements from official surveys of each parcel. Together with title documents and revenue records, these are what authorities and courts use to determine where one property legally ends and the next begins — and they beat personal recollections and “the old tamarind tree” descriptions every time. Definition — Field Measurement Book (FMB): the survey department’s measurement sketch of a single survey number — sides, angles, extent. In a boundary fight it is the closest thing to ground truth on paper. The resolution playbook, step by step 1) Assemble your papers — sale deed, mutation entries, tax receipts, old photographs; download the RoR from the state portal; and FIRST check that the survey number on your deed matches the Record of Rights — a mismatch there gets fixed before anything else. 2) Apply for an official government survey — a certified surveyor measures and marks the actual boundary on site; the report becomes central evidence in any later proceeding. 3) Talk first — holding a government survey report changes the conversation from your word against theirs to a neutral document; direct dialogue and state mediation services resolve more than people expect. 4) Legal notice — if the survey supports you, a notice puts your position on record and signals escalation. 5) Revenue authority or civil court — a permanent injunction (Specific Relief Act, s.38) stops ongoing encroachment; a declaratory suit (s.34) establishes ownership and fixes the line; a possession suit recovers taken land. Courts often appoint a local commissioner (CPC Order XXVI Rule 9) to measure and report — influential, though weighed with all the other evidence. About 95% of RoRs are computerised — the TEXT record is usually a download. But cadastral maps sit at ~68%, geo-referencing at ~49%, only 11 states/UTs have finished map digitisation, and ULPIN covers a bit over 30% of parcels. An encroachment tolerated politely for a decade is quietly becoming the neighbour’s land. Acting early is not aggression; it is how the limitation law forces you to behave. Example: A family “adjusts” with a neighbour’s shed two metres over the line for fifteen years, then sells — and the buyer’s survey triggers the fight. 2026-09-23|ls-death-transfer: How to transfer land ownership after the owner’s death Land School — an original Deccan Ledger lesson · source & further reading: How to Transfer Land Ownership After the Owner's Death — 1acre.in Key Highlights Title does not shift automatically at death — the record keeps the dead owner’s name until someone files for mutation. Probate stopped being MANDATORY anywhere in India on 20 December 2025 (Repealing and Amending Act, 2025 removed Section 213) — but banks and buyers still ask for it. Without a will, PERSONAL law decides: Hindu, Muslim and Christian families on the same street follow different rules. A succession certificate covers bank accounts and securities — NOT land. India has no transfer-on-death deed; the nearest equivalent is a registered settlement or gift deed made while the owner is alive. Why ownership does not transfer automatically An heir does not become the recorded owner by grief alone — someone has to FILE, and the filing is mutation: updating the revenue and municipal record so the state knows who now owes land revenue and property tax. The application goes to the concerned revenue authority with the death certificate, proof of heirship, and the existing land records. With a will vs without one With a will: land passes directly to named beneficiaries through the executor — sometimes involving probate. Without a will (intestate): ownership follows the personal succession law of the deceased’s religion — the Hindu Succession Act for Hindus (daughters holding EQUAL coparcenary rights since 2005), Muslim personal law with its fixed shares, the Indian Succession Act for Christians and Parsis. The intestate route usually needs court-issued heirship paperwork, making it slower — which is the practical argument for a will. Definition — Probate: a court’s certification that a will is genuine. Since 20 December 2025 it is mandatory NOWHERE in India — the old Section 213 requirement (which bound certain wills, notably in the presidency towns) was repealed. But the market has memory: banks and cautious buyers still ASK for probate on willed property, so sometimes heirs obtain it for smoothness even though the law no longer compels it. Legal-heir certificate vs succession certificate Constantly confused, differently scoped. A legal-heir certificate establishes WHO the heirs are — used for utility transfers, pensions, bank formalities, and as the heirship proof in land mutation. A succession certificate , issued by a civil court, authorises the holder to collect the deceased’s DEBTS, SECURITIES and MOVABLE assets — it does not itself convey land. For immovable property, courts and offices weigh the succession certificate alongside other documents, but the land transfer runs on heirship proof + mutation (or a court partition where heirs contest). Documents required ☐ Death certificate — first, everything waits on it. ☐ Legal-heir certificate (or the will + executor papers). ☐ The land records — deed, RoR/passbook, tax receipts. ☐ Co-heirs’ written NOCs where one heir applies. ☐ EC — checking for loans or claims riding on the land. ☐ For heirs abroad: a PoA that SPECIFICALLY authorises applying for the heir certificate and mutation — generic property clauses stall at the counter. Why India has no transfer-on-death deed — and the substitute Several countries let owners name a death-beneficiary on the deed itself; India does not. The working equivalent: a registered settlement or gift deed executed while the owner is alive , reserving a LIFE INTEREST — the owner keeps possession until death, and the property vests in the named person automatically afterwards. Stamped, registered, and it takes effect without anyone approaching a court later. For families who know exactly where land should go, it converts a future dispute into a present document. The steps, in order 1) Death certificate. 2) Establish heirship — get the legal-heir certificate proactively, not when an office finally asks. 3) Co-heirs’ NOCs in writing BEFORE filing — one heir applying alone invites an objection. 4) Pull the EC and revenue record — surface any loan or claim now. 5) File mutation with the revenue authority. 6) Only then list, sell, or borrow. Example: Three siblings inherit; the eldest files mutation alone “to keep it simple”. A sister objects, the revenue officer freezes the entry, and the file crosses into civil-court territory — two years gone. The written NOCs would have cost a week. Selling inherited land Most inherited land eventually reaches the market — and that is where unfinished mutation surfaces, because any buyer’s verification matches seller against record, and the record still names the deceased. Heirs who complete mutation BEFORE listing sell on their own timeline; those who do not discover the gap at the sub-registrar, in front of their buyer. Quick answers (FAQ) Does ownership pass automatically to heirs? By succession law, beneficially yes — but the RECORD moves only on filing. Is probate mandatory? No, since 20 Dec 2025 — though lenders and buyers may still request it. No will? Personal law distributes; heirship certificate + mutation execute. Transfer-on-death deed? Not in India — use a registered settlement/gift deed with life interest. Do daughters have equal rights? Yes — equal coparcenary rights in Hindu law since 2005. How long does it take? Clean, cooperative files: weeks to a few months; contested ones: years. Bottom line Death moves rights; paperwork moves records. Certificate, heirship, NOCs, EC, mutation — done early, in order, it is administration; done late or out of order, it is litigation. For you: Half the parcels you negotiate are inherited — so your first question to any selling family is “is mutation complete in the CURRENT generation’s names?”. If not, your timeline is not theirs to promise. And structurally: an incomplete heir set signing your agreement is a future injunction on your layout — collect every heir’s signature or a court partition first. 2026-09-23|ls-capital-gains: Capital gains tax on agricultural land sale Land School — an original Deccan Ledger lesson · source & further reading: Capital Gains Tax on Agricultural Land Sale in India — 1acre.in Key Highlights Rural agricultural land is NOT a capital asset under Section 2(14)(iii) — its sale attracts no capital gains tax at all. The rural test is mechanical: the nearest municipality’s census population, and aerial distance of 2 / 6 / 8 km. Urban agricultural land is taxed like any property; long-term starts at 24 months. Section 54B exemption needs TWO years of actual farming before sale, reinvestment in farmland within two years, and a three-year lock-in on the new land. Section 50C lets the taxman substitute the stamp-duty value when you sell below it. When the tax applies at all One question decides everything: is the land RURAL or URBAN under the Income Tax Act? Rural agricultural land is excluded from the very definition of a capital asset by Section 2(14)(iii) — no capital asset, no capital gain, nothing to tax. Urban agricultural land gets no carve-out and is taxed like any other asset. Two owners can sell what looks like the same plot and one pays nothing while the other owes tax on the whole gain — purely because of where the land sits. The rural test — mechanical, not agricultural Nothing to do with how the land is farmed; everything to do with location and population. Land is RURAL if it lies outside a municipality or cantonment of 10,000+ people, AND outside these aerial distances from those limits: 2 km where the population is 10,000–1 lakh; 6 km where it is 1–10 lakh; 8 km where it exceeds 10 lakh. Population comes from the last published census; distance is measured AERIALLY — as the crow flies, not as the road winds. Inside the limits = urban agricultural land = taxable. One nuance: the exemption attaches to the LAND — a farmhouse, well or standing trees sold in the same deal are valued and treated separately. Example: Two farmers sell near Hyderabad (population >10 lakh, so the 8 km band applies). One’s land sits 9 km aerially from the municipal limit — rural, gain fully exempt. The other’s sits 7 km out — urban, fully taxable. Same crop, same buyer profile, two kilometres of geometry worth lakhs in tax. The second test: was it actually farmed? Classification decides the tax; CULTIVATION decides whether your claim survives scrutiny. Revenue records carry seasonal cultivation entries — the evidence that agricultural operations actually happened — and Section 54B leans on exactly that record for its two-year farming condition. Land held bare as pure investment is where exemption claims die at assessment. How the gain is computed Sale price minus purchase cost and expenses. Held 24+ months: long-term. The current long-term regime taxes gains at 12.5% without indexation (indexation having been withdrawn for post-July-2024 sales). And Section 50C looms over the price itself: sell below the stamp-duty value and the department can treat THAT value as your deemed sale price, subject to a tolerance margin — the guideline value quietly setting your tax floor. Rural vs urban at a glance Aspect Rural agricultural land Urban agricultural land Capital asset? No — s.2(14)(iii) excludes it Yes Capital gains tax None LTCG/STCG as applicable TDS on sale (194-IA) Expressly excluded 1% at ₹50 lakh+ (resident seller) Exemption routes Not needed 54B (farmland), 54EC (bonds) The exits: 54B and 54EC Section 54B — individuals and HUFs: reinvest the gain in NEW agricultural land within two years, provided the sold land was farmed for the two years before sale; money not yet reinvested by the return-filing date parks in a Capital Gains Account Scheme; the new land locks in for three years — sell early and the exemption unwinds. Section 54EC — the alternative for long-term gains: NHAI/REC/PFC/IRFC bonds within six months (₹50 lakh cap, five-year lock). The taxes that ride alongside TDS: buyers deduct 1% under 194-IA on urban agricultural land at ₹50 lakh+ — rural land is expressly outside the section. NRI sellers: Section 195 instead, at much higher rates — plan with a lower-deduction certificate. 50C: as above, the stamp-value floor. Quick answers (FAQ) Is rural agricultural land exempt? Fully — it is not a capital asset. How is “rural” defined? The census-population + aerial-distance test above. Indexation still available? Not under the current 12.5% regime. Urban land exemptions? 54B with the farming and lock-in conditions; 54EC bonds. TDS on farmland? Urban yes (₹50L+), rural no. Don’t want to buy farmland again? 54EC bonds, or pay the 12.5% and stay liquid. Bottom line Before selling any farmland, establish three things in writing: the aerial distance to the nearest 10,000+ municipality, the census figure that sets the band, and the cultivation record. Those three lines decide whether the tax is zero, exempt-with-conditions, or fully payable — get a CA’s letter where kilometres decide lakhs. For you: For your JD landowner partners this is THE conversation: many Ranga Reddy parcels sit inside Hyderabad’s 8 km band — urban, taxable — while one village further out is exempt. Knowing which side of the line a family’s land falls (and flagging 54B’s two-year farming condition early) makes you the developer who saved them lakhs before the deal even signed. Glossary — every term, simply TGIIC (Telangana Industrial Infrastructure Corporation) The state-owned body that buys, develops and allots industrial land across Telangana — think of it as the state’s own land bank and real-estate arm for factories, tech parks and industrial estates, previously named TSIIC. CCESDM (Consultative Committee on Electronics System Design & Manufacturing) A government committee that reviews and approves land allotments for electronics-manufacturing investors, reportedly at a concessional rate below general market pricing — a real category of state industrial policy meant to attract a specific kind of high-value manufacturing investment. Shell company A company that exists mostly on paper, with little or no real staff, operations or revenue — not automatically illegal, but a common vehicle for disguising who actually controls an asset when combined with a hidden (benami) ownership arrangement. Benami arrangement When someone holds or controls property or a company in another person’s name specifically to hide the real owner’s identity — illegal under India’s Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Act. This is the underlying legal category BRS’s allegation implies, even though the word itself is not always used in the coverage. Lokayukta A state-level statutory ombudsman empowered to investigate complaints of corruption or maladministration against public officials — a check outside the normal government chain of command, but one that can only recommend, not itself cancel a decision or punish anyone. CIN (Corporate Identification Number) The unique registration number India’s Ministry of Corporate Affairs (MCA) assigns every registered company — the closest thing a company has to a permanent ID card, used to look up its official filings, directors and financial statements. Paid-up capital The actual money shareholders have put into a company in exchange for shares, as opposed to any larger amount they might be authorised to contribute later — a company with only ₹1 lakh in paid-up capital has put in a token, minimal amount of its own money, which is unusual for a company that has just bought a multi-crore asset. FIR (First Information Report) The formal document Indian police register when they first receive information about a cognisable (arrestable) offence — the starting point of a criminal investigation, filed here against Krishank over his social-media post. Remand A court’s order sending an arrested person into police or judicial custody for further investigation; a court rejecting a remand request, as happened here, means the judge was not satisfied the arrest met legal requirements. BNSS (Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita) & Section 35(3) India’s new criminal procedure code, replacing the older CrPC nationwide since 2024. Section 35(3) requires police, for offences carrying under 7 years’ imprisonment, to first issue a formal notice asking the person to appear — arrest is meant to be a last resort for minor offences, not a first response. Adjournment motion A legislative procedural tool letting members demand the House set aside its scheduled business to urgently discuss a specific matter — a presiding officer can accept or reject it, as Telangana’s Legislative Council Chairman did here. Agricultural land-ceiling limit A 1970s-era cap (roughly 10–27 acres depending on land quality) on how much agricultural land one family can legally hold, with anything above meant to be surrendered for redistribution — the legal benchmark Revanth Reddy’s counter-allegation against the KCR family (S13) is measured against. CMRS-style third-party clearance (contrast) Not part of this story directly, but worth noting by contrast: unlike a metro line’s safety clearance (see today’s Bengaluru Real Estate zone), a land allotment like this one has no equivalent mandatory independent technical sign-off before the deal closes — which is exactly why disputes like this one can only be resolved after the fact, through bodies like the Lokayukta or the courts. Beneath the dated sequence sit two deeper forces. First, a structural one: TGIIC land deals have already been politically sensitive in 2025, independent of Tesseract, after BRS alleged a separate corporate-status change made it easier to mortgage TGIIC land elsewhere — so this is not the first time the agency’s land decisions have drawn opposition fire. Second, a tit-for-tat one: both major parties are now running near-mirror-image “the other family has too much land” campaigns within the same fortnight — Revanth’s 440-acre allegation against the KCR family landed just two days before Krishank’s T-shirt moment revived the Tesseract story, which suggests each side is at least partly responding to, not just independently pursuing, the other’s attack. What a longtime follower of Telangana politics knows that a first-time reader doesn’t: land-allotment and land-holding allegations against a sitting CM’s family are a recurring genre in this state’s politics, not a one-off — KCR’s own family faced very similar allegations (including the Erravalli/Farmhouse Files land-survey stories covered in earlier editions) while in power, and rarely have such allegations, from either side, been pursued all the way to a conclusive, independently verified finding within the same news cycle that produced them. So what — stakes and consequences If the family-connection allegation is true, it would mean a sitting Chief Minister’s brother benefited from a steep, policy-justified discount on state industrial land — a serious conflict-of-interest finding that would likely force some combination of allotment cancellation, a criminal referral, or real political damage to Revanth Reddy personally. If it is false or unproven, BRS gains a highly visible, if ultimately unresolved, campaign line, and Krishank’s repeated arrests generate genuine sympathy and due-process attention regardless of the underlying land dispute’s merits. The Congress government, meanwhile, gains a mirror-image land allegation of its own (the KCR family’s 440 acres) to point to whenever Tesseract comes up, which risks turning both stories into mutually-cancelling political noise rather than either one reaching a real, independently verified conclusion. Watch: whether the Lokayukta issues any finding or even a procedural update on the 15 August complaint (most likely outcome: continued silence for weeks, based on how such complaints have moved historically); whether Krishank’s 28 September CCS appearance produces a fresh arrest attempt or escalation, given the High Court’s standing order (moderate likelihood, given the pattern of repeated police action against him); and whether any independent, court-ordered valuation of the Raviryala land or MCA-verified director list for Tesseract ever surfaces publicly (low likelihood in the near term, since neither side currently has an incentive to settle the underlying numbers dispute). What this means for you: (a) For Hyderabad/Telangana real estate: this is a live reminder that TGIIC and other state land-allotment bodies can and do sell land at steep, policy-justified discounts to qualifying investors — a legitimate tool, but one whose eligibility criteria and paperwork trail you should always ask to see in full if you are ever evaluating a similarly discounted government land deal, precisely because “the minister said it followed the rules” is not the same as a published, checkable policy document. (b) For business/investment generally: a company’s registered director list is not always the last word on who actually controls it — when evaluating any counterparty, especially one linked to a large asset transfer, treat a thin capital base and no visible operations as a flag worth investigating further, not proof of wrongdoing by itself. The beginner mistake here is picking a side based on which number (₹7.5 crore or ₹200 crore) sounds more dramatic. The sharper, expert read is to notice that neither side has produced the one document that would actually settle this — an independent valuation of the land and a verified, current MCA director list for Tesseract — and that until one of those surfaces, this remains an unresolved allegation on both the price and the family link, however confidently either side states it. Coverage of this story is genuinely two-sided in sourcing, but not evenly weighted: BRS-aligned outlets (Telangana Today, Namasthe Telangana) generated most of the specific numbers and documents in circulation, while independently-owned outlets mostly corroborate the bare procedural facts (the arrest, the court orders, the Lokayukta complaint’s existence) without independently verifying BRS’s valuation or ownership claims. Readers should weigh the story accordingly. The 20% that gives you 100% — your keep-forever map The Telangana government sold 5 acres of industrial land to a thinly-capitalised company for ₹7.5 crore, under a policy that allows discounted rates for electronics-manufacturing investment. The opposition says the buyer is secretly run by the Chief Minister’s brother and that the land is really worth around ₹200 crore, but has not produced a document proving either the valuation or the ownership link. The government denies the family connection and defends the price as policy-compliant, but has not published the underlying approval paperwork either. The fight over these unresolved facts has spilled into a Lokayukta complaint, a blocked Assembly motion, a disputed police-station confrontation, and the repeated arrest of a BRS spokesperson under India’s new criminal-procedure code — while the ruling party runs a nearly identical land-holdings allegation against the opposition’s own founding family at the same time. 2026-09-24|ls-dlc-calc: How to calculate land value from the DLC / circle rate Land School — an original Deccan Ledger lesson · source & further reading: How to Calculate Land Value from DLC / Circle Rate — 1acre.in Key Highlights The DLC rate is the government-fixed minimum for registering land — the same thing other states call circle rate or guidance value. The formula: rate per unit area × total area = the official minimum value. One locality often carries TWO rates — exterior (main-road-facing) higher, interior lower. The result is the FLOOR for stamp duty: registration cannot happen below it, whatever the real price. Rates revise periodically — calculate only from the current figure on the official portal. What the DLC / circle rate represents A government-fixed number, not a market estimate: the minimum value at which land can be officially registered, set to prevent under-declaration. “DLC” (District Level Committee) is Rajasthan’s name; the identical concept is the circle rate, guidance value or ready-reckoner rate elsewhere — and Telangana’s “market value” on the IGRS portal. Which authority fixes it varies by state; what it does never does. The formula, applied Official value = rate per unit × total area — quoted per square metre, square foot, square yard or per acre depending on property type. Example: Rate ₹3,000/sq ft, plot 1,000 sq ft → ₹30 lakh official minimum. If your negotiated price is ₹25 lakh, duty is still charged on ₹30 lakh. If your price is ₹40 lakh, duty follows the ₹40 lakh. The floor pushes up, never down. Why one locality can have two rates Position inside the locality matters as much as the locality. Parcels are classified exterior (beside a main road) or interior (set back) — across residential and commercial categories alike — and exterior rates run higher, pricing frontage exactly as the market does. Confirm your parcel’s classification BEFORE calculating; the wrong one wrecks the whole valuation. How this value drives stamp duty Duty is charged on the HIGHER of the calculated official value and the actual transaction value. Running the calculation before finalising a deal tells you in advance which number you will be taxed on — so registration cost is budgeted, not discovered at the SRO counter. Where to check the current rate The state registration portal (IGRS Telangana, Kaveri Karnataka, e-Panjiyan Rajasthan and their siblings): pick district, urban/rural, then the SRO or village to read the applicable rate. The local SRO’s printed rate booklet works offline. Rates revise periodically — a bookmarked figure from last year is a trap. Red flags An outdated rate (always the current year’s figure); interior/exterior misclassification; unit mix-ups (a per-sq-m rate applied to sq ft produces confident nonsense); and treating agricultural, residential and commercial rates as interchangeable — each type carries its own rate even in the same locality. Interior vs exterior rate Aspect Interior rate Exterior rate Applies to Plots set back from the main road Plots facing or beside a main road Set by The same committee — applied by physical position Same Legal weight Equal for registration Equal for registration Level Lower for the same general area Higher — frontage and access priced in Pre-calculation checklist ☐ Current rate pulled from the official portal for the exact locality. ☐ Interior/exterior classification confirmed. ☐ Units matched (convert before multiplying). ☐ Result compared against the negotiated price — the higher figure is the duty base. ☐ SRO consulted if the numbers land far from expectation. Quick answers (FAQ) Is DLC rate the same as circle rate? Yes — regional names for one benchmark. Can I register below the calculated value? Duty is assessed on at least the notified value, regardless of the declared price. Does it apply to agricultural land? Yes — with its own rate class. How often does it update? Periodically, state by state — which is why “current portal figure” is the only safe input. Bottom line The formula never fails; the INPUTS do. Current rate, right classification, matching units — three checks that keep the stamp-duty bill boring, which is exactly what a stamp-duty bill should be. For you: Keep the current rate for every village in your pipeline in one sheet — revisions move project costs overnight, and the market-to-official GAP is itself a scouting signal: where deals run far above the official rate, a revision (and higher friction for everyone) is coming. Farmers, tenant farmers, sharecroppers, SHG members and women applicants all have defined qualifying paths. Banks typically fund 70–85% of valuation at roughly 7–12% a year; tenures can stretch to 15 years. What the bank checks is your land record: deed, RoR, mutation, survey match, valuation, classification. Under interest subvention, prompt repayers on eligible loans can reach an effective ~4%. You do NOT need to already own land — a registered sale agreement on a clean-title plot gets the file moving. What this loan is Secured credit for buying, developing or cultivating farmland, offered under India’s priority-sector framework by public banks, private lenders, NBFCs and regional rural banks. The distinction worth stating plainly: a land purchase loan is a one-time TERM loan secured on the land; a Kisan Credit Card is revolving working capital for crop seasons. Both are “agricultural credit”, which is why they get conflated — but no bank sanctions a land purchase against a KCC limit. Coverage extends to developing fallow land, horticulture and dairying moves, and irrigation or soil improvement on land already owned. What the bank actually verifies Borrower’s capacity — farm records, bank statements or ITRs. Seller’s title — sale deed, Record of Rights, mutation and revenue records. Encumbrances that would block a fresh mortgage. Survey number and boundary matching the paper. An approved valuer’s price. And classification still AGRICULTURAL — reclassified land needs a different product entirely. Definition — Record of Rights (RoR): the state’s core revenue record of who holds each parcel — pattadar passbook in Telangana, 7/12 in Maharashtra, patta in Tamil Nadu. Every bank wants the latest one, whatever the local name. Who can apply RBI priority-sector norms shape it: applicants ~18–65 at maturity; active farmers the default category (a credible farm business plan can work with some lenders); marginal farmers (up to a hectare) often prioritised, small farmers (1–2 ha) eligible; tenant farmers, sharecroppers and landless labourers enter through self-help or joint-liability groups where collective liability replaces collateral; women qualify on equal terms, with several public banks prioritising distress applicants and widows. And you need not own land already — a registered sale agreement on the target plot, with clean seller title, starts the process. Documents you will need Identity (Aadhaar/PAN/Voter ID); address proof; the land file — sale deed, revenue record, survey report; the registered sale agreement; and repayment evidence — bank statements or ITRs. Above ₹3 lakh, add a valuer’s report and legal clearance certificate. The universal requirement under many names: the latest RoR plus updated mutation entries. How the application runs Compare a few nearby lenders → assemble the file BEFORE the branch visit → apply (often online) → the bank verifies documents, inspects the land, orders valuation — larger loans get a legal title search → sanction letter → funds on creation of the mortgage. With clean paper, public banks finish in three to six weeks; unclear land records are the number-one stall. Pitfalls and red flags Survey number not matching ground boundaries — the most common holdup; land quietly reclassified non-agricultural — rules out the product; an undisclosed encumbrance surfacing in the legal search — weeks lost; an UNregistered sale agreement — dead end at most lenders; and chain gaps — the slowest of all to clear. Example: Use the bank as your unpaid second lawyer: even buying with your own cash, run the parcel through a lender’s eyes. A sanction is a quality certificate; a refusal names the defect the seller did not. Rates, amounts, repayment 70–85% of valuation funded; 7–12% yearly by lender and size; tenure to 15 years (7–10 typical); repayment often aligned to harvest cycles rather than flat EMIs; minimal prepayment charges on floating rates; processing fees commonly waived below ₹3 lakh. Government schemes that cut the cost KCC — subsidised revolving credit, useful working capital alongside an acquisition. Modified Interest Subvention — up to ₹3 lakh at a concessional 7%, with a 3% prompt-repayment incentive taking the effective rate to ~4%. RKVY — state-channelled land-development funding. PM Fasal Bima — crop insurance tied to loans, protecting repayment when a season fails. The direction of policy is expansion: agricultural credit targets keep rising year on year. Pre-application checklist ☐ Classification confirmed agricultural in current records. ☐ Survey number and boundaries matching deed AND ground. ☐ Encumbrances, liens, litigation searched. ☐ Sale agreement REGISTERED before it goes to the bank. ☐ 6–12 months of statements / income records assembled. ☐ Subvention eligibility checked before signing. Quick answers (FAQ) Can a first-time farmer get a purchase loan? Yes — eligibility paths exist without prior ownership; the plan and the plot’s paper carry the file. How much will the bank fund? 70–85% of ITS valuation — usually conservative against your negotiated price; budget the gap. What if the survey number mismatches the ground? Fix it before applying; it will stall everything else anyway. Bottom line The loan is accessible and, with schemes, cheaper than it looks. Speed is decided upstream — by the state of the land’s paperwork before the application. Title, survey and encumbrance sorted early turn a three-month file into a three-week one. For you: Financeability is a quality grade on the LAND, not just the borrower — it widens your exit, because your future buyer probably needs the loan even if you never did. Unfinanceable land trades at a structural discount at BOTH ends; price that honestly. Original Deccan Ledger lesson; full source article on 1acre.in (links above). WebFetch was blocked network–wide for every one of these domains during research, so every fact below is built from search–engine snippets of the original reporting, cross–checked across 3+ independent outlets wherever possible — no article was read in full, and single–source or unconfirmed figures are flagged as such throughout. The story, explained from zero — fact by fact S1 · The order itself On 24 September 2026, Telangana’s Revenue Department issued an order permitting registration of open plots, independent houses and flats currently listed under Section 22–A of the Registration Act, provided the property already carries a valid layout, building or apartment permission from GHMC, HMDA, DTCP, a municipality, or another urban or rural local body. Plain English: If your plot or flat is on Telangana’s do–not–register blacklist, but the government itself already approved the layout or building you built on it, you can now go register it. Mechanics: Works through the existing sub–registrar network — same office that refused you before, now with a proof–of–permission attached to the file. Incentives: Cheapest possible political win for the government — it gives away no actual government land, because by definition these are properties an arm of the state already vetted. Numbers: ≈1 lakh property owners in and around Hyderabad estimated to qualify (cross–checked across Deccan Chronicle, Hyderabad Mail, The South First — a projection, not an audited count). S2 · The link document Applicants must submit a “link document” connecting the specific plot/flat back to the original statutory permission. Plain English: Saying “my colony is approved” isn’t enough — you need the actual paper tying your plot number to that approval. Mechanics: A documentary threshold, not a blanket amnesty — no link document, no registration, regardless of how legitimate the surrounding colony looks. Incentives: Protects the government from fresh fabricated–approval claims riding on genuine cases, and gives sub–registrars a paper–based reason to refuse ineligible files — insulating them from favouritism charges. S3 · The CM’s 16 September promise Nine days earlier, CM A. Revanth Reddy told the Assembly that 22–A grievances would be fast–tracked, unveiling a 12–point plan addressing the government’s own list of the twelve most common ways legitimately developed land ended up on the prohibited list. Plain English: The CM promised, on the record, a systematic fix — not case–by–case firefighting. Incentives: BRS had spent weeks turning 22–A into a street and Assembly issue; a floor promise converts a defensive government into a proactive one before more damage accumulates. Numbers: 12 recurring problem categories identified. S4 · The 18 September committee Revenue Minister Ponguleti Srinivas Reddy announced a high–level committee chaired by CCLA D.S. Lokesh Kumar, with Law Secretary Papi Reddy and IG of Stamps & Registration Rajeevgandhi Hanumanthu as members, to sort the 12 issues. Plain English: The promise got named officials and (reportedly) a deadline. Mechanics: Reportedly tasked with resolving the 12 categories within a month of formation (per Telangana Today; not independently confirmed elsewhere in this research — flagged). Incentives: A CCLA–led panel signals the state’s most senior land officer, not a junior desk, is on it. S5 · District–level committees Alongside the state panel, district committees — Collector, additional collector, district registrar, and an HMDA/municipal/local–body representative — were set up to clear individual cases. Plain English: The state panel sets policy categories; these local committees decide your actual file. Incentives: Keeps case–level judgment close to local land records, which a state panel can’t realistically review file–by–file across a state with lakhs of affected survey numbers. S6 · The 12–point plan’s categories Cross–checked reporting (chiefly The South First) lists the twelve categories as: Urban Land Ceiling (ULC) surplus land; government land inside otherwise–approved layouts; Singareni coal–belt housing; GO 59 cases; GO 118 cases; houses on assigned land; Indiramma–scheme houses on government plots and on owners’ own land; land assigned to freedom fighters/ex–servicemen; Bhoodan land; private patta land with unpaid NALA (land–conversion) charges; government–land encroachments and unauthorised layouts; and Secunderabad cantonment leasehold properties. Plain English: 22–A isn’t one problem — it’s a dozen different historical accidents that all funnelled onto the same blacklist. Numbers: 12 categories — exact wording/order varies slightly by outlet; this is the fullest list found, flagged as not verified against the original GO text. S7 · The ≈1 lakh beneficiaries The relief is projected to help roughly one lakh Hyderabad–area owners who built or bought on land that went through legitimate HMDA/GHMC/DTCP approval but discovered — often only when trying to sell, mortgage or get a bank loan — that their survey number had been swept onto the 22–A list. Plain English: About 100,000 households/plot owners who did everything right on paper are who this order targets. Numbers: ≈1,00,000 — a reported projection, not an audited count of verified applications. S8 · What the order does NOT do — the fee route A separate proposal — reportedly a fee of about 15% of government market value, for 22–A properties WITHOUT valid permissions — is explicitly not part of this order and remains under legal/administrative examination. Plain English: If your land was never properly approved by anyone, this order does nothing for you yet. Incentives: Splitting “approved” (easy, fixed now) from “unapproved” (hard, deferred, to be monetised) lets the government bank a quick win while taking more time on the legally riskier half — badly handled, a pay–to–regularise scheme can look like laundering encroachments. Numbers: ≈15% of government market value (reported as still being finalised — not confirmed as final policy). S9 · The list’s scale, for context Cross–checked reporting describes the 22–A list swelling to roughly 2.5 crore acres notified statewide, of which about 1.01 crore acres fall into permanently prohibited categories (≈77 lakh acres government/assigned/forest/endowment/irrigation/road/residential land; ≈18 lakh acres agricultural land without pattadar passbooks; ≈3 lakh acres agricultural land converted to non–agricultural use). Plain English: The blacklist got so large — over a crore acres — that it stopped being a narrow anti–fraud tool and started catching ordinary, legitimately developed private property. Numbers: Officials’/reported figures, not independently audited here; different outlets round these slightly differently — flagged. S10 · The political backdrop — GO 134 One day earlier, on 23 September 2026, the government issued G.O. Ms. No. 134, forming a panel to probe alleged land irregularities of BRS leaders K. Chandrashekar Rao (KCR), K.T. Rama Rao (KTR) and T. Harish Rao — following Revanth Reddy’s Assembly claim that KCR’s extended family holds ≈440 acres of assigned land. BRS answered by demanding counter–probes into Revanth’s brother’s firm (Tesseract Advanced Systems, reportedly ≈5 acres of government land allotted for ≈₹7 crore against an estimated ≈₹200 crore market value) and Ponguleti Srinivas Reddy’s son’s firm, Raghav Developers. Plain English: A day before delivering good news to ordinary property owners, the government also opened a land–probe fight with its main rivals — who instantly demanded equal treatment for the CM’s own family, so this relief order landed inside an already–blazing political war over land. Incentives: Timing blunts any BRS claim that 22–A relief is pure political cover; BRS matching every accusation keeps the fight symmetrical. Numbers: ≈440 acres and ≈₹200 crore figures are political allegations from opposing sides, not adjudicated facts — flagged. Glossary — every term, simply Section 22–A A rule in Telangana’s Registration Act letting the government put certain land categories on a “do not register” list to stop fraudulent sales of government/temple/Waqf/Bhoodan/disputed land. Example: an HMDA–approved plot in Boduppal can still get flagged if its old revenue survey number also covers nearby government or assigned land, because the flag hits the whole survey number, not just the disputed part. Registration Act, 1908 The central law (in force since 1 Jan 1909) making registration of documents like sale deeds compulsory for property transactions above a small value, giving them legal weight. Example: a Hyderabad flat sale deed must be registered at the local Sub–Registrar’s Office under this Act to count as legal proof of ownership. Link document A paper connecting a specific plot/flat to the original government permission that made it legal to build there. Example: for a house in an HMDA–approved layout, this might be the original sale deed from the developer to the first buyer, referencing the layout approval. Survey number A unique ID the Revenue Department gives a land parcel during a cadastral survey, used as the primary reference in official records. Example: two unrelated pieces of land in Medchal–Malkajgiri could sit under the same old survey number until it’s formally split. Subdivision (revenue records) Formally splitting one large survey number into several new, distinct ones, usually after a mutation. Example: a 10–acre field developed into a 40–plot layout should get its survey number subdivided into 40+ new numbers — but this step is often skipped for years, a root cause of the 22–A mess. Layout approval vs. building permission Layout approval sanctions how land is divided into plots/roads/open spaces (HMDA/DTCP/municipality); building permission separately sanctions construction on one specific plot (GHMC/municipality). Example: Vivek needs layout approval to sell plots; a buyer building a house on one of those plots separately needs building permission. Urban Land Ceiling Act (repealed) A 1976 law capping urban land ownership and letting government take “surplus” land; repealed nationally in 1999, in undivided Andhra Pradesh only in 2008. Example: land declared “surplus” decades ago can still surface as a 22–A category today because the old paperwork was never closed out. GO (Government Order) The formal, numbered instrument through which a state government issues a binding policy decision (e.g., G.O. Ms. No. 134). Example: GO 59 and GO 118 are numbered BRS–era orders setting out different unauthorised–land regularisation schemes. Bhoodan land Land voluntarily donated for redistribution to landless families, following Vinoba Bhave’s movement started at Pochampally (Nalgonda district) in 1951. Example: a family holding an old Bhoodan plot may struggle to sell it today because it carries its own transfer restrictions and often lands on the 22–A list. Assigned land Government land handed to landless poor people for farming/housing under a 1977 Telangana law making it non–alienable — usable and inheritable, but not sellable. Example: a house built on originally–assigned land is a common 22–A dispute category, since any later “sale” was technically never valid. Waqf/endowment land Property permanently dedicated to a religious or charitable purpose (Waqf under Islamic law; endowment more broadly), which by definition can’t be privately sold. Example: a plot near an old mosque or temple in Hyderabad may be flagged even if it has informally changed hands for years. Stamp duty A state tax charged as a percentage of a property’s value at registration, collected by the Registration & Stamps department. Example: stamp duty, registration fee and transfer duty together add several percentage points to a Hyderabad plot’s cost — none collectible while registration is blocked. Sale deed The legal document transferring ownership from seller to buyer, valid only once registered under the Registration Act. Example: without a registered sale deed, a buyer has no legally enforceable ownership even if money has changed hands. Mutation Updating government land records to reflect a change of ownership after a sale, inheritance or subdivision. Example: after registering a sale deed, a buyer still needs the Bhu Bharati record mutated in their name. DTCP (term) Directorate of Town and Country Planning — the state authority approving layouts outside HMDA’s jurisdiction under the Telangana Urban Area Development Act, 1975. Example: a plotting venture beyond HMDA’s outer boundary would typically need DTCP, not HMDA, approval. The backstory — how we got here Date Event 1908/1909 Registration Act, 1908 enacted, in force from 1 Jan 1909 — includes the 22–A power to prohibit registration of certain land categories. 1951 Bhoodan movement launched at Pochampally, Nalgonda — creates the “Bhoodan land” category later entangled in 22–A. 1976 Central Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act enacted, capping urban land holdings. 1977 Telangana Assigned Lands (Prohibition of Transfers) Act bars sale of government–assigned land. 1999 Parliament repeals the Urban Land Ceiling Act nationally; undivided Andhra Pradesh does not adopt the repeal. 2008 (27 Mar) Andhra Pradesh formally repeals ULC Act (G.O. Ms. No. 603); already–taken “surplus” land stays with government. 2014 (2 Jun) Telangana state formed; later used as an eligibility cut–off date for GO 58/59 regularisation. 2020 Dharani portal launched as Telangana’s unified land–records/registration system. 2025 (Aug) Telangana High Court, facing thousands of 22–A petitions, orders the list made public rather than kept opaque; officials compile a fresh list exceeding 1 crore acres. 2025 (Jan assent – Apr in force) Telangana Bhu Bharati (Record of Rights in Land) Act, 2024 replaces the Dharani–era framework; Bhu Bharati portal goes live (14 April 2025). 2026 (Aug) Harish Rao/BRS escalate 22–A into public campaign: “30% commission” and “back–door ULC revival” allegations; colony protests (Tirumala Meadows, Lakshmi Ganapathi, Hemanagar/Boduppal). 2026 (Sept 2–) BRS announces street protests over 22–A and other grievances. 2026 (Sept 16) CM Revanth Reddy promises Assembly fast–track fix + 12–point plan; alleges KCR family holds ≈440 acres of assigned land. 2026 (Sept 18) Ponguleti announces CCLA–led committee (Lokesh Kumar, Papi Reddy, Rajeevgandhi Hanumanthu); district committees also formed. 2026 (Sept 23) G.O. Its property rules now live in the Non-debt Instruments Rules, 2019. How the source of funds decides repatriation The question nobody asks until selling: where did the purchase money COME from? NRE/FCNR (foreign currency) funding: full repatriation of proceeds — but only for two residential properties in a lifetime without special approval. NRO funding or Indian income: repatriation capped at USD 1 million per financial year, whatever the property count. Bought while still a resident: the same 1-million-per-year route through an NRO account. The account choice at purchase becomes irreversible history at sale. Even after a legitimate sale, repatriation follows the standard annual framework. Sale proceeds land in an NRO account — the mandatory starting point. 2. File the income-tax return for the sale year. 3. A chartered accountant issues Form 15CB confirming capital-gains tax is paid. 4. Submit Form 15CA online with the sale deed and bank statements. 5. The bank verifies, converts, remits. Not one bank visit — a CA, a bank and the tax department all signing off; budget weeks, not days. Red flags Cash, or any channel outside normal banking — an outright FEMA violation; every rupee must move through banks. Skipped or botched 15CA/15CB filings — transfers block. Repatriation limits by funding route How the property was funded What can leave India The cap that applies NRE / FCNR (foreign funds) Full sale proceeds Two residential properties per LIFETIME; beyond that, RBI approval NRO account / Indian income Proceeds via NRO USD 1 million per financial year, any property count Bought while a resident Proceeds via NRO USD 1 million per year Inherited property Proceeds via NRO USD 1 million per year + inheritance proof + tax clearance Foreign funding suits a buyer who will sell at most two properties in a lifetime. 2026-09-25|ls-guideline-value: Guideline value vs market value: what every land buyer should know Land School — an original Deccan Ledger lesson · source & further reading: Guideline value vs market value: what every land buyer should know — 1acre.in Key Highlights Stamp duty is charged on the HIGHER of the guideline value and the price you pay. Guideline value usually lags the market — but in stagnant pockets it can sit ABOVE what land is worth. The Income Tax Act calls every state’s version the “stamp duty value”, whatever its local name. Buying BELOW the benchmark can create taxable income in your hands under Section 56(2)(x). A bank-transfer token on the agreement date can LOCK the benchmark at that date — cash cannot. Market value for land runs on registered comparables, frontage, road access and zone. The two numbers, defined Guideline value (circle rate, ready-reckoner rate, unit rate — the name varies by state): the registration department’s benchmark valuation for each locality and land type, existing to stop parties under-declaring prices to dodge duty. The Income Tax Act sweeps all the local names into one term: the stamp duty value . Market value : what a willing buyer actually pays a willing seller — set by demand, not by notification. Duty runs on the higher number Duty is computed on the guideline value or the declared price, WHICHEVER IS HIGHER. Declaring a lower price does not help — where the declared figure falls below the benchmark, the department simply applies the benchmark. Exact rates vary by state; calculate with your jurisdiction’s numbers. The trap: buying below the guideline value Buying ABOVE the benchmark costs you duty; buying BELOW it can cost you INCOME TAX. Under Section 56(2)(x), where you buy immovable property for less than its stamp-duty value, the shortfall is treated as YOUR income under “Income from Other Sources” (subject to the tolerance band). A genuine bargain thus gets taxed as if the discount were a gift to you. One protective mechanism: where agreement and registration dates differ, the benchmark ON THE AGREEMENT DATE can be adopted — but only if part of the consideration moved by cheque, draft or electronic transfer on or before that date. A CASH token does not qualify. And states revise values periodically, so always verify the figure on the date that matters to YOUR transaction. Example: You agree a plot at ₹60 lakh in March by handshake; the state revises the guideline to ₹75 lakh in April; you register in June. Duty computes on ₹75 lakh — and 56(2)(x) can tax ₹15 lakh as your income. Had you paid even a ₹1 lakh token by BANK TRANSFER with a written agreement in March, the March benchmark could have locked. The transfer mode of one token payment carried lakhs of consequence. What moves the guideline value Location does most of the work — established and fast-developing pockets carry higher benchmarks because demand is already on record. Then: zoning — what the land may legally be used for feeds the assessed band; infrastructure — a new road or transit line lifts the benchmark, but only at the NEXT revision; and revision frequency itself varies by state, which is why benchmarks drift from reality in both directions. What determines market value For land the drivers are physical and legal, not cosmetic: frontage and road width; corner position; whether the survey number matches the ground; the master-plan zone and whether conversion is complete; and above all, what comparable parcels nearby actually REGISTERED for — a different number from what they were advertised at. The two values compared Aspect Guideline value Market value Fixed by State registration department Buyers and sellers, deal by deal Decides Duty floor, TDS thresholds, 56(2)(x)/50C exposure The price you negotiate Moves At periodic state revisions Continuously, with demand Evidence Published departmental tables Registered comparable sales Typical relationship Lags the market Leads — except in stagnant pockets When to rely on which number Use the GUIDELINE value to budget duty and to check where your price sits against the tolerance band. Use MARKET value to negotiate and to judge whether a price is defensible. And note the third opinion in the room: a lender’s own valuation — where it lands well below the asking price, confirm the bank’s figure before you commit; banks are paid to be unromantic. Quick answers (FAQ) Is duty on guideline or market value? The higher of guideline and declared price. What if I buy below guideline? Duty on the benchmark anyway — plus possible 56(2)(x) income in your hands. Is guideline always lower than market? Usually, not always — stagnant pockets invert it, and there you pay duty on more than the land is worth. How do I find it? The state registration portal, by village/survey number (Telangana: the IGRS unit-rate search). Negotiate on which? Market value — built from registered comparables; the guideline only tells you the state’s floor. Bottom line Two numbers, two jobs: the state’s benchmark sets the floor for duty and tax; registered comparables set the truth for price. The gap between them decides duty, TDS and tax exposure — verify the benchmark with the registration department before making any offer, and take professional advice where price and benchmark diverge sharply. For you: You live in this gap professionally. Rising guideline values in your belts raise buyers’ closing costs — get grandfathering by locking agreements with BANK-transferred tokens before revision dates. And watch revisions as market intelligence: the state raising a village’s benchmark is the state telling you where it sees demand going.
